## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date (national level):** Civil registration of all births and deaths began **1 January 1864** across Ireland. Non-Catholic marriages were registered from **1 April 1845**; all marriages from **1 January 1864**. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Ireland Church Records confirms 1864 as when civil registration was introduced. Source: [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records).
- **What exists:** For 1864–1870, civil birth, marriage, and death registers at the district level (Coleraine superintendent registrar's district covers this area). Before 1864, no civil vital registration exists — church records are the only source.
- **Where held:** General Register Office (Northern Ireland) — GRONI — holds registers for the six counties of Northern Ireland. Copies from 1864 onward: GRONI, Oxford House, 49–55 Chichester Street, Belfast BT1 4HL; Tel: +44 28 9025 2000; https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/searching-birth-marriage-and-death-records. The IRISHGENEALOGY.IE portal (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/en/) provides some indexed civil records online, but its coverage focuses on Kerry, western Cork, and Dublin — not County Antrim. For Antrim, use GRONI directly or check PRONI's partnered access.
- **Gaps:** The entire period 1780–1863 has no civil registration. The Church records below are the only primary vital sources for those decades.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers of all denominations (see below); Griffith's Valuation (1856–1857 for County Antrim); Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837); census substitutes.

### Church records

**This is the critical record class for 1780–1870.** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Billy Civil Parish ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records)) contains only denominational section headers with no register-specific start dates or volume identifiers. The information below is drawn from the Ireland Church Records page and the PRONI guidance.

#### Church of Ireland

- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials. Confirmation registers also exist for some parishes.
- **Crucial loss note:** Two-thirds of all Church of Ireland registers were destroyed in the Public Record Office fire in Dublin on 30 June 1922. Source: [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records). It is not possible to confirm from any tool result whether Billy's specific CoI registers survived; this must be verified at the repositories below.
- **Where the originals are held:** PRONI holds microfilm or original copies of many Ulster CoI registers that were deposited before 1922. The Representative Church Body (RCB) Library in Dublin also holds transcripts and surviving registers.
- **Surviving register access:**
  - PRONI's Guide to Church Records (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf) identifies which registers survive for each parish and their date ranges.
  - PRONI Digitised Church Records: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1
  - RCB Library (holds surviving transcripts): Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735; Tel: +353 (0)1 492 3979; Email: library@ireland.anglican.org; Request a search: https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy; List of surviving parish registers: https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf
- **Digitization level:** Dependent on whether registers survived 1922. For surviving Ulster registers, many have been digitised and are accessible via PRONI's online portal.

#### Presbyterian

- **Record types:** Baptism and marriage registers. Presbyterian and other non-conformist churches in Ireland typically did **not** maintain burial registers. Source: [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records).
- **Congregations:** Billy parish had at least one Presbyterian congregation and a separate Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) congregation. The FamilySearch Wiki page confirms meeting houses for both. Specific register start dates for Billy are not stated on the wiki page.
- **Average register start:** The average start date for Irish Presbyterian registers is around 1830, though numerous registers date from the 1600s. Source: [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records). The earliest years of this guide (1780–1830) may therefore lack Presbyterian register coverage for Billy.
- **Where held:** Original registers typically remain in the custody of the local congregation. Microfilm copies are held at PRONI. FamilySearch Library also holds microfilm of some County Antrim Presbyterian registers (example from the adjacent Ballylinny parish: FamilySearch film number 973220 covers baptisms/marriages from 1837; PRONI film MIC 1P/327 covers from 1851).
- **Online access:**
  - PRONI Digitised Church Records portal: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1
  - FindMyPast: Ireland, Non-Conformist Births & Baptisms: http://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/ireland-non-conformist-births-and-baptisms (subscription)
  - FindMyPast: Ireland, Non-Conformist Marriages: http://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/ireland-non-conformist-marriages (subscription)
  - FindMyPast: Ireland, Non-Conformist Congregational Records: http://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/ireland-non-conformist-congregational-records (subscription)
  - Ulster Historical Foundation (AncestryIreland): http://www.ancestryireland.com/ — indexes many County Antrim church and civil records (subscription)

#### Roman Catholic

- **Record types:** Baptism and marriage registers. Catholic registers typically do **not** include burial registers. Source: [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records).
- **Parish jurisdiction:** Billy civil parish's Roman Catholic population belonged to the district of Coleraine. The RC ecclesiastical parish boundaries differ from civil parish boundaries; the Coleraine RC parish should be searched for births/marriages/deaths, not a register filed under "Billy." Source: [Billy Civil Parish wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#History).
- **Register start dates:** Most rural Irish Catholic parishes did not begin record-keeping until after Catholic Emancipation (1829). Source: [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records). The Coleraine RC register start date is not stated in any tool result from this session.
- **Online access:**
  - National Library of Ireland Catholic registers (microfilm-based, free): https://registers.nli.ie/
  - Ancestry: Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1655–1915: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61039/ (subscription; index and images)
  - FindMyPast: Ireland Roman Catholic Parish Marriages: https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-records/ireland-roman-catholic-parish-marriages (subscription)

#### Wesleyan Methodist

- **Record types:** Baptism and marriage registers, and sometimes class lists or circuit records.
- **Where held:** Methodist registers for Ireland are held at PRONI (for Northern Ireland) and at the Methodist Church archives. The FindMyPast Non-Conformist Marriages and Burials databases cover Methodist records.
- **Online access:**
  - FindMyPast: Ireland, Non-Conformist Births & Baptisms (includes Methodist): http://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/ireland-non-conformist-births-and-baptisms
  - FindMyPast: Ireland, Non-Conformist Burials: http://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/ireland-non-conformist-burials
  - PRONI Digitised Church Records: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1

#### Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian)

- **Record types:** Baptism and marriage registers. Reformed Presbyterian records for Ulster are generally less well digitised than mainstream Presbyterian registers.
- **Where held:** Originals with the local congregation; microfilm at PRONI. Check PRONI's Guide to Church Records for the specific Billy congregation's survival status.

### Census records

- **All-Ireland census:** Taken 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, and 1871. The 1821 and 1831 originals were almost entirely destroyed in the 1922 fire; 1841 and 1851 originals were destroyed by government order in the early 20th century. Fragments survive at PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland. The 1861 and 1871 originals were similarly destroyed, but some local transcripts survive.
- **1901 and 1911 censuses** (outside the target period) are fully available online at the National Archives of Ireland: https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/
- **Household census returns for 1851:** Some returns for Antrim survive in limited form. PRONI should be consulted.
- **Access:** No County Antrim census original is fully available online for 1780–1870 from any tool result in this session. PRONI holds surviving fragments; the census substitutes below (Tithe Applotment, Griffith's Valuation) are the practical alternatives.
- **Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864):** Treated as the primary census substitute for most of Ireland. County Antrim was surveyed c. 1856–1857. Searchable free at AskAboutIreland: https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/ and at Ancestry. Lists all land and property occupiers.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Cover all landholders, usable as a mid-period census substitute. Free online at the National Archives of Ireland: https://www.titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie/

### Probate and court records

- **Before 1858:** Probate jurisdiction was ecclesiastical. Wills for Billy parish (in the diocese of Connor, Province of Armagh) were proved before the Prerogative Court (for high-value estates) or the Consistorial Court of Connor. Nearly all records of both courts were destroyed in 1922.
- **After 1858:** District Probate Registries were established across Ireland. The Londonderry (Derry) District Probate Registry had jurisdiction over County Antrim. Calendars of wills and grants of administration from 1858 onward survive and are available at PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland.
- **Online access:** Ancestry holds the Ireland, Indexes to Wills, Probate Administration, Marriage Bonds and Licences, 1591–1866 collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/62077/), which provides pre-1858 index data (not the original documents, most of which are lost). Betham Genealogical Abstracts at FindMyPast (https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-records/betham-genealogical-abstracts) contain abstracts from some pre-1922 wills and are a substitute for lost originals.
- **Testate vs intestate:** Wills go in the will books (probate registries); intestate estates go in the administration bond books. Both series are indexed in the surviving calendars at PRONI.

### Land records

- **System:** All Ireland operated a metes-and-bounds system. Land distribution and tenure for County Antrim reflect the 17th-century Ulster Plantation grants.
- **Registry of Deeds (Dublin):** All registered land transactions from 1708 onward are indexed at the Registry of Deeds, Henrietta Street, Dublin 1; https://www.registryofdeeds.ie/. Deeds were registered voluntarily, so coverage is not complete, but large landholders and some tenants appear.
- **Estate papers:** Many Antrim estates deposited their papers at PRONI. Search PRONI's eCatalogue (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni) for estate records relevant to the townlands within Billy parish.
- **Griffith's Valuation** (see Census substitutes above) lists every occupier and maps each holding to a townland — the most comprehensive land-occupancy survey for c. 1856–1857.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** (see above) list landholders subject to tithe.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The 1798 United Irishmen Rebellion affected County Antrim; the Napoleonic Wars (to 1815) and later British Army service throughout the period.
- **Record types:** Militia and yeomanry muster rolls (at PRONI for Ulster); British Army service records (at The National Archives, Kew, England); pension records.
- **Online access:** Findmypast and Ancestry hold British Army service records; The National Archives (UK) catalogue is at https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/. PRONI holds many local militia records.

### Cemetery records

- **Denominations:** Church of Ireland and Presbyterian cemeteries are present in the Billy area. Catholic burials often took place in older pre-Reformation churchyard sites or in the RC parish churchyard at Coleraine.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) and BillionGraves (https://billiongraves.com/) carry some County Antrim headstone transcriptions; coverage for Billy specifically is not confirmed in any tool result from this session. The PRONI tombstone register index should also be checked.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's books, where they survive, are held either by the individual congregation or at PRONI.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Coleraine Chronicle* (founded 1844) and the *Belfast News-Letter* (founded 1737, the oldest surviving English-language newspaper in Ireland) covered County Antrim throughout the target period. The *Coleraine Chronicle* published marriage notices, death notices, and legal announcements.
- **Online access:** The British Newspaper Archive (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/) (subscription) holds digitised issues of the *Belfast News-Letter* and other Ulster papers. The *Belfast News-Letter* 1737–1900 is also indexed at FindMyPast.
- **Physical records:** PRONI and the Linen Hall Library (Belfast) hold microfilm and bound copies.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** County Antrim had significant emigration throughout 1780–1870: post-1798 political emigration, the 1847–1852 Famine emigration, and ongoing chain migration to North America and Australia.
- **Relevant ports:** Belfast, Londonderry/Derry, and Larne were the main Ulster departure points. Liverpool was a transit port for many.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (held at NARA for US arrivals), assisted emigration records, Famine-era relief lists, naturalisation petitions in the destination country.
- **Online access:** Ancestry Passenger Lists collections; the Ellis Island database (for post-1892 arrivals); FamilySearch passenger list collections; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for US military and naturalisation records.
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests list every person aboard, including infants and young children. When searching for a family, examine the full manifest — not just the head of household.

### Tax records

- **Hearth Money Rolls (1660s):** County Antrim Hearth Money Rolls survive at the Irish Manuscripts Commission and PRONI. They list householders and are a useful pre-1780 substitute, with direct bearing on which families were established in Billy by the research period.
- **Griffith's Valuation and Tithe Applotment** (see Census and Land records above) serve as tax-list census substitutes for the target period.
- **Street directories:** *Pigot's Commercial Directory* (1820s) and *Slater's Directory* cover Bushmills and Coleraine and list traders, which can pin a family to a townland when register evidence is thin.

### Other record types

- **School records:** National School registers were established from the 1830s. Many survive at PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland. They give children's names, ages, religion, and father's occupation.
- **Poor Law records:** The Coleraine Poor Law Union records (from 1838) at PRONI record names of persons receiving relief — especially relevant for the Famine years 1845–1852.
- **Church of Ireland vestry minute books:** Vestry books for Billy (where they survive) record local tax assessments, charity distributions, and sometimes family data. PRONI holds many Ulster vestry books.
- **Marriage licence bonds and banns:** FamilySearch holds the index: Ireland, Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds Indexes, 1623–1866 (collection ID 3460239), at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3460239 — free, indexed and images.

## Records NOT online

- **Original church registers for Billy civil parish congregations (CoI, Presbyterian, Covenanter, Methodist):** The Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch Wiki page's church records section contains only blank headers — no register start dates, PRONI film numbers, or digitisation status are listed for any Billy congregation. The extent of online coverage cannot be confirmed from this session's tool results. Use PRONI's Guide to Church Records PDF and the PRONI Digitised Church Records portal to establish what has been digitised.
- **Pre-1858 wills and probate records:** Most originals were destroyed in the 1922 PRO fire. Abstract collections at FindMyPast (Betham, Crossle, Thrift) and the Ancestry wills index are the best substitutes, but coverage is fragmentary.
- **Estate papers for Billy/Lower Dunluce estates:** Landlord papers at PRONI are physical only and must be searched on-site or via PRONI's copy service.
- **Vestry minute books** (Church of Ireland): Physical at PRONI.
- **Poor Law Union records (Coleraine Union):** Physical at PRONI; not comprehensively digitised.
- **Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) registers:** Less well digitised than mainstream Presbyterian; inquire directly at PRONI and the local congregation.

## Known record losses

- **Church of Ireland registers — 1922 fire:** Two-thirds of all Church of Ireland registers were destroyed in the fire at the Public Record Office of Ireland, Dublin, on 30 June 1922. Source: [Ireland Church Records wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records). Whether the Billy CoI registers were destroyed, survived in PRONI's custody (which held many Ulster registers separately), or were transcribed, cannot be confirmed from any tool result in this session — check the RCB Library register list and PRONI's Guide to Church Records.
- **Census originals 1821–1871:** The 1821 and 1831 census originals were almost entirely lost in the 1922 fire. The 1841 and 1851 originals were destroyed by government order. The 1861 and 1871 originals were similarly destroyed. Only fragments and transcripts survive. No tool result specifies what, if anything, survives for Billy specifically — confirm at PRONI.
- **Pre-1858 wills and probate:** See Probate section above. Substitute sources include the Betham, Crossle, and Thrift abstract collections at FindMyPast, and the Ancestry index collection 62077.

---

## Research tips

1. **Check PRONI's Guide to Church Records first.** Before searching any register, download the PRONI Guide to Church Records (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf) and look up Billy parish. It identifies which congregations' registers survive, their date ranges, and whether they are on microfilm at PRONI or in the original at the local church — saving many fruitless searches.

2. **Search all denominations, not just the expected one.** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Ireland Church Records ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)) explicitly advises: search available Church of Ireland records even if your family was not Church of Ireland. Families of all denominations sometimes appear in CoI registers because CoI was the established church and legal marriages before 1845 for non-Catholics required CoI ceremony or a licence.

3. **The RC ecclesiastical parish is not the Billy civil parish.** Roman Catholics in Billy civil parish belonged to the district of Coleraine for registration purposes. Source: [Billy Civil Parish wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#History). Search for Coleraine RC baptisms and marriages, not a "Billy" RC register.

4. **Before 1864, use Griffith's Valuation and Tithe Applotment as locating tools.** These two series (free at askaboutireland.ie and titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie) let you pinpoint which townland within Billy parish a family occupied at c. 1823–1837 and c. 1856–1857. Once the townland is known, the correct church register congregation becomes much easier to identify.

5. **For 1780–1830, expect thin Presbyterian coverage.** The average Irish Presbyterian register starts around 1830. Source: [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records). If you cannot find a Presbyterian baptism or marriage before c. 1830, this is a known gap — supplement with marriage licence bonds (FamilySearch collection 3460239, indexed 1623–1866), estate records, and the Hearth Money Rolls at PRONI.

6. **Cross the county line into Londonderry (Derry) for the Coleraine area records.** The poor law union of Coleraine straddles the Antrim/Londonderry border, and the RC parish of Coleraine is based in Londonderry. Some register series, estate papers, and civil records for the Bushmills / Dunserverick area may be filed under County Londonderry as well as County Antrim. Search PRONI collections for both counties.

---

The guide was compiled using two FamilySearch Wiki pages retrieved in full: the [Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy) and the [Ireland Church Records page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records). The `wiki_place_page` tool (all four sections: home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned a generic fallback page rather than Ireland-specific content, so those sections are recorded as not found. The `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and `external_links_search` tools returned no Ireland-specific data because the place-search tool could not resolve County Antrim or Ireland to a standardPlace in this session. Those are coverage gaps in this guide, not evidence that FamilySearch has no relevant collections.

---

Billy civil parish sits in the barony of Lower Dunluce near the north Antrim coast — its post town is Bushmills — and it had Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Covenanter, Methodist, and Roman Catholic communities in the period 1780 to 1870. The whole of that span predates Ireland's national civil registration, which only began in 1864, so church registers are the essential source for births, marriages, and deaths; however, the parish's own FamilySearch Wiki page lists only empty register headers with no confirmed start dates, meaning you must check PRONI's published Guide to Church Records before searching. Two-thirds of Church of Ireland registers across Ireland were destroyed in 1922, and it is not confirmed from this survey's tool results whether Billy's CoI registers survived; PRONI in Belfast holds many Ulster registers separately. The main repositories for this parish are PRONI (Belfast), the RCB Library (Dublin) for Church of Ireland, the National Library of Ireland's online Catholic register portal, and PRONI's own digitised church records portal for Presbyterian and Methodist material.

The next step would be to consult PRONI's Guide to Church Records for Billy parish specifically, establish which denomination's registers survive and from what year, and then build a targeted research plan around the gaps identified.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton Counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated, driving rapid in-migration
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, Welsh, English, and German immigrant populations (coal industry workers)
- **Key events:** 1840s–1860s coal boom; Civil War (1861–1865)

---

## Available Record Types

### ✅ Federal Census Records *(Most Accessible)*
- **1850 and 1860 federal censuses** cover Schuylkill County
- DGS 007621224 — **96% name-indexed and full-text searchable** (strongest digitization in this period)
- Mortality schedules accompany both censuses, recording deaths in the preceding year
- Also on Ancestry: [1850 US Federal Census – Schuylkill County](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/)

### ✅ Church Records
- **Lutheran Church Records, 1840–1875** (DGS 004288771) — 198 images, **browse-only** (0% name-indexed); contains German-language entries
- Broader collection: "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (1708–1985, ~982,000 persons), searchable on FamilySearch
- Covers baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations
- Church records are the **primary substitute for civil vital records** in this period

### ✅ Probate Records
- DGS 004812990 — **Probate Records, 1845–1880** — 286 images, **full-text searchable** (4% name-indexed)
- Collection: "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (3.2 million images) on FamilySearch — browse-only at collection level
- Names heirs, guardians, creditors — valuable for family reconstruction
- Physical originals: Schuylkill County Register of Wills, Pottsville

---

## Record Types Held Physically (Not Online for This Period)

These record types were **not found in any digitized online collection** for 1840–1869 — they exist physically but require in-person or written requests:

| Record Type | Where Held |
|---|---|
| **Vital records** (civil births, marriages, deaths) | County courthouse, Pottsville |
| **Land/deed records** | Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds; state-level warrants at Pennsylvania State Archives |
| **Tax records** | County courthouse, Pottsville |
| **Military records** (service, pensions, Civil War draft) | NARA (Philadelphia/Washington DC); Pennsylvania State Archives |
| **Naturalization records** | Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas; Pennsylvania State Archives |
| **Newspaper records** | Schuylkill County Historical Society; Chronicling America (some years) |

> **Note:** Absence from online databases is a *coverage gap*, not evidence of record loss.

---

## Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, probate originals, court minute books, naturalization records, tax lists |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State-level records, warrant surveys, military records, county record copies |
| NARA (Philadelphia / Washington DC) | Federal census originals, military service & pension files, passenger lists |
| Individual church archives | Parish registers beyond digitized Lutheran volume |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Local histories, newspapers, photographs, family files |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Church records first, civil records second.** No civil vital registration volumes for the 1840s–1860s were found. The Lutheran volume (DGS 004288771) must be browsed image by image and includes German-language entries.

2. **Federal censuses are the most accessible starting point.** The 1850 and 1860 censuses are 96% indexed and searchable on both FamilySearch and Ancestry. Use mortality schedules to identify deaths in the prior year.

3. **Don't overlook probate records.** The probate series (1845–1880) is full-text searchable and names heirs, guardians, and creditors — very useful when vital records are missing.

4. **Immigrant mining families:** Schuylkill County had heavy Irish, Welsh, and German immigration. Search Philadelphia and New York passenger lists for arrivals; check the local Court of Common Pleas for pre-1906 naturalizations.

5. **Neighboring counties:** Schuylkill County borders Berks, Lebanon, Dauphin, Northumberland, Columbia, and Luzerne Counties. Events (marriages, purchases) often crossed county lines — check those records too.

---

## Summary

The **two most accessible digitized record sets** for Schuylkill County in the 1840s–1860s are:
- **Federal census images for 1850 and 1860** (96% indexed, on FamilySearch and Ancestry)
- **Lutheran church registers, 1840–1875** (browse-only, some German-language entries)

Civil vital registration (births, marriages, deaths) does not appear to have been required at the county level during this period, making church records the primary substitute. Land records, tax lists, military files, and naturalization papers for this period are held physically at the county courthouse, Pennsylvania State Archives, and NARA.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811, from Berks and Northampton Counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this place and period; no figures can be stated.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated the county during the 1840s–1860s, driving rapid in-migration.
- **Ethnic composition:** The coal industry drew Irish, Welsh, English, and German immigrant labor in large numbers during this period, producing records in multiple languages.
- **Religious denominations:** Lutheran congregations are confirmed by digitized records (DGS 004288771 covers 1840–1875); other denominations served the diverse immigrant population but did not return specific digitized volumes in this survey.
- **Key historical events:** The 1840s–1860s coal boom and the Civil War (1861–1865) generated military, pension, and draft records relevant to the county.

## Boundary changes

- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 and its boundaries were stable throughout the 1840–1869 target period. No boundary changes during the target period were returned by the tools.
- Records from before 1811 will be found under the predecessor jurisdictions of Berks County and Northampton County.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey (url: `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records`); no Pennsylvania-specific registration start date or level can be stated from a tool-returned page. The FamilySearch Wiki should be consulted directly at `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records` to confirm when and at what level civil registration began in Pennsylvania.
- **What exists for 1840s–1860s:** Because Pennsylvania statewide civil registration was not confirmed to have been required during this period by any tool-returned wiki page, church registers are likely the primary vital record source for births, marriages, and deaths in these decades.
- **Where held:** County courthouse (Pottsville) for any locally recorded events; church registers held by individual congregations, their denominational archives, and FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Gaps:** No civil registration volumes for births, marriages, or deaths in the 1840–1869 range appeared in `volume_search` results; this is a coverage gap in the digitized record set.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Lutheran confirmed by digitized volume (DGS 004288771, 1840–1875). Other denominations served the community but did not return separate digitized volumes in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Digitized volume:** DGS 004288771 — Lutheran Church Records, Schuylkill County, 1840–1875, 198 images. This volume is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). It must be worked through image by image with no name search.
- **Language:** Records in this volume are in English and German. Researchers must be prepared to read German-language entries.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (collection id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, labeled "synthetic test fixture" in the tool result — researchers should verify this collection's status on FamilySearch directly), covering 1708–1985, with 982,415 persons and 1,245,830 records. URL: `https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/SYNTH-PA-CHURCH`.
- **Where else held:** Denominational archives (e.g., the Lutheran Theological Seminary Archives, the Pennsylvania State Archives) and local congregational records.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1850 and 1860 federal censuses cover Schuylkill County. DGS 007621224 covers Schuylkill County federal census images 1850–1860 (412 images, **96% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — the strongest digitization level in this survey). This is the most accessible digitized record set for the period.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850 and 1860 censuses included mortality schedules recording deaths in the year preceding enumeration; these supplement the absence of civil death registration.
- **External link:** Ancestry also hosts the 1850 United States Federal Census for Schuylkill County at `https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/`.
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census volumes for this period returned from `volume_search`.
- **Access:** Federal census is **indexed + images** via FamilySearch (DGS 007621224) and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; held at the county level.
- **Digitized volume:** DGS 004812990 — Probate Records, Schuylkill County, 1845–1880, 286 images. This volume is **4% name-indexed** but **full-text searchable** — meaning it is not reliably found by a name search but can be searched as text. Classify as full-text searchable, not name-indexed.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (id 1999196), covering the full county with 3,200,560 images and 0 indexed records — **browse-only** at the collection level despite the volume being full-text searchable. URL: `https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196`.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** When a decedent left a will (testate), search the will books; when they died without one (intestate), search the administration files. Both series fall within the above volume and collection.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Register of Wills, Pottsville (originals); FamilySearch for digitized images.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania uses metes and bounds (not the rectangular survey system). Land grants and patents for Pennsylvania were issued by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. The Pennsylvania State Archives (Bureau of Land Records) holds the original warrant and survey records.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content** in this survey; no tool result confirmed the specific repositories or record series for Schuylkill County land records beyond the general framework.
- **Types:** Deeds (at the county level, Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville), patents and warrants (at the state level, Pennsylvania State Archives), mortgages, and tax records.
- **Date range:** County deed books begin at county formation (1811). The Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville holds originals.
- **Digitization:** No land record volumes for the 1840–1869 period appeared in `volume_search` for Schuylkill County. Land records are likely physical or microfilm only for this period and place.
- **External resource:** Ancestry hosts "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801" at `https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/` — this predates the 1840s–1860s target window but may provide background on property-owning ancestors before the target period.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848), Civil War (1861–1865). The Civil War produced the largest military record sets — service records, pension files, and (for 1863 onward) draft registrations — for men in Schuylkill County.
- **Record types:** Union service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants are held at the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). Pennsylvania adjutant general records may be at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Draft:** The Civil War draft (1863) produced Consolidated Lists of draft-eligible men, held at NARA.
- **Digitization:** No military record volumes for 1840–1869 returned from `volume_search` for Schuylkill County. Military records for this period are likely physical (NARA, Pennsylvania State Archives) or accessible via Ancestry/Fold3 but were not returned in the external links for this time window.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** No specific cemetery names were returned by tools for Schuylkill County during this period.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves index many Pennsylvania cemetery inscriptions and should be searched; neither appeared in the curated external links returned for this place and period.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual cemeteries and churches. Church burial registers overlap with the Lutheran volume (DGS 004288771, browse-only).

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Schuylkill County had active local newspapers during the coal boom years (the Miners' Journal, Pottsville, is the most prominent). No newspaper volumes returned from `volume_search` for this period and place.
- **Where held:** The Miners' Journal archive and Pennsylvania newspaper collections are accessible through Chronicling America (Library of Congress) for some years, and through the Pennsylvania State Library. Neither appeared in the curated external links returned for this survey.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (sheriff's sales, estate notices), and mining accident reports name individuals not found in other records.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** The major port of entry for Irish, Welsh, and German miners coming to Schuylkill County was Philadelphia; some came through New York (Castle Garden, then the Battery/Barge Office).
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (held at NARA and online via Ancestry and FamilySearch); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions filed at the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas (pre-1906, any court of record could naturalize); alien registrations.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.
- **Digitization:** No immigration or naturalization volumes returned from `volume_search` for Schuylkill County in 1840–1869. Naturalization records from the local court may be within the county courthouse or the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax lists, maintained at the county level.
- **Date range:** County tax records begin at county formation (1811); no digitized county tax volumes for 1840–1869 returned from `volume_search`.
- **Substitute value:** Annual county tax lists can substitute for missing census years, confirming residence, property ownership, and (for poll taxes) adult male presence year by year.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse (originals); Pennsylvania State Archives may hold copies.

### Other record types

- **Occupational records:** The anthracite coal industry generated company employment records, mine inspector reports, and accident lists specific to this region. These are not standard genealogical series but can document miners who do not appear prominently in other records.
- **Court records:** The Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas minute books and equity dockets are held at the county courthouse. These include naturalization petitions (important for the large immigrant mining population), guardianship orders, name changes, and civil suits that name family members.
- **County and local histories:** 19th-century county histories (published in the 1880s–1890s for most Pennsylvania counties) often reprint early records and provide biographical sketches of residents who were living or recently deceased; some are the only surviving transcription of records since lost.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 10, 1798, from Lincoln and Green counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Somerset
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by tools for this county and period.
- **Economy:** South-central agricultural county; the Cumberland River runs through the county
- **Ethnic composition:** Specific data not returned by tools
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian (the four largest Kentucky denominations per the FamilySearch Kentucky Church Records wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records)
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861–1865) — Kentucky was a Union border state with divided loyalties, so residents may appear in both Union and Confederate military records; courthouse disasters destroyed some records in 1838 and 1871

## Boundary changes
- Pulaski County shows a single stable representation from its 1798 formation through the target period (confirmed via place_search_all). No boundary changes occurred during or near 1840–1880.
- Pre-formation records (before December 1798) should be sought in Lincoln County and Green County.

## Available record types

All registration dates below are taken from the FamilySearch Kentucky Vital Records wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records and the Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates:** Births and deaths at county level: 1853–1862, 1874–1878, and 1892–1910 (compliance was minimal throughout). Marriages: from county formation (1799). Statewide registration began 1911; general compliance achieved by approximately 1917.
- **What exists within 1840–1880:** Marriage bonds and licenses from 1799 (covering the entire target period); scattered birth and death records only for 1853–1862 and 1874–1878 — no civil registration of births or deaths for 1840–1852, 1863–1873, or 1879–1880.
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street, #208, Somerset, KY 42502); Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA, Frankfort) for microfilmed copies; FamilySearch has marriage bonds and consent forms 1799–1871 digitized online.
- **Gaps:** The 1838 and 1871 courthouse disasters destroyed some records, including potentially early civil vital records. Large periods of the 1840–1880 window have no civil birth or death registration at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); mortality schedules in the 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses; family bibles; cemetery records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, Presbyterian — the four largest Kentucky denominations during this period
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, membership lists, minutes
- **FamilySearch online collections (from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records):** Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995 (index and images, incomplete); Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960 (index only); Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979 (index only); Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970 (index only)
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Historical Society (most comprehensive local collection of church records); FamilySearch Library (microfilmed records from many Kentucky congregations); Kentucky Historical Society (Frankfort, manuscript church records); Filson Historical Society (Louisville, Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian records); denominational archives — Southern Baptist Historical Library (Nashville), Methodist conference archives, Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia)
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 enumerations all fall within the target period and are fully available
- **Mortality schedules:** 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record deaths in the year preceding each census; valuable during periods when civil death registration lapsed
- **State census:** No Kentucky state census for this period is noted by tools
- **Access:** Indexed and browsable on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, letters of administration, guardianship files, court orders
- **Date range:** Probate from 1801; court records from 1799
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse; KDLA (microfilmed copies); FamilySearch has will books 1801–1929 digitized and searchable online
- **Losses:** The 1871 courthouse disaster destroyed some probate and court records; if an expected record is absent, the Historical Society surname files and church records should be checked.

**Key Jurisdictional Context**

The Alabama region around 1800 was not yet a state — it was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (until March 1817), so records are scattered across two states' archives rather than one. Searching under "Alabama" alone will miss most of what exists; always search **"Mississippi Territory"** at both the Alabama and Mississippi state archives.

**Main Record Repositories**

- **Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery)** — Holds the Mississippi Territory censuses of **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810**. These are not online and must be accessed directly.
- **FamilySearch** — Has four indexed collections starting as early as 1803 (county marriages, probate records, a census-substitute index, and church records), plus two **unindexed digitized volumes for 1803–1819** that must be browsed page by page.
- **Mobile area special case** — Mobile was under **Spanish administration until 1813**. Colonial church registers, land grants, and census returns are held in archives in **Seville and Aix-en-Provence**, with copies at the **Library of Congress** and the **Mobile Municipal Archives**.

**Practical Caveat**

County formation in Alabama mostly happened 1818–1820, so pre-statehood coverage in county-level records is thin.

**Recommended Next Step**

Identify the specific county or area of Alabama where your ancestor lived. That will determine which territorial census year is most likely to list them and which repositories to contact for a targeted research plan.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory separated from Mississippi Territory March 3, 1817; Alabama statehood December 14, 1819
- **County seat / administrative center:** St. Stephens (Washington County) was the earliest territorial seat; Mobile was the main Gulf Coast settlement; Huntsville emerged as a major interior center by 1810
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), then Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
- **Population during period:** No tool data returned for this period
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence agriculture; cotton emerging by end of period; Mobile as a Gulf Coast trade port
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (interior); Anglo-American settlers migrating from Georgia, the Carolinas, and Virginia (interior, accelerating after Creek War 1813–1814); Spanish Creole and French Creole populations in the Mobile area; enslaved African Americans
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes in Mobile (French and Spanish era); Methodist circuit riders and Baptist congregations in the interior (established from ca. 1800)
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813–1814 opened large portions of central Alabama to rapid Anglo-American settlement; U.S. acquisition of Mobile from Spain in 1813; Mississippi Territory created 1798

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763: French claimed the Mobile area (established 1702). Britain held the region 1763–1780. Spain controlled the Mobile District 1780–1813; the interior was also claimed by Georgia and contested.
- 1798–1817: The Mississippi Territory, created by Congress in 1798, covered both present-day Alabama and Mississippi. All territorial government records are under Mississippi Territory, not Alabama.
- March 3, 1817: The Alabama Territory was separated from the Mississippi Territory. Records from March 1817 to December 1819 are under Alabama Territory.
- December 14, 1819: Alabama became the 22nd state. County-level records begin only from each individual county's formation date — most Alabama counties were not organized until 1818–1820 or later.
- Pre-U.S. Mobile: The Mobile District was separately administered by Spain until U.S. acquisition in 1813; its colonial records are not in U.S. repositories.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and gives no specific start year. No statewide civil registration of births or deaths existed during the pre-statehood period. Church records are the primary substitute for vital events.
- **What exists:** County marriage records begin from county formation. FamilySearch holds "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (612,345 records, indexed + images), covering the earliest surviving county-level marriage registers.
- **Where held:** Original registers at county probate courts; FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408)
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration in this era. County coverage begins only at county formation, most of which occurred 1818–1820 or later.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; family bibles; territorial census substitutes; tax lists

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, serving French-era parishes); Methodist and Baptist circuits in the interior (from ca. 1800)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (156,789 records, indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396). Catholic records for the Mobile area are held by the Archdiocese of Mobile and include Spanish- and French-era registers. French colonial church records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France) and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Language:** Mobile-area colonial church records may be in French or Spanish

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covers the Mississippi Territory (present Alabama) and the 1820 census is the first to cover Alabama as a state. These are indexed in "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (287,634 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756).
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810, covering settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held physically at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). They are not available in any online database.
- **Other enumerations:** Territorial tax lists (ca. 1800–1817) function as census substitutes and are at ADAH.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch compiled index is name-searchable online. Physical territorial census records at ADAH require in-person or mail inquiry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration; territorial court records
- **Date range:** Washington County records begin 1803–1820; most other counties' probate records begin after 1818–1820 when counties were organized
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (438,210 records, indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764). Two browse-only digitized volumes covering the pre-statehood period specifically:
  - Volume 004512889 (214 images): Territorial court and land records, 1808–1819, Alabama — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
  - Volume 004512890 (96 images): Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820 — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
- Mississippi Territory court records (1798–1817) are also at MDAH in Jackson, Mississippi.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state using the Public Land Survey System (rectangular survey). Earlier colonial grants used metes-and-bounds descriptions.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** After U.S. acquisition, federal land offices distributed land; patents searchable at the BLM GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov/). Spanish colonial land grants for the Mobile area were administered by Spain and are documented at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville), with copies at the Library of Congress, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Types:** Federal land patents (from ca. 1806); Spanish and British colonial grants; county deed transfers; tax records
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (https://glorecords.blm.gov/); ADAH (territorial and early state land records); Archivo General de Indias and Library of Congress (Spanish colonial grants)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813–1814; War of 1812 (defense of Mobile, 1813); colonial-era conflicts
- **Record types:** Service and pension records; bounty land warrants (War of 1812); militia rolls for the Mississippi Territory
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal service and pension records (https://www.archives.gov/). Territorial militia rolls are at ADAH. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) hosts many digitized pension and service record images.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Early frontier and church graveyards; Mobile-area Catholic cemeteries with French and Spanish interments
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes Alabama cemeteries, though coverage for pre-1820 graves is sparse
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for formal cemeteries are rare for this period; grave markers in family and church graveyards often are the primary record

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile area had newspapers by the early 1800s; the interior had no newspapers before statehood
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and ADAH hold historical Alabama newspaper runs
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sales, death notices; very sparse for the pre-statehood interior

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast); Pensacola (Spanish Florida); Atlantic coast ports (Charleston, Savannah) for overland migrants
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists for Mobile; naturalization petitions in territorial courts
- **Where held:** NARA holds passenger lists and naturalization records (https://www.archives.gov/). Pre-1820 passenger lists for Gulf Coast ports are fragmentary.
- **Content note:** Most settlers arrived overland from Georgia, the Carolinas, and Virginia — passenger lists are less relevant than migration chain evidence in land, church, and court records. For families traveling together, examine the territorial census lists for all members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial tax lists (Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory); early county property tax records
- **Date range:** Territorial period tax lists from ca. 1800–1819
- **Where held:** ADAH in Montgomery; published transcriptions exist in some genealogical society publications
- **Substitute value:** Territorial tax lists are the primary census substitute for years between territorial enumerations (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810)

### Other record types
- **Colonial records (Mobile area):** Spanish district census returns, church registers, and land grants at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence), with copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Native American records:** Records involving Creek and Cherokee nations in this period are mainly U.S. treaty and agency records at NARA; tribal nation archives may hold additional materials

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (612,345 records); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (438,210 records); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (287,634 records); Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (156,789 records) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (includes 1810 Mississippi Territory, 1820 Alabama) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (War of 1812, Creek War pensions and service records) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from ca. 1806 | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Alabama newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, military pensions, passenger lists | In-person / online ordering |

**Coverage of this survey:** Two digitized but entirely browse-only volumes (310 images total) specifically cover the pre-statehood period in FamilySearch's volume repository. These are the complete matching set (totalResults: 2). The four indexed FamilySearch collections listed above extend back as early as 1803 but have primary coverage beginning at or after county formation (generally 1809+).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); tax lists; territorial court records; state records | In-person; mail inquiry; some digital finding aids |
| Mississippi Dept. of Archives and History (MDAH), Jackson, MS | Mississippi Territory records 1798–1817 (covers pre-Alabama-Territory period) | In-person; mail inquiry |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal court records; military service and pension files; land office records | In-person; mail request |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers, some extending to French/Spanish colonial era | Contact archives directly |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial church records | In-person |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial land grant records | In-person; some digitized holdings online |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District (census, church, land grants) | In-person; some digitized at pares.mcu.es |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial church records for the Mobile area | In-person; written request |

## Records NOT online
- Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) — physical at ADAH; not in any indexed online database
- Territorial tax lists (1800–1817) — physical at ADAH
- Territorial court minute books and case files — physical at ADAH and MDAH
- Spanish colonial land grants and district census returns — at Archivo General de Indias, with copies at Library of Congress (partially digitized)
- French colonial church registers for Mobile — at Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- Catholic parish registers for early Mobile — at Archdiocese of Mobile; not fully digitized

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey names a specific destroyed record set for pre-statehood Alabama. Absence from an online database is a coverage gap, not confirmed loss — the records named above exist in physical repositories and some have been only partially microfilmed or digitized.

## Research tips
- **Search under 'Mississippi Territory,' not 'Alabama,' for any event before March 3, 1817.** Most territorial government records, court files, and tax lists created before the Alabama Territory was separated are filed under Mississippi Territory. Check both ADAH and MDAH. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Use the four Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) as your first enumeration tool.** Held at ADAH in Montgomery, these are the primary head-of-household lists for pre-statehood Alabama residents. They are not available online. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Research the Mobile area separately from the interior.** The Mobile District had Spanish administration until 1813 and a colonial record lineage running through Seville, Aix-en-Provence, and the Mobile Municipal Archives. Interior Alabama settlers have an entirely different record trail rooted in Virginia, Georgia, and the Carolinas. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Check BLM GLO for federal land patents from ca. 1806.** Alabama is a public-domain land state, so land was distributed through federal land offices. The GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov/) is free and fully indexed by name.
- **Browse the two FamilySearch pre-statehood volumes image by image.** Volumes 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808–1819) and 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — there is no name-search shortcut.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama-specific pages all returned only generic content during this survey.** Re-run or visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy directly for the full Alabama-specific guidance before relying on their absence.

- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), then Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
- **Population during period:** No tool data returned for this period
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence agriculture; cotton emerging by end of period; Mobile as a Gulf Coast trade port
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (interior); Anglo-American settlers migrating from Georgia, the Carolinas, and Virginia (interior, accelerating after Creek War 1813–1814); Spanish Creole and French Creole populations in the Mobile area; enslaved African Americans
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes in Mobile (French and Spanish era); Methodist circuit riders and Baptist congregations in the interior (established from ca. 1800)
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813–1814 opened large portions of central Alabama to rapid Anglo-American settlement; U.S. acquisition of Mobile from Spain in 1813; Mississippi Territory created 1798

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763: French claimed the Mobile area (established 1702). Britain held the region 1763–1780. Spain controlled the Mobile District 1780–1813; the interior was also claimed by Georgia and contested.
- 1798–1817: The Mississippi Territory, created by Congress in 1798, covered both present-day Alabama and Mississippi. All territorial government records are under Mississippi Territory, not Alabama.
- March 3, 1817: The Alabama Territory was separated from the Mississippi Territory. Records from March 1817 to December 1819 are under Alabama Territory.
- December 14, 1819: Alabama became the 22nd state. County-level records begin only from each individual county's formation date — most Alabama counties were not organized until 1818–1820 or later.
- Pre-U.S. Mobile: The Mobile District was separately administered by Spain until U.S. acquisition in 1813; its colonial records are not in U.S. repositories.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and gives no specific start year. No statewide civil registration of births or deaths existed during the pre-statehood period. Church records are the primary substitute for vital events.
- **What exists:** County marriage records begin from county formation. FamilySearch holds "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (612,345 records, indexed + images), covering the earliest surviving county-level marriage registers.
- **Where held:** Original registers at county probate courts; FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408)
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration in this era. County coverage begins only at county formation, most of which occurred 1818–1820 or later.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; family bibles; territorial census substitutes; tax lists

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, serving French-era parishes); Methodist and Baptist circuits in the interior (from ca. 1800)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (156,789 records, indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396). Catholic records for the Mobile area are held by the Archdiocese of Mobile and include Spanish- and French-era registers. French colonial church records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France) and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Language:** Mobile-area colonial church records may be in French or Spanish

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covers the Mississippi Territory (present Alabama) and the 1820 census is the first to cover Alabama as a state. These are indexed in "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (287,634 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756).
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810, covering settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held physically at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). They are not available in any online database.
- **Other enumerations:** Territorial tax lists (ca. 1800–1817) function as census substitutes and are at ADAH.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch compiled index is name-searchable online. Physical territorial census records at ADAH require in-person or mail inquiry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration; territorial court records
- **Date range:** Washington County records begin 1803–1820; most other counties' probate records begin after 1818–1820 when counties were organized
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (438,210 records, indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764). Two browse-only digitized volumes covering the pre-statehood period specifically:
  - Volume 004512889 (214 images): Territorial court and land records, 1808–1819, Alabama — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
  - Volume 004512890 (96 images): Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820 — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
- Mississippi Territory court records (1798–1817) are also at MDAH in Jackson, Mississippi.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state using the Public Land Survey System (rectangular survey). Earlier colonial grants used metes-and-bounds descriptions.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** After U.S. acquisition, federal land offices distributed land; patents searchable at the BLM GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov/). Spanish colonial land grants for the Mobile area were administered by Spain and are documented at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville), with copies at the Library of Congress, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Types:** Federal land patents (from ca. 1806); Spanish and British colonial grants; county deed transfers; tax records
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (https://glorecords.blm.gov/); ADAH (territorial and early state land records); Archivo General de Indias and Library of Congress (Spanish colonial grants)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813–1814; War of 1812 (defense of Mobile, 1813); colonial-era conflicts
- **Record types:** Service and pension records; bounty land warrants (War of 1812); militia rolls for the Mississippi Territory
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal service and pension records (https://www.archives.gov/). Territorial militia rolls are at ADAH. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) hosts many digitized pension and service record images.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Early frontier and church graveyards; Mobile-area Catholic cemeteries with French and Spanish interments
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes Alabama cemeteries, though coverage for pre-1820 graves is sparse
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for formal cemeteries are rare for this period; grave markers in family and church graveyards often are the primary record

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile area had newspapers by the early 1800s; the interior had no newspapers before statehood
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and ADAH hold historical Alabama newspaper runs
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sales, death notices; very sparse for the pre-statehood interior

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast); Pensacola (Spanish Florida); Atlantic coast ports (Charleston, Savannah) for overland migrants
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists for Mobile; naturalization petitions in territorial courts
- **Where held:** NARA holds passenger lists and naturalization records (https://www.archives.gov/). Pre-1820 passenger lists for Gulf Coast ports are fragmentary.
- **Content note:** Most settlers arrived overland from Georgia, the Carolinas, and Virginia — passenger lists are less relevant than migration chain evidence in land, church, and court records. For families traveling together, examine the territorial census lists for all members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial tax lists (Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory); early county property tax records
- **Date range:** Territorial period tax lists from ca. 1800–1819
- **Where held:** ADAH in Montgomery; published transcriptions exist in some genealogical society publications
- **Substitute value:** Territorial tax lists are the primary census substitute for years between territorial enumerations (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810)

### Other record types
- **Colonial records (Mobile area):** Spanish district census returns, church registers, and land grants at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence), with copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Native American records:** Records involving Creek and Cherokee nations in this period are mainly U.S. treaty and agency records at NARA; tribal nation archives may hold additional materials

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (612,345 records); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (438,210 records); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (287,634 records); Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (156,789 records) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (includes 1810 Mississippi Territory, 1820 Alabama) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (War of 1812, Creek War pensions and service records) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from ca. 1806 | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Alabama newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, military pensions, passenger lists | In-person / online ordering |

**Coverage of this survey:** Two digitized but entirely browse-only volumes (310 images total) specifically cover the pre-statehood period in FamilySearch's volume repository. These are the complete matching set (totalResults: 2). The four indexed FamilySearch collections listed above extend back as early as 1803 but have primary coverage beginning at or after county formation (generally 1809+).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); tax lists; territorial court records; state records | In-person; mail inquiry; some digital finding aids |
| Mississippi Dept. of Archives and History (MDAH), Jackson, MS | Mississippi Territory records 1798–1817 (covers pre-Alabama-Territory period) | In-person; mail inquiry |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal court records; military service and pension files; land office records | In-person; mail request |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers, some extending to French/Spanish colonial era | Contact archives directly |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial church records | In-person |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial land grant records | In-person; some digitized holdings online |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District (census, church, land grants) | In-person; some digitized at pares.mcu.es |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial church records for the Mobile area | In-person; written request |

## Records NOT online
- Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) — physical at ADAH; not in any indexed online database
- Territorial tax lists (1800–1817) — physical at ADAH
- Territorial court minute books and case files — physical at ADAH and MDAH
- Spanish colonial land grants and district census returns — at Archivo General de Indias, with copies at Library of Congress (partially digitized)
- French colonial church registers for Mobile — at Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- Catholic parish registers for early Mobile — at Archdiocese of Mobile; not fully digitized

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey names a specific destroyed record set for pre-statehood Alabama. Absence from an online database is a coverage gap, not confirmed loss — the records named above exist in physical repositories and some have been only partially microfilmed or digitized.

## Research tips
- **Search under 'Mississippi Territory,' not 'Alabama,' for any event before March 3, 1817.** Most territorial government records, court files, and tax lists created before the Alabama Territory was separated are filed under Mississippi Territory. Check both ADAH and MDAH. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Use the four Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) as your first enumeration tool.** Held at ADAH in Montgomery, these are the primary head-of-household lists for pre-statehood Alabama residents. They are not available online. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Research the Mobile area separately from the interior.** The Mobile District had Spanish administration until 1813 and a colonial record lineage running through Seville, Aix-en-Provence, and the Mobile Municipal Archives. Interior Alabama settlers have an entirely different record trail rooted in Virginia, Georgia, and the Carolinas. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Check BLM GLO for federal land patents from ca. 1806.** Alabama is a public-domain land state, so land was distributed through federal land offices. The GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov/) is free and fully indexed by name.
- **Browse the two FamilySearch pre-statehood volumes image by image.** Volumes 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808–1819) and 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — there is no name-search shortcut.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama-specific pages all returned only generic content during this survey.** Re-run or visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy directly for the full Alabama-specific guidance before relying on their absence.
