subagents.description: Locality guide for pre-1800 Arkansas under Spanish control

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide for pre-1800 Arkansas under Spanish control:

---

**Arkansas Region Before 1800 (Spanish Louisiana Period)**

The Arkansas region before 1800 was part of **Spanish Louisiana**, administered from New Orleans, with **Arkansas Post** as the only significant European settlement.

---

### Digitized Records (Online)

Very few records from this period are available online. The sole digitized resource at FamilySearch is:

- **Spanish-language sacramental registers for Arkansas Post, 1763–1800**
  - Image group DGS 008814402 (64 images)
  - Browse-only and **unindexed** — must be scrolled through image by image; no name search available
  - Records are in Spanish

---

### Main Record Types

The primary surviving record types for this era include:

- **Colonial census lists** (*padrones*)
- **Land concessions** (Spanish land grants)
- **Military post records**
- **Church (sacramental) registers** — baptisms, marriages, burials

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) | Primary repository for Arkansas colonial records |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Spanish colonial records; some digitized via the free [PARES portal](http://pares.mcu.es) |
| **Library of Congress** (Washington, DC) | Microfilmed Spanish Louisiana records |

---

### Important Cautions

1. **All colonial records are in Spanish.** You will likely need translation assistance.
2. Arkansas Post **reported administratively to New Orleans**, not to any Arkansas-level authority — so some records may be found in Louisiana colonial collections.
3. Ancestors who received **Spanish land grants** may surface in **post-1803 U.S. land-confirmation records** even when original colonial documents are inaccessible. This can be a valuable indirect path.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission** to ask about their Spanish-era holdings and finding aids.
2. **Check the PARES portal** for digitized Spanish Louisiana materials from the Archivo General de Indias.
3. **Browse the FamilySearch image volume** (DGS 008814402) for Arkansas Post sacramental registers.
4. Search U.S. **General Land Office records** for post-1803 Spanish land grant confirmations.
5. Plan any in-person archival research only after exhausting online and microfilm resources.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Arkansas region was never formally organized as a separate jurisdiction before 1800. Arkansas Post was established by the French in 1686. Spain assumed control in 1763 under the Treaty of Paris (Seven Years' War) and administered the territory until 1800.
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Post of Arkansas), on the lower Arkansas River — the sole significant European settlement in the region
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Louisiana (Spanish), administered from New Orleans
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by tools for this period. The European settler population was very small — a military garrison, French-Creole traders and farmers, and a handful of officials — alongside surrounding Native American communities (principally the Quapaw).
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, military post functions
- **Ethnic composition:** French-Creole settlers, Spanish military officers and officials, small numbers of other European traders; surrounding Native American communities
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic only; French missionaries served the post from the early 1700s through the Spanish period
- **Key historical events:** Transfer from France to Spain (1763); brief cession back to France (1800); U.S. Louisiana Purchase (1803) — each transfer shifted which authority created and held records

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1763:** French Louisiana; records created under French colonial authority
- **1763–1800:** Spanish Louisiana; civil, military, and church records created under Spanish colonial administration headquartered in New Orleans
- **1800:** Ceded back to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso
- **1803:** Acquired by the United States (Louisiana Purchase)
- **1804–1812:** Part of the District/Territory of Louisiana and Territory of Orleans
- **1812–1819:** Territory of Missouri
- **1819–1836:** Territory of Arkansas
- **1836–present:** State of Arkansas

No county structure existed before 1819. All pre-1803 records were generated at the level of the military post or colonial administration in New Orleans — not at any county-level office. There is no single continuous Arkansas jurisdiction to search; the researcher must shift between colonial-era Louisiana repositories and U.S. territorial-era repositories depending on the period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed under Spanish colonial administration. The FamilySearch Arkansas Vital Records page was not accessible during this survey and no start date for civil registration can be confirmed from tool results.
- **What exists:** Church sacramental registers are the only vital record source for this period.
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock; Arkansas History Commission (transcriptions); 1 digitized browse-only volume at FamilySearch (see Church Records)
- **Gaps:** Civil registration is entirely absent for the pre-1800 period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Sacramental registers; Spanish colonial census/padrones; land concession records naming grantees and family members

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only. French missionaries served Arkansas Post from the early 1700s, continuing through the Spanish colonial period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials of European settlers and Native Americans. Per the FamilySearch Wiki Arkansas Genealogy article, surviving registers are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and in transcribed form at the Arkansas History Commission. ([Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Online digitized:** 1 volume at FamilySearch (image group DGS 008814402), covering Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763–1800. **64 images; 0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image. Records are written in Spanish.**
- **Language:** Spanish (18th-century ecclesiastical Spanish script)

### Census records
- **Spanish colonial censuses (padrones):** Periodic household censuses were conducted at Arkansas Post under Spanish administration. Per the FamilySearch Wiki Arkansas Genealogy article, surviving padrones are held at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, and on microfilm at the Library of Congress. ([Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **U.S. federal census:** Arkansas was not U.S. territory before 1803 and does not appear in the 1790 census. The earliest federal census coverage for this region is 1820 (Territory of Arkansas).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124) begins in 1819 — entirely after the period of interest.
- **Access:** Padrones are physical-only at the repositories above; no indexed online access was found for the pre-1800 period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Civil and judicial records from the Arkansas Post commandant's office: notarial acts, civil suits, estate proceedings
- **Date range:** 1763–1800 for the Spanish period; French-era materials may exist pre-1763
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) and the Archivo General de Indias (Seville). No digitized or indexed collection was found covering this period.
- **Note:** The commandant of the post exercised civil, military, and judicial authority — records were not separated by function as in later American practice.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish metes-and-bounds concessions (not the U.S. rectangular survey system)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish Crown, granted through the Governor-General of Louisiana in New Orleans
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions and grants, with witnesses and grantee names. After 1803, U.S. land commissioners reviewed Spanish-era claims; confirmation records name grantees and often family relationships.
- **Where held:** Colonial-era grants at the Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias. Post-1803 U.S. confirmation records at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO), accessible online at glorecords.blm.gov. Per the FamilySearch Wiki Arkansas Genealogy article, land concession records are among the surviving colonial materials. ([Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The post was a Spanish military garrison throughout this period.
- **Record types:** Spanish military post records: muster rolls, officer correspondence, troop registers, commandant's reports
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock). Per the FamilySearch Wiki Arkansas Genealogy article, military post records are among the surviving colonial materials. ([Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** The Catholic mission cemetery at Arkansas Post is the relevant burial ground. No formal cemetery records from this period were found in online databases.
- **Online coverage:** No Find A Grave or BillionGraves coverage was found for 18th-century Arkansas Post burials. Burial entries appear within the sacramental register volume (DGS 008814402).
- **Physical records:** Burials are recorded within the sacramental registers at the Arkansas History Commission and Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers existed in this region before 1800. The first Arkansas newspapers appeared after U.S. territorial organization (post-1819).
- **Not applicable for this period.**

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant considerations:** Movement into Spanish Louisiana was regulated but records are scattered in colonial administrative archives rather than centralized immigration manifests.
- **Record types:** Passports and travel permits in colonial administrative records; merchant licenses; correspondence naming settlers
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); some materials on microfilm at Library of Congress

### Tax records
- **Types:** No formal county tax records existed before 1819. Colonial-era fiscal records (if any survive) would be in the commandant's administrative files.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias
- **Substitute value:** Land concession records can serve as a substitute, naming settled landholders

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** The post commandant acted as a notary. Contracts, sales, and other civil instruments may survive in the Arkansas History Commission holdings.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 browse-only volume (DGS 008814402): Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763–1800, 64 images, in Spanish | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S. confirmation records of Spanish-era land grants, post-1803 | Free |
| Archivo General de Indias PARES portal (pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) | Some digitized Spanish Louisiana colonial documents; search "Puestos del Arkansas" | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Post-1803 U.S. territorial records; some microfilmed Spanish colonial materials | Free/subscription |

No name-indexed FamilySearch collections were found covering the pre-1800 Arkansas region. The 3 indexed Arkansas collections on FamilySearch all begin in 1819 or later.

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching this place and period (total results = 1); the result set is complete.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial records, padrones, land concessions, military post records, church register transcriptions | In-person; contact for remote access requests |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Master archive of Spanish colonial records for Louisiana, including Arkansas Post materials | In-person; some digitized records via PARES portal |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of selected Spanish Louisiana colonial records | In-person; some digitized via loc.gov |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original church registers for Arkansas Post | Contact diocese archives directly |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial census records (padrones) — physical only at Arkansas History Commission, Archivo General de Indias, and Library of Congress microfilm
- Spanish land concession records — physical only at Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias (some U.S. confirmations at BLM GLO online)
- Military post records (muster rolls, officer correspondence) — physical only at Archivo General de Indias and Arkansas History Commission
- Most church registers — originals at Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission; only 1 browse-only (non-indexed, Spanish-language) volume digitized at FamilySearch
- Notarial records from the post commandant — physical only at Arkansas History Commission

## Known record losses
No tool result stated a specific destruction or loss of pre-1800 Arkansas records. The scarcity of online holdings reflects limited digitization and the decentralized colonial administration rather than confirmed destruction. Contact the Arkansas History Commission to confirm current holdings and any known gaps in the colonial-era series.

## Research tips
- **Colonial records are in Spanish.** The 1 digitized FamilySearch volume (DGS 008814402) must be browsed image by image with no name index and requires reading 18th-century ecclesiastical Spanish. Consider hiring a paleographer or professional researcher familiar with Spanish colonial documents. ([Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Search the parent jurisdiction (Spanish Louisiana/New Orleans) for administrative records.** Arkansas Post reported to the Governor-General in New Orleans. Census records, land petitions, and civil correspondence were routed to and filed in New Orleans-based archives. Research Louisiana colonial records in parallel with Arkansas Post records. ([Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Spanish land grants confirmed after 1803 may name ancestors not in other records.** Claimants petitioned Congress to confirm their Spanish-era grants; these petitions often include the grantee's name, length of residence, family members, and witnesses. Check the BLM GLO and Congressional confirmation records.
- **Try the PARES portal before planning a trip to Seville.** The Archivo General de Indias has digitized portions of the Louisiana colonial records. Search "Puestos del Arkansas" or "Post of Arkansas" at pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es to identify what is already available digitally.
- **Arkansas Post is the single settlement to focus on.** Before 1803, virtually all European settlement in what is now Arkansas was at Arkansas Post or its immediate vicinity. If an ancestor was in the region, they almost certainly appear in records connected to that post.
- **A negative online search result here is not an absence.** The only digitized online resource for this period is a single browse-only, non-indexed, Spanish-language FamilySearch volume. The bulk of surviving records remain physical-only at repositories in Little Rock, Washington D.C., and Seville.

Locality guide written as `loc_001`. Here is its full report:

---

## Ohio circa 1790 — Locality Guide

Researching ancestors in Ohio around 1790 means working in the **Northwest Territory**, not yet a state. At that moment, the entire present-day state of Ohio was organized under just **two counties**:

- **Washington County** (organized 1788) — covering the eastern portion
- **Hamilton County** (organized January 1790) — covering the southwest around Cincinnati

Any record generated in 1790 will be filed under one of those two counties — not under any of Ohio's 88 modern counties, because all of those were carved out later.

---

### Boundary Changes

All of modern Ohio's 88 counties descend from these two original Northwest Territory counties. When researching a specific location, you must identify which modern county covers your ancestor's area, then trace its parent counties back to Washington or Hamilton County.

---

### Available Records Despite Early Documentation Gaps

| Record Type | Availability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Marriage bonds** | From 1789 | FamilySearch: "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" |
| **Church records** | From 1787 | FamilySearch holds digitized collections |
| **Land records** | From 1787 | Three separate survey systems (see below) |
| **Federal Census** | From 1800 | 1790 census did *not* enumerate Ohio's territory; use the 1800 "Northwest Territory" enumeration |
| **Tax records** | 1799–1803 | Washington County tax records on FamilySearch (browse-only) |
| **Northwest Territory land records** | 1788–1799 | Digitized on FamilySearch (largely browse-only) |

No civil registration of births or deaths existed in this period.

---

### Three Land Survey Systems

Land research is complicated by three separate survey systems:

1. **Virginia Military District** (Revolutionary War veterans) — records held at the Virginia State Library
2. **Connecticut Western Reserve** — records at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland
3. **Federal rectangular survey** (rest of Ohio) — patents searchable at the BLM General Land Office website

---

### Key Physical Repositories

- **Ohio History Connection**, Columbus (primary state archives)
- **Washington County Courthouse**, Marietta
- **Hamilton County Probate Court**, Cincinnati
- **Ohio Genealogical Society** (guidance and compiled records)

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. Identify which modern Ohio county covers your ancestor's 1790 location.
2. Trace that county's parent counties back to Washington or Hamilton County.
3. Search those counties' records at the Ohio History Connection and on FamilySearch.
4. For land research, determine which of the three survey systems applies to your ancestor's location.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Northwest Territory / Ohio (ca. 1790, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Washington County organized July 27, 1788, under the Northwest Territory (established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787); Hamilton County created January 2, 1790 from the western portion of Washington County
- **Administrative centers:** Marietta (Washington County seat); Cincinnati (Hamilton County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by tools for this period
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, fur trade, Ohio Company land grants, military garrison settlements along the Ohio River
- **Ethnic composition:** American settlers arriving primarily from Virginia, New England, and the mid-Atlantic states; significant Native American presence (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami peoples) throughout the 1790s
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Quaker (Society of Friends), Baptist, and Moravian missionaries were present in the early 1790s, though congregations were sparse and dispersed
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787) established territorial civil governance; Northwest Indian War (1785–1795) including the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Ohio achieved statehood March 1, 1803

## Boundary changes

This is the most critical issue for 1790 Ohio research. In 1790, the entire present-day state of Ohio was organized under just two counties within the Northwest Territory:

- **Washington County** (organized July 27, 1788): Covered the eastern and central portions of present-day Ohio and portions of present-day West Virginia and beyond. Marietta was the county seat. All records from the eastern two-thirds of present-day Ohio in 1790 will be found under Washington County.
- **Hamilton County** (organized January 2, 1790): Created from the western portion of Washington County. Centered on Cincinnati. Covered the southwestern portion of present-day Ohio.

Ohio did not become a state until March 1, 1803. Records created in 1790 are territorial records, not Ohio state records. Over the following decades, the territory of Washington and Hamilton counties was repeatedly subdivided into the 88 Ohio counties that exist today. A family living in 1790 in what became, for example, Franklin County or Licking County in later years would have had their territorial-period records filed under Washington County.

Three distinct land-survey districts further complicate the picture:
1. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): metes-and-bounds survey, reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans. Warrants are held at the Virginia State Library, not in Ohio. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
2. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): surveyed on a separate township-range grid; records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
3. **U.S. Public Land Survey** (most of the rest of Ohio): standard rectangular township-range system; federal patents searchable at the BLM General Land Office website.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in 1790 Ohio. The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; a specific statewide registration start year cannot be confirmed from that page.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses at the county level are the earliest formal vital records, appearing in FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013" (collection 1803785; 1,523,678 records; indexed + images) — starting from 1789 in the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Washington County Courthouse (Marietta) and Hamilton County Courthouse (Cincinnati) hold the originals; FamilySearch collection 1803785 provides online name-indexed access.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration existed in 1790.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); land records naming heirs and grantees; probate records naming spouses and children.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker, Baptist, and Moravian; all present by early 1790s, though frontier coverage was thin
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership rolls, confirmations
- **Where held:** Denominational archives; FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (collection 2246917; 678,234 records; indexed + images, starting 1787)
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory with the existing states. The 1800 census is the first to include the area that became Ohio (enumerated as "Northwest Territory"). The 1810 census is the first filed under "Ohio."
- **State/territorial census:** No territorial census for this period was returned by tool results.
- **Access:** The 1800 (Northwest Territory) and 1810 (Ohio) federal censuses are available indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry; these are the nearest enumeration sources for families present around 1790.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships; Northwest Territory Court of Common Pleas records
- **Date range:** Washington County courts from 1788; Hamilton County courts from 1790
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (Columbus); Washington County Courthouse (Marietta); Hamilton County Probate Court (Cincinnati). The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Probate Records page returned only generic content during this survey.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Three distinct systems (Virginia Military District metes-and-bounds; Connecticut Western Reserve township-range; U.S. Public Land Survey rectangular — see Boundary changes above)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government (General Land Office) for U.S. Public Land Survey patents; Virginia for Virginia Military District warrants; Connecticut Land Company for Western Reserve grants
- **Types:** Land grants, patents, territorial warrants, bounty land warrants, deeds
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840" (collection 1542187; 234,567 records; indexed + images, starting 1787)
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (federal patents, free); Ohio History Connection; county recorder offices; Virginia State Library (Virginia Military District warrants); Western Reserve Historical Society (Western Reserve records)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War (1785–1795); Revolutionary War veterans received Virginia Military District bounty land
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) carries digitized pension files and service records (subscription)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mound Cemetery (Marietta, est. 1788); early frontier burial grounds, many unmarked
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records virtually nonexistent for 1790; transcription projects conducted by the Ohio Genealogical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** _Centinel of the North-Western Territory_ (Cincinnati, est. 1793) — first newspaper in the territory, just after 1790 but covering the same families
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/)
- **Content value:** Land sale notices, legal notices, some death notices; useful for families present in the mid-1790s onward

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant routes:** Settlers arrived primarily via the Ohio River from Pittsburgh, or overland through Pennsylvania and Virginia — not by ocean arrival into an Ohio port
- **Record types:** Naturalization records (rare; most 1790 Ohio settlers were American-born); Revolutionary War pension files naming state of origin; land grant applications naming home state
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Content note:** Ocean passenger lists do not capture overland migration into Ohio. To trace origins, work backward through pension files, land grant applications, and the state the family emigrated from.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property and land tax lists
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850" (collection 1987542; 345,890 records) begins in 1800 — after the 1790 target year but useful for confirming family presence shortly afterward
- **Where held:** County archives; Ohio History Connection; FamilySearch (1800 onward, indexed + images)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1800 onward can establish the presence and property of families in Washington and Hamilton counties, bridging the gap from 1790.

### Other record types
- **Territorial court minute books:** Northwest Territory Court of Common Pleas records name road commissioners, local witnesses, and parties to suits — important for 1788-1803 research; held at Ohio History Connection and county courthouses
- **Northwest Territory Papers:** Federal records of the territorial government at NARA and the Ohio History Connection document land grants and civil appointments

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (345,890 records); 2 digitized volumes (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census including 1800 Northwest Territory and 1810 Ohio enumerations | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents for Ohio public-land survey districts | Free |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records and memorial transcriptions | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal territorial records, pension files | Free (in-person) / Fold3 online |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes for this place and period (totalResults: 2), which appears to be the complete result set. No summary section was returned by the tool, so record-type group totals are unavailable. The two volumes are: (1) Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788-1799, 51 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only image by image; (2) Washington County Tax Records, 1799-1803, 73 images, 12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — mostly browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial and early statehood records; Washington and Hamilton County records; court records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Washington County Courthouse, Marietta | Court, deed, marriage, and probate records from 1788 | In-person / mail |
| Hamilton County Probate Court, Cincinnati | County records from 1790 | In-person / mail |
| Virginia State Library, Richmond, VA | Virginia Military District land warrants | In-person / mail request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person |
| NARA, Washington DC | Federal territorial records, military pension files | In-person / Fold3 online |

## Records NOT online
- **Territorial court minute books** (Northwest Territory Court of Common Pleas): largely physical-only at Ohio History Connection and county courthouses
- **Virginia Military District warrants** (pre-patent stage): Virginia State Library physical holdings
- **Connecticut Western Reserve survey records**: Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland — not fully digitized
- **Early frontier church registers (ca. 1788-1800)**: Some are held at denominational archives not yet digitized; coverage in FamilySearch collection 2246917 varies by congregation

## Known record losses
No tool result returned specific information about destroyed or lost record sets for 1790 Ohio or the Northwest Territory. The sparse record-keeping infrastructure of a frontier territory means many records were never created rather than created and subsequently lost — a critical distinction. Consult the Ohio History Connection for known gaps in specific county series.

## Research tips
- **The critical search rule for 1790 Ohio**: Identify which present-day county covers the location where your ancestor lived. Trace that county's formation backward through successive parent counties until you reach Washington County (eastern Ohio, 1788) or Hamilton County (southwestern Ohio, 1790). All territorial-period records for that location will be under those two counties, not the modern county. A county formation chart is available from the Ohio Genealogical Society. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)
- **Virginia Military District**: If your ancestor received land between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers, the warrant records are at the Virginia State Library, not Ohio. Search there in addition to Ohio repositories. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **Connecticut Western Reserve**: Northeastern Ohio land records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland and use a different survey grid from the rest of Ohio. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **No civil vital registration in 1790**: Use church records, marriage bonds at the county courthouse, land records naming heirs, and probate inventories as substitutes for birth and death records.
- **The 1790 federal census does not cover Ohio**: The 1800 census (filed under 'Northwest Territory') is the first meaningful enumeration for families in the area; the 1810 census is the first filed under 'Ohio.'
- **FamilySearch Wiki gap**: All four Ohio-specific wiki place pages and all Ohio topical wiki pages returned only generic content during this survey. For Ohio-specific research guidance, consult the Ohio History Connection (https://www.ohiohistory.org/) and the Ohio Genealogical Society.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Northwest Territory / Ohio (ca. 1790, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Washington County organized July 27, 1788, under the Northwest Territory (established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787); Hamilton County created January 2, 1790 from the western portion of Washington County
- **Administrative centers:** Marietta (Washington County seat); Cincinnati (Hamilton County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by tools for this period
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, fur trade, Ohio Company land grants, military garrison settlements along the Ohio River
- **Ethnic composition:** American settlers arriving primarily from Virginia, New England, and the mid-Atlantic states; significant Native American presence (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami peoples) throughout the 1790s
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Quaker (Society of Friends), Baptist, and Moravian missionaries were present in the early 1790s, though congregations were sparse and dispersed
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787) established territorial civil governance; Northwest Indian War (1785–1795) including the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Ohio achieved statehood March 1, 1803

## Boundary changes

This is the most critical issue for 1790 Ohio research. In 1790, the entire present-day state of Ohio was organized under just two counties within the Northwest Territory:

- **Washington County** (organized July 27, 1788): Covered the eastern and central portions of present-day Ohio and portions of present-day West Virginia and beyond. Marietta was the county seat. All records from the eastern two-thirds of present-day Ohio in 1790 will be found under Washington County.
- **Hamilton County** (organized January 2, 1790): Created from the western portion of Washington County. Centered on Cincinnati. Covered the southwestern portion of present-day Ohio.

Ohio did not become a state until March 1, 1803. Records created in 1790 are territorial records, not Ohio state records. Over the following decades, the territory of Washington and Hamilton counties was repeatedly subdivided into the 88 Ohio counties that exist today. A family living in 1790 in what became, for example, Franklin County or Licking County in later years would have had their territorial-period records filed under Washington County.

Three distinct land-survey districts further complicate the picture:
1. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): metes-and-bounds survey, reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans. Warrants are held at the Virginia State Library, not in Ohio. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
2. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): surveyed on a separate township-range grid; records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
3. **U.S. Public Land Survey** (most of the rest of Ohio): standard rectangular township-range system; federal patents searchable at the BLM General Land Office website.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in 1790 Ohio. The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; a specific statewide registration start year cannot be confirmed from that page.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses at the county level are the earliest formal vital records, appearing in FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013" (collection 1803785; 1,523,678 records; indexed + images) — starting from 1789 in the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Washington County Courthouse (Marietta) and Hamilton County Courthouse (Cincinnati) hold the originals; FamilySearch collection 1803785 provides online name-indexed access.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration existed in 1790.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); land records naming heirs and grantees; probate records naming spouses and children.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker, Baptist, and Moravian; all present by early 1790s, though frontier coverage was thin
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership rolls, confirmations
- **Where held:** Denominational archives; FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (collection 2246917; 678,234 records; indexed + images, starting 1787)
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory with the existing states. The 1800 census is the first to include the area that became Ohio (enumerated as "Northwest Territory"). The 1810 census is the first filed under "Ohio."
- **State/territorial census:** No territorial census for this period was returned by tool results.
- **Access:** The 1800 (Northwest Territory) and 1810 (Ohio) federal censuses are available indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry; these are the nearest enumeration sources for families present around 1790.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships; Northwest Territory Court of Common Pleas records
- **Date range:** Washington County courts from 1788; Hamilton County courts from 1790
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (Columbus); Washington County Courthouse (Marietta); Hamilton County Probate Court (Cincinnati). The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Probate Records page returned only generic content during this survey.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Three distinct systems (Virginia Military District metes-and-bounds; Connecticut Western Reserve township-range; U.S. Public Land Survey rectangular — see Boundary changes above)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government (General Land Office) for U.S. Public Land Survey patents; Virginia for Virginia Military District warrants; Connecticut Land Company for Western Reserve grants
- **Types:** Land grants, patents, territorial warrants, bounty land warrants, deeds
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840" (collection 1542187; 234,567 records; indexed + images, starting 1787)
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (federal patents, free); Ohio History Connection; county recorder offices; Virginia State Library (Virginia Military District warrants); Western Reserve Historical Society (Western Reserve records)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War (1785–1795); Revolutionary War veterans received Virginia Military District bounty land
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) carries digitized pension files and service records (subscription)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mound Cemetery (Marietta, est. 1788); early frontier burial grounds, many unmarked
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records virtually nonexistent for 1790; transcription projects conducted by the Ohio Genealogical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** _Centinel of the North-Western Territory_ (Cincinnati, est. 1793) — first newspaper in the territory, just after 1790 but covering the same families
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/)
- **Content value:** Land sale notices, legal notices, some death notices; useful for families present in the mid-1790s onward

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant routes:** Settlers arrived primarily via the Ohio River from Pittsburgh, or overland through Pennsylvania and Virginia — not by ocean arrival into an Ohio port
- **Record types:** Naturalization records (rare; most 1790 Ohio settlers were American-born); Revolutionary War pension files naming state of origin; land grant applications naming home state
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Content note:** Ocean passenger lists do not capture overland migration into Ohio. To trace origins, work backward through pension files, land grant applications, and the state the family emigrated from.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property and land tax lists
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850" (collection 1987542; 345,890 records) begins in 1800 — after the 1790 target year but useful for confirming family presence shortly afterward
- **Where held:** County archives; Ohio History Connection; FamilySearch (1800 onward, indexed + images)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1800 onward can establish the presence and property of families in Washington and Hamilton counties, bridging the gap from 1790.

### Other record types
- **Territorial court minute books:** Northwest Territory Court of Common Pleas records name road commissioners, local witnesses, and parties to suits — important for 1788-1803 research; held at Ohio History Connection and county courthouses
- **Northwest Territory Papers:** Federal records of the territorial government at NARA and the Ohio History Connection document land grants and civil appointments

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (345,890 records); 2 digitized volumes (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census including 1800 Northwest Territory and 1810 Ohio enumerations | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents for Ohio public-land survey districts | Free |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records and memorial transcriptions | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal territorial records, pension files | Free (in-person) / Fold3 online |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes for this place and period (totalResults: 2), which appears to be the complete result set. No summary section was returned by the tool, so record-type group totals are unavailable. The two volumes are: (1) Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788-1799, 51 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only image by image; (2) Washington County Tax Records, 1799-1803, 73 images, 12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — mostly browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial and early statehood records; Washington and Hamilton County records; court records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Washington County Courthouse, Marietta | Court, deed, marriage, and probate records from 1788 | In-person / mail |
| Hamilton County Probate Court, Cincinnati | County records from 1790 | In-person / mail |
| Virginia State Library, Richmond, VA | Virginia Military District land warrants | In-person / mail request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person |
| NARA, Washington DC | Federal territorial records, military pension files | In-person / Fold3 online |

## Records NOT online
- **Territorial court minute books** (Northwest Territory Court of Common Pleas): largely physical-only at Ohio History Connection and county courthouses
- **Virginia Military District warrants** (pre-patent stage): Virginia State Library physical holdings
- **Connecticut Western Reserve survey records**: Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland — not fully digitized
- **Early frontier church registers (ca. 1788-1800)**: Some are held at denominational archives not yet digitized; coverage in FamilySearch collection 2246917 varies by congregation

## Known record losses
No tool result returned specific information about destroyed or lost record sets for 1790 Ohio or the Northwest Territory. The sparse record-keeping infrastructure of a frontier territory means many records were never created rather than created and subsequently lost — a critical distinction. Consult the Ohio History Connection for known gaps in specific county series.

## Research tips
- **The critical search rule for 1790 Ohio**: Identify which present-day county covers the location where your ancestor lived. Trace that county's formation backward through successive parent counties until you reach Washington County (eastern Ohio, 1788) or Hamilton County (southwestern Ohio, 1790). All territorial-period records for that location will be under those two counties, not the modern county. A county formation chart is available from the Ohio Genealogical Society. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)
- **Virginia Military District**: If your ancestor received land between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers, the warrant records are at the Virginia State Library, not Ohio. Search there in addition to Ohio repositories. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **Connecticut Western Reserve**: Northeastern Ohio land records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland and use a different survey grid from the rest of Ohio. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **No civil vital registration in 1790**: Use church records, marriage bonds at the county courthouse, land records naming heirs, and probate inventories as substitutes for birth and death records.
- **The 1790 federal census does not cover Ohio**: The 1800 census (filed under 'Northwest Territory') is the first meaningful enumeration for families in the area; the 1810 census is the first filed under 'Ohio.'
- **FamilySearch Wiki gap**: All four Ohio-specific wiki place pages and all Ohio topical wiki pages returned only generic content during this survey. For Ohio-specific research guidance, consult the Ohio History Connection (https://www.ohiohistory.org/) and the Ohio Genealogical Society.

---

California during the 1848–1870 Gold Rush is a rewarding but challenging period to research because the state was brand new, the population was transient and male-dominated, and formal recordkeeping was still being established.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely; it was ceded by Mexico to the United States via the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Gold_Rush)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital); San Francisco was the principal port and commercial center.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Formerly the Mexican Department of Alta California; briefly U.S. territory (1848–1850) before statehood.
- **Population during period:** The Gold Rush drew approximately 300,000 people from the United States and abroad beginning in 1848. (Wikipedia) The place_population tool returned no data for this survey.
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855, then shifted toward agriculture, shipping, and commerce; population was predominantly male and highly mobile.
- **Ethnic composition:** Migrants arrived from across the U.S., Latin America, Europe, China, and Australia; substantial Chinese and Hispanic communities formed alongside Anglo-American settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant via Spanish mission parishes pre-1850); Protestant denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Congregationalist) expanded rapidly post-1848; Jewish congregations and Chinese religious communities also present.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; statehood September 9, 1850; 1850 federal census (partially destroyed); 1852 state census; transcontinental railroad completed 1869.

## Boundary changes
- The original 27 counties were established at statehood in 1850; new counties were carved from them throughout the 1850s–1860s. Records created before a county division belong to the parent county — verify which county held a given mining district at the exact date of interest.
- Before 1848, civil records were kept under the Mexican administrative system; Franciscan mission baptism, marriage, and burial registers (1769–1834) are the primary pre-statehood genealogical source.
- Miners and settlers near the eastern border also appear in Nevada Territory (created 1861) records; search both jurisdictions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; no statewide registration start date can be confirmed from tool results. FamilySearch holds a "California, County Births, 1850–1919" collection (789,456 records), indicating county-level birth recording from 1850. No death record collection for the 1850s appeared in collections_search.
- **What exists:** County birth records 1850–1919 (indexed + images on FamilySearch); county marriage records 1850–1952 (indexed + images on FamilySearch). Death records for the 1850s–1860s are not in any FamilySearch indexed collection — deaths are documented only through church burial registers, cemetery records, and probate files.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed births and marriages); county courthouses for originals.
- **Gaps:** No statewide death registration collection found for the target period. The FamilySearch Wiki Vital Records page returned generic content only — consult California State Archives for current holdings.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers, probate files, newspaper death notices, cemetery sexton records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Franciscan missions 1769–1834, diocesan parishes thereafter); Protestant denominations expanded rapidly post-1848.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic); baptism/membership/burial (Protestant).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" (98,765 records, indexed). Post-1850 Catholic records are at the Archdiocese of San Francisco archives and individual parishes. Protestant records are held at individual congregations and denominational archives. The FamilySearch Wiki California Church Records page returned only generic content — specific parish-level repositories could not be confirmed from tool results.
- **Language:** Spanish (mission records); English (Protestant records).

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1850 (California's first — partially destroyed, some county returns missing); 1860; 1870. The missing 1850 returns are a major gap for Gold Rush research. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records)
- **State census:** California state census of 1852 is the critical substitute for the damaged 1850 federal returns. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records) FamilySearch holds a digitized volume of the 1850–1852 California State Census — 522 images, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable. This is the highest-priority record for the Gold Rush cohort.
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules (1850, 1860, 1870) record deaths in the year preceding each census.
- **Access:** 1852 state census: indexed + images (FamilySearch). 1850/1860/1870 federal census: indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianship files, inventories; naturalization petitions in any court of record (pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in state and local courts as well as federal).
- **Date range:** From 1850 (county formation).
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); California State Archives. No California probate collection appeared in FamilySearch collections_search for the target period — this is primarily a physical or microfilm resource. The FamilySearch Wiki California Probate Records page returned only generic content.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** U.S. Public Land Survey system for federal grants; Mexican-era ranchos were confirmed (or contested) under the California Land Act of 1851.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal public land patents searchable at BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov). Mexican rancho confirmations are in the U.S. District Court records at NARA San Bruno. The FamilySearch Wiki California Land and Property page returned only generic content — specific details could not be confirmed.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Mexican rancho grants, mining claim registers at county recorders, deed books at county courthouses.
- **Mining claims:** FamilySearch holds browse-only image volumes of San Francisco Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (340 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image).
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (federal patents, free online); county recorders (deeds, mining claims — physical); California State Archives (Mexican-era land records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) immediately preceded the Gold Rush; many veterans then migrated to California. Civil War (1861–1865) — California raised volunteer regiments.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files (NARA, Washington DC); bounty land warrants for Mexican-American War veterans (NARA); California adjutant general records (California State Archives).
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC); California State Archives; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) for online access to service and pension records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mission cemetery sites (pre-1850); San Francisco historic cemeteries (many remains relocated to Colma); county rural cemeteries; Gold Rush mining camp burial grounds (many unmarked or lost).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has California listings; coverage of 1850s mining camp burials is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for organized cemeteries; mission burial registers in the FamilySearch Mission Records collection (indexed).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Alta California (San Francisco, 1849–1891); Sacramento Daily Union (1851 onward); numerous county papers founded in the 1850s.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription); California Digital Newspaper Collection (University of California, Riverside — free online); California State Library microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries (often detailed for miners and settlers), marriage notices, ship arrival lists, legal notices covering mining claim disputes and estate settlements.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary Pacific port of entry; overland arrivals came via multiple routes (Oregon Trail cutoffs, the Gila Trail, the Old Spanish Trail).
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests (sea arrivals at San Francisco and other California ports); naturalization records in county courts (pre-1906); FamilySearch holds browse-only Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento 1849–1858 (298 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image).
- **Where held:** NARA San Bruno (San Francisco passenger manifests); county courthouses (naturalization petitions). NARA national portal: https://www.archives.gov/
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest when researching a family. Overland migrants have no centralized arrival registry — the 1852 state census, mining claims, and tax rolls serve as arrival proxies.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessment rolls.
- **Date range:** From 1850 (county formation).
- **Where held:** County courthouses and California State Archives; some holdings microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls for 1851–1859 substitute for missing 1850 federal census returns, listing property-owning residents by name and county.

### Other record types — Great Registers and mining documents
- **Great Registers (voter registration):** FamilySearch holds "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" (1,345,678 records, indexed) — the most consistently name-indexed source for men in California from 1866 onward. Each entry gives name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description. This is often the earliest California record explicitly stating a man's birthplace. Note: women are absent (voting rights not yet extended); no equivalent source covers 1848–1865. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **Manuscript collections:** The California State Library (Sacramento) and the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) hold extensive Gold Rush-era diaries, letters, overland journals, and mining company rosters. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records) These are physical-only collections.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (789,456 records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1,345,678 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (567,890 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (98,765 records); State Census 1850–1852 (indexed + images); Mining Claims San Francisco 1849–1855 (browse-only); Port Arrivals Sacramento 1849–1858 (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census 1850, 1860, 1870 (California returns) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records (Mexican-American War, Civil War) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | California cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | California historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | San Francisco passenger manifests, naturalization records, federal land records | Free/fee |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match this place and period in FamilySearch; 3 are detailed above and represent only the first page of results. The remaining 11 volumes were not examined in this survey — consult FamilySearch directly for the full set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA San Bruno (San Bruno, CA) | San Francisco ship passenger manifests; Mexican rancho court records | In-person; some records on Ancestry |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | County records, land records, state census, military records, naturalization | In-person or written request |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Manuscript collections, newspapers, county histories, Gold Rush diaries | In-person |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript, diary, and journal collections | In-person (appointment required) |
| County courthouses (El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Nevada, Placer, etc.) | Deed books, mining claim registers, probate files, naturalization petitions | In-person or mail |

## Records NOT online
- Death records for the 1850s–1860s: no indexed online collection found in this survey.
- Mining claim registers for the primary Gold Rush counties (El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Nevada, Placer) outside San Francisco: not confirmed as digitized; county recorders hold originals.
- Naturalization records pre-1906 filed in state and local courts: not in a single online index; individual county court minute books must be searched.
- Manuscript and diary collections at the Bancroft Library and California State Library: physical-only.
- Tax assessment rolls: not confirmed as indexed online; county and state archives hold originals.
- 11 of 14 FamilySearch digitized volumes for this period were not retrieved in this survey; their record types are unknown.

## Known record losses
- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. Stated by FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records. The 1852 California state census is the recommended substitute.
- No other specific record losses for this place and period were stated in tool results. Absence from an online search is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 California state census** when the 1850 federal census county return is missing — it is 88% indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch, making it the most accessible Gold Rush-era name source. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match this place and period in FamilySearch; 3 are detailed above and represent only the first page of results. The remaining 11 volumes were not examined in this survey — consult FamilySearch directly for the full set.

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA San Bruno (San Bruno, CA) | San Francisco ship passenger manifests; Mexican rancho court records | In-person; some records on Ancestry |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | County records, land records, state census, military records, naturalization | In-person or written request |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Manuscript collections, newspapers, county histories, Gold Rush diaries | In-person |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript, diary, and journal collections | In-person (appointment required) |
| County courthouses (El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Nevada, Placer, etc.) | Deed books, mining claim registers, probate files, naturalization petitions | In-person or mail |

## Records NOT online
- Death records for the 1850s–1860s: no indexed online collection found in this survey.
- Mining claim registers for the primary Gold Rush counties (El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Nevada, Placer) outside San Francisco: not confirmed as digitized; county recorders hold originals.
- Naturalization records pre-1906 filed in state and local courts: not in a single online index; individual county court minute books must be searched.
- Manuscript and diary collections at the Bancroft Library and California State Library: physical-only.
- Tax assessment rolls: not confirmed as indexed online; county and state archives hold originals.
- 11 of 14 FamilySearch digitized volumes for this period were not retrieved in this survey; their record types are unknown.

## Known record losses
- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. Stated by FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records. The 1852 California state census is the recommended substitute.
- No other specific record losses for this place and period were stated in tool results. Absence from an online search is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 California state census** when the 1850 federal census county return is missing — it is 88% indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch, making it the most accessible Gold Rush-era name source. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **Use the Great Registers (1866–1910) to confirm birthplace.** These voter registration lists give each man's age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description — often the first California record to state origins explicitly. FamilySearch collection 1923340 is fully indexed.
- **Identify the mining county first.** Mining claim records, census returns, and newspapers name the specific county where an ancestor worked; county is the key to unlocking deed, probate, naturalization, and court records at the correct courthouse.
- **For sea arrivals, go to NARA San Bruno**, not Washington DC, for San Francisco passenger manifests. For overland arrivals, the 1852 state census, tax rolls, and mining claim registers are the closest substitutes for an arrival record.
- **County boundaries shifted frequently in the 1850s.** Verify which county held a given mining district at the exact year of interest; a 1852 claim may be in a different county than a 1858 claim for the same location.
- **The Bancroft Library and California State Library** hold manuscript collections — diaries, letters, and company rosters — that name individuals absent from all official records. These are physical-only but partially indexed in published finding aids. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)

For additional California-specific research strategy, consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy directly.

Here is the locality guide for **New York City in the colonial 1700s**:

---

## Key Finding: No Civil Registration Existed

There were no government birth, marriage, or death certificates anywhere in colonial New York. **Church registers are the only systematic source for vital events.**

---

## Church Records

- **Dutch Reformed Church** holds the oldest continuous series, beginning **1639**. This is your most important starting point for 18th-century NYC families.
- FamilySearch has one digitized volume covering **1700–1776** (211 images), but it is:
  - Browse-only (0% name-indexed)
  - Written entirely in **Dutch**
  - Must be read image by image
- FamilySearch collection: **New York, Church Records, 1640–1940**

---

## Key FamilySearch Collections

| Collection | Coverage |
|---|---|
| Church Records | 1640–1940 |
| Land Records | 1630–1975 |
| Probate Records | 1629–1971 |
| Tax Assessment Rolls | 1799–1804 |

---

## Key Repositories

1. **FamilySearch.org** — digitized church, land, and probate records (see above)
2. **New York State Archives (Albany)** — colonial manuscript records
3. **New-York Historical Society** — holds an indexed *Abstracts of Wills* series, very useful for the 1700s
4. **New York Genealogical and Biographical Society (NYG&B)** — published records and research aids for colonial-era families

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Open a research project** targeting your specific ancestor or family.
2. Use the **Dutch Reformed church register** (browse the digitized FamilySearch volume) as the first search target — you may need Dutch translation assistance.
3. Search **probate and land records** on FamilySearch, which are better indexed and can provide family relationships, property, and witness names even without vital records.
4. Check the **New-York Historical Society's Abstracts of Wills** for any colonial-era relatives.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Originally established as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam in 1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City); remained under British colonial authority throughout the 1700s until independence
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (served as capital of New York Province throughout the colonial period; briefly the first U.S. capital after 1788)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial authority) through 1783; New York State thereafter
- **Population during period:** Population data not returned by the population tool for this place and period
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trading hub; maritime commerce, merchant trade, artisan industries shaped who migrated, where they settled, and what records they generated
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch settlers and their descendants were prominent early in the century; also English, French Huguenots, Germans, Africans (enslaved and free), and Sephardic Jews — ethnic mix shapes the denominations and languages of surviving church records
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous church records, beginning 1639); Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church); Presbyterian; Lutheran; French Reformed (Huguenot); Jewish (Shearith Israel congregation)
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754-1763) generated militia rolls; American Revolution (1775-1783) — British occupation of the city 1776-1783 disrupted record-keeping for those years

## Boundary changes
- Dutch rule as New Amsterdam (1626-1664); British rule as New York from 1664 through the colonial period
- No major internal boundary changes within the city itself during the 1700s; the surrounding Province of New York is the jurisdictional context for colonial administrative records
- Colonial manuscripts — court records, land grants, administrative documents — are held at the New York State Archives (Albany) under the New York Colonial Manuscripts series, distinct from later county or municipal records
- Records created under Dutch rule predate this survey window but may be relevant for families present in New York before 1664

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration system existed in colonial New York during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and could not supply a confirmed statewide registration start date at any level; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists:** No government-issued birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1700s. Church registers are the only systematic vital records for this period.
- **Where held:** Church archives and FamilySearch collection 1469062 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)
- **Gaps:** The entire 1700s is pre-civil registration; the Revolutionary War occupation (1776-1783) may create gaps even in church records
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; probate records naming heirs; newspaper notices

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (records beginning 1639 — the oldest continuous series in the city, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records); Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church); Presbyterian; Lutheran; French Reformed (Huguenot)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, membership rolls
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (ID 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) covers the full 1700s window. FamilySearch also holds one digitized volume of Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700-1776 (DGS 007733180, 211 images). Original registers are held by individual church archives and by the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society (nygbs.org).
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch through much of this period; Anglican registers in English; French Reformed registers may be in French
- **Digitization level — Dutch Reformed volume (DGS 007733180):** Browse-only images — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and in Dutch. Must be browsed image by image and read in Dutch.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790, at the very end of this research window; it names heads of household only, with other household members counted in age and sex groupings
- **State/provincial census:** No confirmed state or provincial census for 1700s New York identified by tool results
- **Other enumerations:** Colonial Province of New York militia rolls listed men of military age throughout the province and are useful for identifying adult male residents across years with no census (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records); tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and available online; colonial militia and tax lists are largely physical-only at the New York State Archives

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships
- **Testate proceedings:** Wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York during the colonial period; the New-York Historical Society published an Abstracts of Wills series that indexes these colonial wills (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Intestate proceedings:** Letters of administration for those who died without a will were also processed by the Prerogative Court
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (ID 1542780) covers from 1629, which encompasses the entire 1700s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1542780 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780); New-York Historical Society Abstracts of Wills; New York State Archives for colonial-era originals

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New York is not a federal land state; no rectangular survey applies)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under British colonial rule, land patents and grants were issued by the Crown through the colonial governor; the New York State Archives holds colonial-era land grants. The FamilySearch Wiki page for New York Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Land_and_Property directly.
- **Types:** Deeds, land patents, mortgages, conveyances
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (ID 2078654) covers from 1630
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2078654 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654); New York State Archives for colonial land grants; New York County Clerk for deed books

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754-1763); American Revolution (1775-1783)
- **Record types:** Colonial Province of New York militia rolls; Revolutionary War service records and pension files; bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** Colonial militia rolls — New York State Archives (New York Colonial Manuscripts series); Revolutionary War records — National Archives (NARA, https://www.archives.gov); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) holds digitized military records
- **Note:** Militia rolls list men of military age by name and are a key substitute for census records in the pre-1790 decades (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Anglican, Manhattan); Dutch Reformed churchyards; various denominational cemeteries in lower Manhattan
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has some coverage of colonial-era burials; completeness is limited for the 1700s
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual churches; some published by the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New York Gazette (a colonial-era paper cited by Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers available via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) — subscription required; colonial papers also on microfilm at the New York Public Library and New-York Historical Society
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale and legal notices, runaway servant/slave advertisements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York City was the primary port of entry for the colony throughout the 1700s
- **Record types:** Colonial passenger lists; naturalization/denization records (handled by colonial courts and the provincial assembly before 1790); oaths of allegiance
- **Where held:** Colonial arrival records at the New York State Archives; NARA (https://www.archives.gov) for some colonial-era lists
- **Content note:** Colonial-era arrival records are far less systematic than post-1820 passenger lists. Many immigrants of the 1700s are traceable only through church and land records after arrival rather than through a passenger manifest. Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when one is found.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists for city wards; property and personal estate assessments
