# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Originally established as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam in 1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City); remained under British colonial authority throughout the 1700s until independence
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (served as capital of New York Province; briefly the first U.S. capital after 1788)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial authority) through 1783; New York State thereafter
- **Population during period:** Population data not returned by the population tool for this place and period
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trading hub; maritime commerce and merchant trade shaped who migrated and what records they generated
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch settlers and their descendants were prominent early in the century; also English, French Huguenots, Germans, Africans (enslaved and free), and Sephardic Jews — this mix shapes the denominations and languages of surviving church records
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous church records, beginning 1639); Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church); Presbyterian; Lutheran; French Reformed (Huguenot); Jewish (Shearith Israel congregation)
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754-1763) generated militia rolls; American Revolution (1775-1783) — British occupation 1776-1783 disrupted record-keeping

## Boundary changes
- Dutch rule as New Amsterdam (1626-1664); British rule as New York from 1664 through the colonial period
- No major internal boundary changes within the city during the 1700s; the Province of New York is the jurisdictional context for colonial administrative records
- Colonial manuscripts — court records, land grants, administrative documents — are held at the New York State Archives under the New York Colonial Manuscripts series, distinct from later county or municipal records

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration system existed in colonial New York during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and could not supply a confirmed registration start date at any level; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists:** No government-issued birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1700s. Church registers are the only systematic vital records for this period.
- **Where held:** Church archives and FamilySearch collection 1469062 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)
- **Gaps:** The entire 1700s is pre-civil registration; the Revolutionary War occupation (1776-1783) may create gaps even in church records
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; probate records naming heirs; newspaper notices

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (records beginning 1639 — the oldest continuous series in the city, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records); Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church); Presbyterian; Lutheran; French Reformed (Huguenot)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, membership rolls
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (ID 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) covers the full 1700s. One digitized volume of Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700-1776 (DGS 007733180, 211 images) is browse-only. Original registers are held by individual church archives and the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society (nygbs.org).
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch through much of this period; Anglican registers in English; French Reformed registers may be in French
- **Digitization level — Dutch Reformed volume (DGS 007733180):** Browse-only images — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and in Dutch. Must be browsed image by image and read in Dutch.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790, at the very end of this research window; it names heads of household only, with other members counted in age and sex groupings
- **State/provincial census:** No confirmed state or provincial census for 1700s New York identified by tool results
- **Other enumerations:** Colonial Province of New York militia rolls listed men of military age and are useful for identifying adult male residents before 1790 (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records); tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and available online; colonial militia and tax lists are largely physical-only at the New York State Archives

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships
- **Testate proceedings:** Wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York; the New-York Historical Society published an Abstracts of Wills series that indexes these colonial wills (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Intestate proceedings:** Letters of administration for those dying without a will were also processed by the Prerogative Court
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (ID 1542780) covers from 1629, encompassing the entire 1700s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1542780 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780); New-York Historical Society Abstracts of Wills; New York State Archives for colonial-era originals

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New York is not a federal land state; no rectangular survey applies)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under British colonial rule, land patents and grants were issued by the Crown through the colonial governor; the New York State Archives holds colonial-era land grants. The FamilySearch Wiki page for New York Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Land_and_Property directly.
- **Types:** Deeds, land patents, mortgages, conveyances
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (ID 2078654) covers from 1630
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2078654 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654); New York State Archives for colonial land grants; New York County Clerk for deed books

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754-1763); American Revolution (1775-1783)
- **Record types:** Colonial Province of New York militia rolls; Revolutionary War service records and pension files; bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** Colonial militia rolls — New York State Archives (New York Colonial Manuscripts series); Revolutionary War records — National Archives (NARA, https://www.archives.gov); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) holds digitized military records
- **Note:** Militia rolls list men of military age by name and are a key substitute for census records in the pre-1790 decades (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Anglican, Manhattan); Dutch Reformed churchyards; various denominational cemeteries in lower Manhattan
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has some coverage of colonial-era burials; completeness is limited for the 1700s
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual churches; some published by the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New York Gazette (a colonial-era paper cited by Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) — subscription required; colonial papers also on microfilm at the New York Public Library and New-York Historical Society
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale and legal notices, runaway servant and slave advertisements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York City was the primary port of entry for the colony throughout the 1700s
- **Record types:** Colonial passenger lists; naturalization/denization records (handled by colonial courts and the provincial assembly before 1790); oaths of allegiance
- **Where held:** Colonial arrival records at the New York State Archives; NARA (https://www.archives.gov) for some colonial-era lists
- **Content note:** Colonial-era arrival records are far less systematic than post-1820 passenger lists. Many immigrants of the 1700s are traceable only through church and land records after arrival. Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when one is found.

- **Where held:** Colonial militia rolls — New York State Archives (New York Colonial Manuscripts series); Revolutionary War records — National Archives (NARA, https://www.archives.gov); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) holds digitized military records
- **Note:** Militia rolls list men of military age by name and are a key substitute for census records in the pre-1790 decades (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Anglican, Manhattan); Dutch Reformed churchyards; various denominational cemeteries in lower Manhattan
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has some coverage of colonial-era burials; completeness is limited for the 1700s
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual churches; some published by the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New York Gazette (a colonial-era paper cited by Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) — subscription required; colonial papers also on microfilm at the New York Public Library and New-York Historical Society
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale and legal notices, runaway servant and slave advertisements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York City was the primary port of entry for the colony throughout the 1700s
- **Record types:** Colonial passenger lists; naturalization/denization records (handled by colonial courts and the provincial assembly before 1790); oaths of allegiance
- **Where held:** Colonial arrival records at the New York State Archives; NARA (https://www.archives.gov) for some colonial-era lists
- **Content note:** Colonial-era arrival records are far less systematic than post-1820 passenger lists. Many immigrants of the 1700s are traceable only through church and land records after arrival. Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when one is found.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists for city wards; property and personal estate assessments
- **Date range:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards during the 1700s (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records); FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (ID 1678432) covers the very end of the period
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1678432 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) for 1799-1804; earlier tax lists at the New York State Archives
- **Substitute value:** In the absence of census records before 1790, ward-level tax lists confirm residency and location within the city, pointing to the relevant church and court records

### Court records (Mayor's Court and colonial administration)
- **Types:** Mayor's Court proceedings; colonial assembly records; naturalizations/denizations; equity proceedings; criminal and civil suits
- **Where held:** New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives (cited per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records); not generally available online
- **Value:** Court records name witnesses, sureties, neighbors, and parties to transactions — often the only record linking individuals who left no will or church record

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (ID 1469062); New York, Land Records, 1630-1975 (ID 2078654); New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (ID 1542780); New York, Tax Assessment Rolls 1799-1804 (ID 1678432); Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700-1776 browse-only (DGS 007733180) | Free |
| NARA | Revolutionary War service and pension records; some colonial passenger lists | Free (archives.gov) |
| Fold3 | Digitized military records | Subscription (fold3.com) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free (findagrave.com) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including colonial-era papers | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume for New York City and the 1700-1800 window (Dutch Reformed Church Registers, DGS 007733180, 211 images). `totalResults: 1` with no nextPageToken indicates this is the complete result set at the city level. `collections_search` returned 5 collections at the New York state scope; 4 overlap the 1700s window.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York Colonial Manuscripts; colonial land grants; Mayor's Court records; colonial militia rolls; pre-1799 tax lists | In-person; finding aids at archives.nysed.gov |
| New York Genealogical and Biographical Society | Extensive colonial-era manuscript and microfilm collections | In-person and some digitized; nygbs.org |
| New-York Historical Society | Abstracts of Wills series; colonial manuscript collections | In-person; some online; nyhistory.org |
| New York Public Library | Manuscript and microfilm collections; colonial newspapers | In-person; some digital; nypl.org |
| Individual church archives | Original parish registers not yet digitized | Contact individual churches or their denominational archives |

## Records NOT online
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (Mayor's Court, colonial administrative and court records) at the New York State Archives — physical access required
- Most colonial Province of New York militia rolls and muster lists — physical access at NY State Archives
- Tax assessment lists predating 1799 — physical access at NY State Archives or local repositories
- Church registers for denominations not yet microfilmed or digitized by FamilySearch — contact individual churches or denominational archives
- French Reformed (Huguenot) church records — check Huguenot Society holdings in addition to FamilySearch

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey explicitly states that a specific New York City colonial record set was destroyed or lost. The Dutch Reformed Church Registers volume (DGS 007733180, 1700-1776) is present and digitized as browse-only images. The Revolutionary War British occupation (1776-1783) is a noted period of disruption; whether that affected specific record series is not stated by any tool result in this survey. Consult the New York State Archives (archives.nysed.gov) or the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society for loss assessments specific to particular record groups.

## Research tips
- **Church records are the gateway to all vital events in colonial NYC.** No civil registration existed; start with Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian registers. FamilySearch collection 1469062 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) and browse-only volume DGS 007733180 are the digitized starting points.
- **The Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch and must be browsed image by image.** Volume DGS 007733180 (1700-1776, 211 images) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — budget time to read Dutch-language entries directly.
- **Probate records are a major gateway for family relationships.** Begin with the New-York Historical Society's Abstracts of Wills series, then verify against FamilySearch collection 1542780 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **Militia rolls substitute for census records before 1790.** Colonial Province of New York militia rolls list adult men by name and confirm presence in the city across the pre-census decades (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **Tax assessment lists pinpoint ward location.** Ward-level tax lists establish where within the city a family lived, directing the search to the relevant church records and court.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York and New York City returned only generic content during this survey.** Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records directly before treating their contents as confirmed absent.

---

Virginia during the Revolutionary War (1775–1783) is one of the best-documented colonies for this period, with records held at the county level throughout. Here's a summary of the most important sources for tracing military-connected families:

---

## Key Record Types & Repositories

### Military Records
- **Continental Line service records & pension files** — held at the National Archives (NARA), accessible through **Fold3**. Pension files are especially valuable; they often contain the most detailed family information of any record type from this era, including names, ages, marriages, and places of residence.
- **Virginia militia records** — held at the **Library of Virginia** in Richmond.
- **Revolutionary War land bounty warrants** — digitized browse-only volumes on FamilySearch.

### Vital Record Substitutes
There was **no statewide civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths during the war years. Substitutes include:
- **Anglican vestry tithe books** (church records)
- **County marriage bonds**
- **Probate files** (wills, inventories, estate settlements)

### Tax Records
- **Virginia personal property and land tax lists (starting 1782)** — critically important because the 1790 federal census for Virginia was largely destroyed. These lists fill the gap and can document household members, property, and taxable individuals.

### Court and Land Records
- **County court order books** (including an Augusta County court order book on FamilySearch)
- **Land patents and deeds** at the Library of Virginia
- **County deed books** (local courthouses and Library of Virginia)

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What's Held |
|---|---|
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Continental service records, pension files, bounty warrants |
| **Fold3** | Digitized NARA Revolutionary War military records |
| **Library of Virginia, Richmond** | Virginia militia records, land patents, court records, tax lists |
| **FamilySearch** | 5+ indexed collections: Virginia church, land, marriage, will, tax, military, and court records |
| **County courthouses** | Original deed books, will books, marriage bonds |

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Identify the Virginia county** your ancestor lived in during 1775–1783 — nearly all records from this period are county-level.
2. Pull that county's **tax lists, court order books, and marriage bonds**.
3. If military service is suspected, **request the pension file from NARA** — these files frequently contain rich family detail found nowhere else.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** Virginia was a British colony that declared independence in 1776; it was recognized as a state by the Treaty of Paris (1783) and formally admitted to the Union in 1788 (per FamilySearch place data).
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital through 1780); Richmond became the state capital in 1780.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Virginia (British Crown) until 1776; thereafter an independent state under the Virginia General Assembly.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools for 1775-1783. The first federal census (1790) is largely destroyed for Virginia (see Census section below).
- **Economy:** Tobacco agriculture dominated; also grain farming, iron production, and shipbuilding — occupational records can reflect this.
- **Ethnic composition:** English majority; also Scots-Irish and German settlers (particularly in the Shenandoah Valley), and a large enslaved African population. Ethnic background affects which church denomination's records apply.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church through the Disestablishment Act of 1786), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker, Lutheran (German communities in the Valley).
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of independence (1776); British invasion and Yorktown campaign culminating in Cornwallis's surrender (October 1781). The war disrupted county court sessions in some tidewater and piedmont areas.

## Boundary changes
- Kentucky County was created from Virginia in 1776 and became the separate state of Kentucky in 1792 — researchers with ancestors in what is now Kentucky should check both Virginia and Kentucky county records.
- West Virginia did not separate from Virginia until 1863; records for the western counties (present-day West Virginia) during 1775-1783 are Virginia records.
- No historical jurisdictional data was returned by place_search_all for this survey; consult the Library of Virginia for specific county formation dates within the period.

## Available record types

All records for this period are created and held at the **county level** in Virginia; Virginia had no statewide civil registration system during 1775-1783.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Virginia had no statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during 1775-1783. The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records directly to confirm when statewide registration began.
- **What exists for this period:** County marriage bonds and minister's returns at the county courthouse; church baptism, marriage, and burial registers. FamilySearch collection 1734285 ("Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900"; 2,567,890 records) includes marriage records.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (marriage bonds, originals); Library of Virginia (microfilm); FamilySearch (collections 1598230 and 1734285 online).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (vestry system with tithe lists), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker, Lutheran.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes, tithe lists (annual household-head enumeration), and parish poor-relief records. Anglican vestry tithe books name every taxable household head and are invaluable for this period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598230 ("Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929"; 1,234,567 records) covers 1680-1929. Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives (Richmond) holds vestry books not yet digitized. Quaker monthly meeting records are at Swarthmore College and Haverford College.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was 1790, just after the war period. Critically, the 1790 Virginia schedules were largely destroyed; reconstructed lists exist but are incomplete. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands), county tax lists from the 1780s are the primary substitute.
- **State enumerations:** Virginia conducted county personal property and land tax enumerations beginning 1782 — the best substitute for the missing 1790 census. FamilySearch volume DGS 005301449 (87 images, 1782-1799) is **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — researchers must use text search rather than name lookup.
- **Access:** DGS 005301449 covers 1782-1799 and is the only census-substitute volume returned by this survey. Tax list collection 1456723 ("Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850"; 456,789 records) is the indexed companion.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate), estate inventories, guardianship records, and county court order books covering a wide range of county business.
- **Date range:** County court records begin from county formation — many Virginia counties date from the 1600s and 1700s, so pre-war and wartime records run continuously.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); FamilySearch collection 2134567 ("Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920"; 1,789,012 records). FamilySearch volume DGS 005301448 (Augusta County court order books, 1775-1795; 158 images) is **61% name-indexed with images** — the only fully indexed volume this survey returned for the war period.
- **Tip:** Wills drafted during 1775-1783 frequently name sons away on military service by name and sometimes unit, providing a direct military connection.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is not a rectangular-survey state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial land grants were issued by the Crown through the Virginia Land Office; after 1776, Virginia issued patents through the state Land Office. Veterans received bounty land warrants entitling them to tracts in the Virginia Military District of Ohio (post-war).
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, bounty land warrants (DGS 005301447 — see below), and mortgages. Collection 1734285 covers land records 1600-1900.
- **Where held:** County recorder of deeds (deed books); Library of Virginia (state land patent books, bounty warrant records). FamilySearch volume DGS 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779-1800; 341 images) is **browse-only** — no name index, no full-text search; must be examined image by image.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783). Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War), Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony.
- **Record types:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls — NARA Record Group 93 (Washington D.C. / College Park); accessible via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)
  - Virginia militia records — Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files — NARA Record Group 15; accessible via Fold3
  - Revolutionary War land bounty warrants — FamilySearch DGS 005301447 (browse-only, 341 images, 1779-1800)
  - Virginia State Navy records — Library of Virginia
  - FamilySearch collection 1945678 ("Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783"; 345,678 records) covers the war period directly
- **Where held:** NARA (service records, pensions); Library of Virginia (militia, navy); Fold3 online for NARA holdings.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Colonial-era Anglican churchyard cemeteries are present throughout the state, often adjacent to surviving parish churches. Many predate the Revolution.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides headstone photographs and transcriptions for many Virginia cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Vestry and sexton burial records are held at individual parishes and the Library of Virginia; many have not been digitized.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) and its successor publications were the primary colonial Virginia newspapers and carried military news, estate sale notices, loyalist/patriot commentary, and legal announcements during 1775-1783.
- **Where held:** Microfilm at major Virginia research libraries; some issues digitized at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/).

Virginia during the Revolutionary War (1775-1783) is one of the best-documented colonies for this period, with records held at the county level throughout. The most important sources for military-connected families are the Continental Line service records and pension files at the National Archives (accessible through Fold3), Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia in Richmond, and the county personal property and land tax lists starting in 1782 — the last being critical because the 1790 federal census for Virginia was largely destroyed and does not exist for most of the state. ## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** Virginia was a British colony that declared independence in 1776; it was recognized as a state by the Treaty of Paris (1783) and formally admitted to the Union in 1788 (per FamilySearch place data).
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital through 1780); Richmond became the state capital in 1780.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Virginia (British Crown) until 1776; thereafter an independent state under the Virginia General Assembly.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools for 1775-1783. The first federal census (1790) is largely destroyed for Virginia (see Census section below).
- **Economy:** Tobacco agriculture dominated; also grain farming, iron production, and shipbuilding — occupational records can reflect this.
- **Ethnic composition:** English majority; also Scots-Irish and German settlers (particularly in the Shenandoah Valley), and a large enslaved African population. Ethnic background affects which church denomination's records apply.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church through the Disestablishment Act of 1786), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker, Lutheran (German communities in the Valley).
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of independence (1776); British invasion and Yorktown campaign culminating in Cornwallis's surrender (October 1781). The war disrupted county court sessions in some tidewater and piedmont areas.

## Boundary changes
- Kentucky County was created from Virginia in 1776 and became the separate state of Kentucky in 1792 — researchers with ancestors in what is now Kentucky should check both Virginia and Kentucky county records.
- West Virginia did not separate from Virginia until 1863; records for the western counties (present-day West Virginia) during 1775-1783 are Virginia records.
- No historical jurisdictional data was returned by place_search_all for this survey; consult the Library of Virginia for specific county formation dates within the period.

The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records directly to confirm when statewide registration began.
- **What exists for this period:** County marriage bonds and minister's returns at the county courthouse; church baptism, marriage, and burial registers. FamilySearch collection 1734285 ("Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900"; 2,567,890 records) includes marriage records.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (marriage bonds, originals); Library of Virginia (microfilm); FamilySearch (collections 1598230 and 1734285 online).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (vestry system with tithe lists), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker, Lutheran.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes, tithe lists (annual household-head enumeration), and parish poor-relief records. Anglican vestry tithe books name every taxable household head and are invaluable for this period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598230 ("Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929"; 1,234,567 records) covers 1680-1929. Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives (Richmond) holds vestry books not yet digitized. Quaker monthly meeting records are at Swarthmore College and Haverford College.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was 1790, just after the war period. Critically, the 1790 Virginia schedules were largely destroyed; reconstructed lists exist but are incomplete. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands), county tax lists from the 1780s are the primary substitute.
- **State enumerations:** Virginia conducted county personal property and land tax enumerations beginning 1782 — the best substitute for the missing 1790 census. ### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate), estate inventories, guardianship records, and county court order books covering a wide range of county business.
- **Date range:** County court records begin from county formation — many Virginia counties date from the 1600s and 1700s, so pre-war and wartime records run continuously.

Here is the locality guide's response on New Orleans early 1800s records:

---

**New Orleans, Early 1800s — What Survived Disasters and Where to Look**

New Orleans presents a layered records situation shaped directly by its disaster history. Two key facts frame everything:

1. **The city fires of 1788 and 1794** destroyed most French colonial-era records *before* the early 1800s even begin, so gaps in the earliest records are often fire-losses, not missing digitization.
2. Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods continued damaging archives throughout the 19th century.

---

### What Survived — and Where to Find It

**Sacramental Registers (St. Louis Cathedral)**
- Survived from 1731 (with some gaps)
- Available on FamilySearch: *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (Collection 1612905) — name-indexed with images
- These are the closest substitute for civil vital records in this period

**Notarial Acts — The Most Important Substitute Source**
- Because Louisiana uses **civil law**, nearly every major life event (marriage contracts, property sales, wills, manumissions of enslaved persons) was recorded by a notary
- Held at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — over 30 million pages dating to 1734
- FamilySearch has digitized only one browse-only volume (1803–1820, 167 images, not name-indexed), so most of this collection requires an in-person or online portal visit to the Notarial Archives

**Cabildo Records (Spanish Colonial Governing Body, 1769–1803)**
- Survived the fires; held at the **Louisiana State Museum** and **Louisiana State Archives**

**Probate / Succession Records**
- FamilySearch: *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* (Collection 2078341) — name-indexed
- **Important vocabulary note:** Because of Louisiana's civil law system, search for "successions," "tutorships," and "interdictions" — not common-law probate terms

---

### For African-Descended Ancestors
- Separate sacramental registers were kept by Catholic churches — these must be sought explicitly
- **Manumission records** in the notarial acts are another critical source

---

### Starting Points on the FamilySearch Wiki
- [Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy)
- [New Orleans Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy)

---

The locality guide has been saved to your project (as **loc_001**). The recommended next step is to build a research plan using this guide as a foundation, or to begin searching within the specific surviving collections identified above.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by the French in 1718. It passed to Spanish control around 1763, briefly returned to France, then came under U.S. authority with the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. Orleans Territory was organized in 1804; Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish; State of Louisiana (from 1812); Orleans Territory (1804–1812)
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by the tools for this place.
- **Economy:** Major port city; sugar and cotton trade; Mississippi River commerce; significant slave market — the record-keeping environment reflects an economy built on enslaved labor and river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Creole (French, Spanish, African descent), Anglo-American, free people of color, enslaved people, Irish and German immigrants (particularly from the 1830s onward) — a multiracial, multilingual population that shaped both the languages of records and the categories in which people were recorded
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic predominant (St. Louis Cathedral established 1727); Protestant denominations present from early 1800s; Jewish community also present
- **Key historical events:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records (predating the target period but explaining major gaps); repeated yellow fever epidemics (including severe outbreaks in 1817, 1819, 1822, 1832, 1833, 1847, and 1853); hurricanes and Mississippi River floods further damaged archival holdings [Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans]

## Boundary changes
- Under France 1718–1763; under Spain 1763–1800; brief return to France 1800–1803; U.S. territory from the Louisiana Purchase (1803); Orleans Territory 1804–1812; State of Louisiana from 1812.
- Louisiana uses **parishes** rather than counties — a legacy of French and Spanish civil law. Orleans Parish is the civil jurisdiction equivalent to a county elsewhere.
- Records created before 1803 are in French or Spanish; early American-period records (1803–ca. 1820) frequently appear in French, English, and sometimes Spanish.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — no specific civil registration start date for births, marriages, or deaths could be confirmed from tool results. The Louisiana Statewide Death Index (FamilySearch collection 1543892) begins in 1819, indicating some form of death recording began by then, but the level (parish, territorial, or state) is not confirmed by any tool result.
- **What exists:** For the early 1800s, the functional equivalent of civil vital records are the sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral and other Catholic churches, which recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials. FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925) covers this period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collection 1612905); Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed many pre-1800 records; sacramental registers survive from 1731 with gaps [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]. The FamilySearch Wiki page on Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content and gave no specific start date.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; notarial acts (marriage contracts, baptismal references); Cabildo records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant); St. Louis Cathedral (established 1727) with sacramental registers from 1731 (with gaps)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925) is name-indexed with images. African-descended ancestors require separate series: Catholic churches in New Orleans maintained registers for enslaved people and free people of color separately from white parishioners.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1612905 (indexed + images); originals at the Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans (in-person access)
- **Language:** Records from the early 1800s are frequently in French or Latin; researchers must be able to read these languages or obtain translations

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census records for Orleans Parish are available from 1810 onward (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860). No specific New Orleans census collection was returned by tools; U.S. federal census records for Louisiana are accessible on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.
- **State/provincial census:** No Louisiana state census information was returned by any FamilySearch Wiki page during this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding the census.
- **Access:** Federal census years 1810–1860 are name-indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com; images available on both platforms

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana's civil law system calls probate records "successions" (not wills and estates). Unique Louisiana record types: successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship of minors), and interdictions (incapacitation). These are filed in civil district courts, not county probate courts as in other U.S. states [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System].
- **Testate or intestate:** Whether the deceased left a will (testate, leading to a succession with a testament) or died without one (intestate, leading to a succession without a testament) determines which sub-series to search within the successions records.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984) covers this period and is name-indexed with images.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2078341; originals at Louisiana State Archives and Orleans Parish Civil District Court

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French arpent system (long lots along waterways) rather than the U.S. rectangular survey. Some metes-and-bounds descriptions appear in Spanish-era grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pre-1803 grants came from French or Spanish colonial authorities. After 1803, U.S. federal land patents applied. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Land and Property returned only generic content — the specific land office and grant series were not confirmed by any tool result.
- **Types:** Notarial acts are the primary vehicle for land conveyances in Louisiana — they document every sale, mortgage, and transfer. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]. FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume of Orleans Parish Notarial Acts 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, browse-only).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical; limited online portal); FamilySearch image group 004990115 (browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and English)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Mexican War (1846–1848); early Louisiana state militia service
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; militia rosters
- **Where held:** NARA (service and pension records); state adjutant general records at Louisiana State Archives; Fold3.com (https://www.fold3.com) for military records online

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (established 1789, above-ground tombs characteristic of New Orleans); St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (established 1823); Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (established 1833, Garden District). Protestant and Jewish cemeteries are also present.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has cemetery listings for New Orleans
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held at the Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans; in-person access required

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (founded 1804), Le Courrier de la Louisiane (French-language), the New Orleans Bee/L'Abeille (bilingual, from 1827), and others were published during this period.
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription); Louisiana State Library and Tulane University hold microfilm; some holdings at the New Orleans Public Library
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, sheriff's sale notices, estate auction notices, succession notices (probate required public posting), and immigration/arrival notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the United States by the mid-1800s, accessible by sea via the Gulf of Mexico and by river up the Mississippi.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA Series M259 covers New Orleans arrivals 1820–1902); naturalization records filed in local civil courts (pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record); declarations of intention and first/second papers in district court records
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov, https://www.archives.gov); Ancestry.com holds New Orleans passenger lists (subscription); FamilySearch has some coverage via general immigration collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed alongside adults.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax (real and personal property) assessed annually at the parish level
- **Date range:** Tax records survive from the territorial period (1804 onward) and earlier under Spanish administration
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; some records at New Orleans City Archives
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for missing census years; confirms presence in New Orleans when other records are silent

### Other record types
**Notarial records (unique to Louisiana):** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734. Notarial acts cover property sales, marriage contracts, manumissions (freeing of enslaved people), apprenticeships, business partnerships, wills, and more — they are a primary research source with no equivalent in common-law states [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]. FamilySearch holds only 1 browse-only volume for 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and English).

**Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body):** The Cabildo records cover Spanish colonial New Orleans (1769–1803) and some early American-period material. They survived the 1788 and 1794 fires and are held at the Louisiana State Museum / Louisiana State Archives. These records name individuals in court proceedings, land grants, and administrative matters.

**Sacramental records of enslaved and free people of color:** St. Louis Cathedral and other New Orleans Catholic churches kept separate sacramental registers for enslaved people and free people of color. These are included for some periods in FamilySearch collection 1612905. Researchers with African-descended New Orleans ancestors must specifically seek these series.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (col. 1612905); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (col. 1543892); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (col. 2078341); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (col. 1798054); Notarial Acts 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | New Orleans passenger lists; U.S. federal census; various Louisiana collections | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery listings for New Orleans cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Louisiana newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists; federal records | Free / in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching New Orleans for the period queried (Notarial Acts 1803–1820, image group 004990115, 167 images, browse-only). This was the complete result set for that query. The tool resolved the search to a narrower date range (1803–1820) than the full 1800–1860 target; volumes covering 1820–1860 may require a broader or re-run search.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; limited online portal |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records; succession/probate records; territorial census; tax records; Cabildo records | In-person; some records via Louisiana Secretary of State online |
| Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans | Sacramental registers of Catholic parishes; cemetery/sexton records | In-person by appointment |
| Louisiana State Museum (Cabildo) | Cabildo records from Spanish colonial through early American period | In-person |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Historical newspapers; local historical and family records | In-person |
| New Orleans Public Library (Louisiana Division) | City directories; newspapers on microfilm; local records | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- The vast majority of the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center's 30+ million pages of notarial acts are not fully online — the single FamilySearch volume (image group 004990115) covers only 1803–1820 with 167 browse-only images.
- Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body, 1769–1803) held at the Louisiana State Museum must be accessed in person or through the Louisiana State Archives.
- Sacramental registers for enslaved people and free people of color not captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905 must be sought at the Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans in person.
- City and parish tax assessment records from the early 1800s must be accessed at the Louisiana State Archives or New Orleans City Archives.
- Most early 19th-century Orleans Parish Civil District Court minute books and case files are physical only at the Orleans Parish Civil District Court or Louisiana State Archives.

## Known record losses

The FamilySearch Wiki states that New Orleans suffered catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 that destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 with gaps caused by those fires [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]. Wikipedia confirms that yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and Mississippi River floods further damaged archival holdings across the 19th century [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans].

The fate of specific individual record series beyond what the FamilySearch Wiki and Wikipedia named was not confirmed by any tool result in this survey. An empty search result for a given year or series is a coverage gap, not confirmation of destruction. Researchers should contact the Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) and the Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans directly to confirm the current status of specific series before concluding they are lost.

**What survived and where copies or substitutes are held:**
- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with fire-gap losses): FamilySearch collection 1612905; originals at Archdiocesan Archives
- **Notarial acts** (marriage contracts, property sales, wills, manumissions, etc., from 1734): New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; FamilySearch image group 004990115 covers 1803–1820 only (browse-only)
- **Cabildo records** (Spanish colonial governing body, 1769–1803): Louisiana State Museum / Louisiana State Archives
- **Federal census** (from 1810): Substitutes for missing parish-level population records
- **Tax records** (from the territorial period): Louisiana State Archives — substitute for missing census years
- **Succession records** (probate/successions from 1756 in FamilySearch collection 2078341): Document family relationships even when vital records are absent

## Research tips
- **Use Louisiana's civil law vocabulary.** When searching the Louisiana State Archives and FamilySearch collection 2078341, search for "successions" not "wills"; "tutorships" not "guardianships"; "interdictions" not "incompetency proceedings." The civil law terminology is not interchangeable with common-law terms and will affect search results [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System].
- **Treat notarial acts as your first substitute source when other records are destroyed.** When vital records or church registers are missing due to the 1788 and 1794 fires or later disasters, the notarial acts document the same life events — marriage contracts instead of marriage registers, testaments instead of probate abstracts, manumissions instead of birth records for freed people. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is the primary repository; FamilySearch image group 004990115 covers only 1803–1820 and must be browsed image by image with no search function [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters].
- **Do not assume pre-1800 records are absent.** The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 despite the fires — the gaps are documented but not total. Always check the surviving portions of the register before concluding a person is unrecorded.
- **Records before 1803 are in French or Spanish; early American-period records are frequently in French.** FamilySearch's single notarial acts volume (image group 004990115) is in French and English. Researchers must read these languages or obtain translations.
- **For African-descended ancestors, seek the separate series.** Catholic churches in New Orleans kept sacramental registers for enslaved people and free people of color separately from white parishioners. Manumission records in the notarial acts name the enslaved person and the enslaver. The Cabildo records also document the free people of color community in the Spanish colonial period.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages** for Louisiana and New Orleans returned only generic content during this survey. Consult the following pages directly before relying on any absence: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy — those pages may contain current guidance not surfaced in this tool run.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by the French in 1718. It passed to Spanish control around 1763, briefly returned to France, then came under U.S. authority with the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. Orleans Territory was organized in 1804; Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish; State of Louisiana (from 1812); Orleans Territory (1804–1812)
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by the tools for this place.
- **Economy:** Major port city; sugar and cotton trade; Mississippi River commerce; significant slave market — the record-keeping environment reflects an economy built on enslaved labor and river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Creole (French, Spanish, African descent), Anglo-American, free people of color, enslaved people, Irish and German immigrants (particularly from the 1830s onward) — a multiracial, multilingual population that shaped both the languages of records and the categories in which people were recorded
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic predominant (St. Louis Cathedral established 1727); Protestant denominations present from early 1800s; Jewish community also present
- **Key historical events:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records (predating the target period but explaining major gaps); repeated yellow fever epidemics (including severe outbreaks in 1817, 1819, 1822, 1832, 1833, 1847, and 1853); hurricanes and Mississippi River floods further damaged archival holdings [Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans]

## Boundary changes
- Under France 1718–1763; under Spain 1763–1800; brief return to France 1800–1803; U.S. territory from the Louisiana Purchase (1803); Orleans Territory 1804–1812; State of Louisiana from 1812.
- Louisiana uses **parishes** rather than counties — a legacy of French and Spanish civil law. Orleans Parish is the civil jurisdiction equivalent to a county elsewhere.
- Records created before 1803 are in French or Spanish; early American-period records (1803–ca. 1820) frequently appear in French, English, and sometimes Spanish.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — no specific civil registration start date for births, marriages, or deaths could be confirmed from tool results. The Louisiana Statewide Death Index (FamilySearch collection 1543892) begins in 1819, indicating some form of death recording began by then, but the level (parish, territorial, or state) is not confirmed by any tool result.
- **What exists:** For the early 1800s, the functional equivalent of civil vital records are the sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral and other Catholic churches, which recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials. FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925) covers this period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collection 1612905); Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed many pre-1800 records; sacramental registers survive from 1731 with gaps [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]. The FamilySearch Wiki page on Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content and gave no specific start date.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; notarial acts (marriage contracts, baptismal references); Cabildo records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant); St. Louis Cathedral (established 1727) with sacramental registers from 1731 (with gaps)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925) is name-indexed with images. African-descended ancestors require separate series: Catholic churches in New Orleans maintained registers for enslaved people and free people of color separately from white parishioners.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1612905 (indexed + images); originals at the Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans (in-person access)
- **Language:** Records from the early 1800s are frequently in French or Latin; researchers must be able to read these languages or obtain translations

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census records for Orleans Parish are available from 1810 onward (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860). No specific New Orleans census collection was returned by tools; U.S. federal census records for Louisiana are accessible on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.
- **State/provincial census:** No Louisiana state census information was returned by any FamilySearch Wiki page during this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding the census.
- **Access:** Federal census years 1810–1860 are name-indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com; images available on both platforms

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana's civil law system calls probate records "successions" (not wills and estates). Unique Louisiana record types: successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship of minors), and interdictions (incapacitation). These are filed in civil district courts, not county probate courts as in other U.S. states [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System].
- **Testate or intestate:** Whether the deceased left a will (testate, leading to a succession with a testament) or died without one (intestate, leading to a succession without a testament) determines which sub-series to search within the successions records.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984) covers this period and is name-indexed with images.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2078341; originals at Louisiana State Archives and Orleans Parish Civil District Court

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French arpent system (long lots along waterways) rather than the U.S. rectangular survey. Some metes-and-bounds descriptions appear in Spanish-era grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pre-1803 grants came from French or Spanish colonial authorities. After 1803, U.S. federal land patents applied. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Land and Property returned only generic content — the specific land office and grant series were not confirmed by any tool result.
- **Types:** Notarial acts are the primary vehicle for land conveyances in Louisiana — they document every sale, mortgage, and transfer. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]. FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume of Orleans Parish Notarial Acts 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, browse-only).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical; limited online portal); FamilySearch image group 004990115 (browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and English)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Mexican War (1846–1848); early Louisiana state militia service
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; militia rosters
- **Where held:** NARA (service and pension records); state adjutant general records at Louisiana State Archives; Fold3.com (https://www.fold3.com) for military records online

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (established 1789, above-ground tombs characteristic of New Orleans); St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (established 1823); Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (established 1833, Garden District). Protestant and Jewish cemeteries are also present.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has cemetery listings for New Orleans
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held at the Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans; in-person access required

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (founded 1804), Le Courrier de la Louisiane (French-language), the New Orleans Bee/L'Abeille (bilingual, from 1827), and others were published during this period.
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription); Louisiana State Library and Tulane University hold microfilm; some holdings at the New Orleans Public Library
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, sheriff's sale notices, estate auction notices, succession notices (probate required public posting), and immigration/arrival notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the United States by the mid-1800s, accessible by sea via the Gulf of Mexico and by river up the Mississippi.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA Series M259 covers New Orleans arrivals 1820–1902); naturalization records filed in local civil courts (pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record); declarations of intention and first/second papers in district court records
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov, https://www.archives.gov); Ancestry.com holds New Orleans passenger lists (subscription); FamilySearch has some coverage via general immigration collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed alongside adults.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax (real and personal property) assessed annually at the parish level
- **Date range:** Tax records survive from the territorial period (1804 onward) and earlier under Spanish administration
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; some records at New Orleans City Archives
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for missing census years; confirms presence in New Orleans when other records are silent

### Other record types
**Notarial records (unique to Louisiana):** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734. Notarial acts cover property sales, marriage contracts, manumissions (freeing of enslaved people), apprenticeships, business partnerships, wills, and more — they are a primary research source with no equivalent in common-law states [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]. FamilySearch holds only 1 browse-only volume for 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and English).

**Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body):** The Cabildo records cover Spanish colonial New Orleans (1769–1803) and some early American-period material. They survived the 1788 and 1794 fires and are held at the Louisiana State Museum / Louisiana State Archives. These records name individuals in court proceedings, land grants, and administrative matters.

**Sacramental records of enslaved and free people of color:** St. Louis Cathedral and other New Orleans Catholic churches kept separate sacramental registers for enslaved people and free people of color. These are included for some periods in FamilySearch collection 1612905. Researchers with African-descended New Orleans ancestors must specifically seek these series.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (col. 1612905); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (col. 1543892); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (col. 2078341); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (col. 1798054); Notarial Acts 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | New Orleans passenger lists; U.S. federal census; various Louisiana collections | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery listings for New Orleans cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Louisiana newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists; federal records | Free / in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching New Orleans for the period queried (Notarial Acts 1803–1820, image group 004990115, 167 images, browse-only). This was the complete result set for that query. The tool resolved the search to a narrower date range (1803–1820) than the full 1800–1860 target; volumes covering 1820–1860 may require a broader or re-run search.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; limited online portal |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records; succession/probate records; territorial census; tax records; Cabildo records | In-person; some records via Louisiana Secretary of State online |
| Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans | Sacramental registers of Catholic parishes; cemetery/sexton records | In-person by appointment |
| Louisiana State Museum (Cabildo) | Cabildo records from Spanish colonial through early American period | In-person |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Historical newspapers; local historical and family records | In-person |
| New Orleans Public Library (Louisiana Division) | City directories; newspapers on microfilm; local records | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- The vast majority of the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center's 30+ million pages of notarial acts are not fully online — the single FamilySearch volume (image group 004990115) covers only 1803–1820 with 167 browse-only images.
- Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body, 1769–1803) held at the Louisiana State Museum must be accessed in person or through the Louisiana State Archives.
- Sacramental registers for enslaved people and free people of color not captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905 must be sought at the Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans in person.
- City and parish tax assessment records from the early 1800s must be accessed at the Louisiana State Archives or New Orleans City Archives.
- Most early 19th-century Orleans Parish Civil District Court minute books and case files are physical only at the Orleans Parish Civil District Court or Louisiana State Archives.

## Known record losses

The FamilySearch Wiki states that New Orleans suffered catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 that destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 with gaps caused by those fires [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]. Wikipedia confirms that yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and Mississippi River floods further damaged archival holdings across the 19th century [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans].

The fate of specific individual record series beyond what the FamilySearch Wiki and Wikipedia named was not confirmed by any tool result in this survey. An empty search result for a given year or series is a coverage gap, not confirmation of destruction. Researchers should contact the Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) and the Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans directly to confirm the current status of specific series before concluding they are lost.

**What survived and where copies or substitutes are held:**
- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with fire-gap losses): FamilySearch collection 1612905; originals at Archdiocesan Archives
- **Notarial acts** (marriage contracts, property sales, wills, manumissions, etc., from 1734): New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; FamilySearch image group 004990115 covers 1803–1820 only (browse-only)
- **Cabildo records** (Spanish colonial governing body, 1769–1803): Louisiana State Museum / Louisiana State Archives
- **Federal census** (from 1810): Substitutes for missing parish-level population records
- **Tax records** (from the territorial period): Louisiana State Archives — substitute for missing census years
- **Succession records** (probate/successions from 1756 in FamilySearch collection 2078341): Document family relationships even when vital records are absent

## Research tips
- **Use Louisiana's civil law vocabulary.** When searching the Louisiana State Archives and FamilySearch collection 2078341, search for "successions" not "wills"; "tutorships" not "guardianships"; "interdictions" not "incompetency proceedings." The civil law terminology is not interchangeable with common-law terms and will affect search results [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System].
- **Treat notarial acts as your first substitute source when other records are destroyed.** When vital records or church registers are missing due to the 1788 and 1794 fires or later disasters, the notarial acts document the same life events — marriage contracts instead of marriage registers, testaments instead of probate abstracts, manumissions instead of birth records for freed people. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is the primary repository; FamilySearch image group 004990115 covers only 1803–1820 and must be browsed image by image with no search function [FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters].
- **Do not assume pre-1800 records are absent.** The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 despite the fires — the gaps are documented but not total. Always check the surviving portions of the register before concluding a person is unrecorded.
- **Records before 1803 are in French or Spanish; early American-period records are frequently in French.** FamilySearch's single notarial acts volume (image group 004990115) is in French and English. Researchers must read these languages or obtain translations.
- **For African-descended ancestors, seek the separate series.** Catholic churches in New Orleans kept sacramental registers for enslaved people and free people of color separately from white parishioners. Manumission records in the notarial acts name the enslaved person and the enslaver. The Cabildo records also document the free people of color community in the Spanish colonial period.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages** for Louisiana and New Orleans returned only generic content during this survey. Consult the following pages directly before relying on any absence: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy — those pages may contain current guidance not surfaced in this tool run.
