- **Where held:** County courthouse for 1870–1905 records; FamilySearch for statewide death certificates from 1906
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration before 1906; county-level registration (from 1870) may have gaps and is not fully indexed online
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; census mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880); coroner's inquest records for accidental or violent deaths

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes: Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish — many established from the 1840s onward); German Lutheran and Reformed; Presbyterian; Episcopal; others ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; some parishes also kept records of the poor and recent immigrants
- **Where held:** The Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds many original parish registers; FamilySearch has microfilmed some holdings; individual parishes may still hold their own books
- **Language:** Many ethnic Catholic registers are in Latin or the immigrant community's language (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian) — these require reading the original language

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Allegheny County is covered from 1800; the 1880 and 1900 censuses are especially valuable for steel-era workers — they capture occupation, parents' birthplaces, and (in 1900) year of immigration and years in the United States ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules list people who died in the year preceding the census, including workplace deaths
- **Access:** Federal censuses 1860–1900 are indexed and available on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch; the 1890 census was largely destroyed but an 1890 Veterans Schedule survives

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** Allegheny County probate records date from 1788
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994) holds 3,200,560 browse-only images — must be browsed image by image with no name index; no separate Allegheny County–specific digitized volume was identified in this survey

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Pennsylvania land and property during this survey; the Pennsylvania State Archives holds patent records; county deed books are at the Allegheny County recorder of deeds
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax assessment records
- **Where held:** Allegheny County recorder of deeds (in-person/mail); Pennsylvania State Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and Civil War draft records at NARA (also on Fold3); the 1890 Veterans Schedule lists veterans by county
- **Where held:** National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides volunteer-submitted transcriptions for Pittsburgh-area cemeteries including Allegheny Cemetery and many ethnic Catholic parish cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual cemeteries and parishes; the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds some burial registers

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had multiple daily papers during the steel era; editions are accessible via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/)
- **Content value:** Obituaries frequently name the employer and length of service; labor news, accident reports, and Homestead Strike coverage document the industrial community; legal notices supplement probate records

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most European immigrants arrived through New York (Castle Garden before 1892, Ellis Island from 1892) and Baltimore
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (indexed on Ancestry.com); naturalization records from the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas (1798–1930) are at the National Archives at Philadelphia; FamilySearch holds a partially indexed volume of Pennsylvania Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 15% name-indexed, browse-only otherwise)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Post-1906 naturalizations:** After September 1906 naturalizations were handled by federal courts and are at NARA; the petition form added significantly more family detail

### Tax records
- **Types:** County tax assessment lists (property tax, personal property)
- **Date range:** Assessment records predate 1860 and continue through the period
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse; Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for the largely destroyed 1890 census and help trace individuals between census years

### Other record types — Occupational and industrial sources
- **City directories:** Pittsburgh city directories begin in 1813 and are held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh; they list individuals by name, occupation, and street address — essential for tracking workers between census years and pinning addresses for church-record searches. Ancestry.com carries many digitized Pittsburgh directories.
- **Company records:** The Senator John Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) houses records of Carnegie Steel and other major industrial firms, including employment ledgers, payroll books, and accident reports. Physical access — contact the Heinz History Center directly.
- **Union records:** Labor union membership records (for trade unions including the Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel, and Tin Workers) may be held by union locals, the Pennsylvania State Archives, or the Heinz History Center; they document member rosters and benefit claims.
- **Coroner's records:** Workplace accidents were common in steel mills. Allegheny County coroner inquest records name the deceased, employer, witnesses, and cause of death; held at the Allegheny County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Pension and benefit records:** Company-sponsored benefit societies (e.g., the Carnegie Relief Fund) generated membership and payment records held in company archives at the Heinz History Center.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 (524,189 records, indexed, coll. 1921317); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records, indexed, coll. 1571957); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 records, indexed, no images, coll. 1502909); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M browse-only images, coll. 1999196); Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M indexed records, coll. 2255317); Pennsylvania Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (15% indexed, vol. 008120443) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census 1860–1910; Pittsburgh city directories; passenger arrival lists | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| FindAGrave | Pittsburgh-area cemetery transcriptions | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Pittsburgh historical newspapers | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Fold3 | Military service, pension, and draft records | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| NARA | Federal records including pre- and post-1906 naturalizations and military | In-person / online request (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes for Pennsylvania covering 1860–1910; this is the complete result set (complete: true). Neither volume_search nor collections_search returned Allegheny County–specific volumes — the Pennsylvania-level results represent a coverage gap for county-specific holdings, which may exist in the FamilySearch Catalog or physical repositories.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Marriage licenses (1885+), deed books, court and probate records, coroner inquests | In-person / mail |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories (1813+), local history collections | In-person |
| Senator John Heinz History Center | Company records (Carnegie Steel, etc.), immigration records, union records | In-person; contact for access |
| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Ethnic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) | Contact Diocese for access |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Allegheny County naturalization records 1798–1930 | In-person / written request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | State vital records (from 1906), land records, tax records, military records | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online
- Company employment ledgers, payroll books, and accident reports (Heinz History Center — physical access only)
- Union membership rosters (various repositories — physical access)
- Allegheny County coroner inquest records (county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives — physical access)
- County-level birth and death registrations (1870–1905) — not confirmed to be fully indexed or digitized online
- Catholic ethnic parish registers in original form (Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives — physical access; some microfilmed by FamilySearch)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified specific record losses for Allegheny County. The absence of Allegheny County–specific digitized volumes in volume_search is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction. The county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives should be contacted to confirm the completeness of coroner and county vital record holdings.

## Research tips
- The 1880 and 1900 federal censuses are the top starting points for steel-era workers: they record occupation, parents' birthplaces, and — in 1900 — year of immigration and years in the United States ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- County-level birth and death registration began in 1870, predating the statewide mandate of 1906 — do not assume records are absent before 1906 ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))
- Pittsburgh city directories (Carnegie Library; Ancestry.com) are the best tool for pinning a worker's exact street address between census years — use that address to identify the neighborhood parish and then search its registers
- Many steel-era families are documented exclusively in ethnic church registers written in non-English languages — identify the congregation by the worker's nationality before searching general Catholic records
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; begin with the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas (1798–1930) at the National Archives at Philadelphia ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- The Senator John Heinz History Center is the single most important repository for occupational and industrial documentation — contact them for employment, payroll, benefit-society, and union records before concluding a worker cannot be traced

Here is what the locality guide found:

---

**Philadelphia, 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic — Records & Repositories**

Philadelphia in 1793 had no civil vital registration — Pennsylvania did not require statewide registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906 — so tracing families affected by the yellow fever epidemic depends almost entirely on church burial registers and a handful of unique epidemic-era sources.

### Primary Epidemic-Era Sources (Named Individuals)
- **Mathew Carey's published account** listing the dead — held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)
- **Minutes of the citizen relief Committee** — Philadelphia City Archives / HSP
- **Bush Hill hospital records** — Philadelphia City Archives / HSP

These three sources are the most direct route to individuals who died or were treated during the outbreak.

### Bracketing the Epidemic with Census & Tax Records
- **1790 federal census** (3 years before) and **1800 federal census** (7 years after) reveal household changes attributable to the epidemic
- **Philadelphia county tax lists** and **city directories** fill the gap years in between (available at HSP and on Ancestry/FamilySearch)

### Estates & Orphan Court
- **Pennsylvania Probate Records (1683–1994)** — a surge of estate filings in 1793 and orphan-court guardianship filings in 1793–1796 can reveal which family members survived. FamilySearch has 3.2 million browse-only images for this collection.

### Church Burial Registers
- **Christ Church** and **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes')** are the core death-documentation sources for the period
- The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia-area church registers, held at HSP

### FamilySearch Digitized Volumes
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750–1800)** — 145 digitized images covering Quaker records, requiring image-by-image browsing

---

If you'd like a full sequenced research plan — which sources to search in what order for a specific family — just say so and the research-plan step can be run next.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 — Yellow Fever Epidemic Context; Survey Window 1780–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1682 by William Penn; both the city and county share the same geographic footprint in this period
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county co-extensive)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793 (Wikipedia: "Yellow fever epidemic of 1793"); no specific figure returned by place_population tool
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port; commercial, merchant, and artisan trades; printing and publishing
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American majority; significant German, Scots-Irish, and free Black communities; diverse immigrant port population
- **Religious denominations:** Quaker, Episcopal (Anglican), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Baptist, Catholic, Jewish, and African Methodist Episcopal congregations all present by 1793
- **Key historical events:** The 1793 yellow fever epidemic struck August–November 1793, killing approximately 5,000 of Philadelphia's 50,000 residents (roughly one-tenth of the population). Philadelphia was the national capital until 1800. The Revolutionary War period (1775–1783) immediately precedes the survey window.

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County was established 1682 and its boundaries were stable throughout the 1780–1810 period.
- The City of Philadelphia and Philadelphia County were co-extensive in 1793; consolidation was formally accomplished in 1854 but the practical overlap was already in place earlier. Records may appear under either label — search both.
- No predecessor jurisdiction issues: Philadelphia is an original Pennsylvania county.

## Available record types

**Critical note for 1793:** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil vital registration in 1793. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection (FamilySearch id 2255317) begins in 1906, which is when statewide death registration is first evidenced in FamilySearch holdings. For 1793, church records and epidemic-specific published sources are the only contemporaneous documentation of births, marriages, and deaths.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed in Pennsylvania at the state level in 1793. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection (id 2255317) begins 1906; no county-level civil registration collection for this period was returned by collections_search. The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania_Vital_Records page returned only generic fallback content during this survey — visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records directly for the confirmed start dates at each level.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for 1793.
- **Gaps:** The entire period 1793 (and the surrounding decades) predates Pennsylvania civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (see Church records below); the 1793 epidemic-specific sources (see below); probate records for deaths; newspaper death notices.

### 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic — Specialty Sources
These sources are unique to the epidemic and directly name individuals who died or were aided:
- **Mathew Carey's published account (1793):** A near-contemporaneous narrative listing names of the dead and relief recipients. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793), this is a key genealogical source. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and many major research libraries; digitized copies exist online.

Here is the locality guide for Chicago families affected by the Great Fire of 1871:

---

**Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire of 1871**

Chicago in 1871 sits at the center of one of genealogy's most significant record-loss events. The **Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871** burned through the Cook County Courthouse, destroying deeds, birth and death registers, court records, probate files, and tax rolls for the entire city's prior history. The good news is that several key sources survived, and specific repositories were built to compensate for that loss:

### Surviving & Reconstructed Record Sources

- **1870 Federal Census** — Originals were safely held in Washington, D.C. This is your most important pre-fire snapshot of Chicago households.
- **City Directories (1840s onward)** — Held at the **Newberry Library**, these can place families in Chicago before, during, and after the fire.
- **Insurance & Title Records** — The **Chicago Title and Trust Company** records are now at the **Chicago History Museum**, and can help trace property ownership and household locations.
- **Church Registers** — Congregations whose buildings were outside the burn zone preserved their registers. These can document births, marriages, and deaths.
- **Burnt Record Act of 1872** — Illinois law allowed property owners to re-record lost deeds. Post-fire property re-recordings survive and can substitute for destroyed deeds.

### FamilySearch Collections

FamilySearch holds indexed collections beginning in 1871:
- **Birth certificates** — ~1.45 million records
- **Death records** — ~980,000 records
- **Marriage records** — ~620,000 records
- **Church records** — ~285,000 records

Additionally, FamilySearch has digitized browse-only/partially indexed volumes covering reconstructed pre-fire court records.

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **Newberry Library (Chicago)** | City directories, newspapers, local histories |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Title records, photographs, local archives |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD)** | Post-fire Cook County court and vital records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indexed vital and church records from 1871 onward |
| **National Archives (Great Lakes Region)** | Federal census, naturalization, and military records |

### Best Starting Point

The **FamilySearch Wiki page for Cook County, Illinois** is the richest online narrative guide:
👉 https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy

---

**Recommended next step:** A research plan targeting Chicago ca. 1871 can sequence these repositories — starting with the 1870 federal census to establish the household pre-fire, then city directories and church registers, then post-fire vital records to pick up the family afterward.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (c. 1860–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837 (formal formation dates not returned by place-search tools — Wikipedia confirms the city's existence by the time of the 1871 fire)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois
- **Population during period:** The 1871 fire left more than 100,000 residents homeless, indicating a major urban center (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire). The place_population tool returned no data for this location.
- **Economy:** Major Midwestern commercial and transportation hub — rail terminus, meatpacking, lumber, grain trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Large immigrant population including Irish, German, Scandinavian, and other European groups — important for identifying records in multiple languages and across church denominations
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant among Irish and German immigrants), Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, and many others
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left 100,000+ homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with the bulk of the city's civil records (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were stable during the 1860–1880 period. No jurisdictional splits during this window affect record-holding.
- The defining event for record access is not a boundary change but a records-destruction event: the Great Chicago Fire of October 1871 eliminated most civil records generated before that date.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Illinois Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — no specific registration level or start year could be confirmed from tool results. Cook County collections on FamilySearch begin in 1871 for births, deaths, and marriages, almost certainly because pre-fire records were destroyed rather than because registration began that year.
- **What exists (post-fire):** FamilySearch holds Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records; collection ID 2024189); Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947 (980,000 records; collection ID 1913456); Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920 (620,000 records; collection ID 1756321). All three are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch (collections_search result, scope: Illinois).
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 vital records are almost entirely absent through civil sources — they were destroyed in the fire. No county-level civil vital records survive from before October 8, 1871.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the primary substitute for pre-fire vital events. The federal census (1850, 1860, 1870) names household members and can establish approximate birth years and places of origin.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, and many others serving the large immigrant population
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 (285,000 records; collection ID 1803978). Catholic parish registers are held at the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories). Some church registers survived the fire; others were destroyed with the rest of the courthouse district.
- **Language:** Many early records are in German, Norwegian, or other immigrant languages depending on the congregation.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, and 1870 are all available. The 1870 federal census for Chicago survived the Great Fire because originals were held in Washington, D.C. — it is the single most reliable pre-fire source for household composition (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The 1880 census covers the post-fire period. Both are indexed and searchable.
- **State census:** Illinois conducted state censuses — the 1865 and 1885 schedules fall within or near the target period and can fill intercensal gaps.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding each census and serve as a substitute for missing death records.
- **Access:** Federal census years (1870, 1880) are indexed and searchable via Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, court suits
- **Date range:** Pre-fire probate and court records were largely destroyed in 1871. Post-1871 records survive.
- **Where held:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University holds Cook County records post-1871 (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories). FamilySearch has digitized one volume of pre-fire reconstructed court records (DGS 009982110: 38 images, 1865–1871) — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image**.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Illinois is a public land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal land patents filed at the General Land Office — available via the BLM GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov/)
- **Types:** Pre-fire deeds were destroyed in the courthouse fire. The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds. FamilySearch holds a partially indexed volume of post-fire property re-recordings (DGS 009982111: 112 images, 1871–1880, 41% name-indexed — searchable by name for roughly half the volume; the remaining images must be browsed individually).
- **Pre-fire substitute:** Insurance company records, particularly the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection held at the Chicago History Museum, are the primary substitute for pre-fire property ownership (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (post-fire originals); IRAD at NEIU; Chicago History Museum (insurance/title records); BLM GLO for federal patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) is the primary conflict for this period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, Civil War draft registrations (1863). These federal records were held in Washington, D.C. and were NOT destroyed in the Chicago fire.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA: https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Several historic Chicago cemeteries date to this period. Specific cemetery names were not confirmed by a tool result in this survey — consult the Chicago History Museum or Newberry Library for cemetery directories.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has extensive Chicago-area coverage.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual cemeteries and potentially at the Chicago History Museum.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago had active newspapers before and after the fire. Some pre-fire papers survived because their offices were outside the burned district; post-fire coverage extensively documented the disaster and its aftermath, including lists of survivors and displaced families.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Chicago newspaper collections. The Newberry Library holds Chicago newspapers on microfilm (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, fire-era casualty and survivor lists (fall 1871), legal notices, property recovery filings under the Burnt Record Act.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is an inland city. Primary ports of entry for families arriving by 1870 were New York, Baltimore, New Orleans, and other coastal ports.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (held by NARA in Washington — unaffected by the fire); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (pre-1906 filed in any court of record; Cook County court naturalizations were largely destroyed in 1871 — also check state and federal courts and neighboring county courts). Alien registrations are a 20th-century record type.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for passenger lists and federal naturalization records. FamilySearch and Ancestry for digitized arrivals.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest page for all family members when researching a family's arrival.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and personal property tax rolls
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls were in the Cook County Courthouse and were destroyed in 1871. Post-fire tax records survive.
- **Where held:** Post-fire tax records at the Cook County Assessor and IRAD at NEIU.
- **Substitute value:** City directories (Newberry Library, 1840s onward) serve as a substitute for missing tax and census years, confirming residence and occupation between enumerations.

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Available from the 1840s onward, held at the Newberry Library (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). These are the primary substitute for any pre-fire civil record — they list heads of household with occupation and street address.
- **Insurance and title records:** The Chicago History Museum holds the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection, the leading source for pre-fire property ownership.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000); Birth Certs 1871–1940 (1,450,000); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000); 2 digitized volumes: browse-only pre-fire court records (DGS 009982110) and partially indexed post-fire property re-recordings (DGS 009982111) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (all years including 1870 and 1880) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Chicago newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records, Civil War pension files | Subscription |
| NARA | Passenger lists, federal court records, military records (unaffected by fire) | Free in-person; some online via Fold3/Ancestry |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 matching digitized volumes for Cook County 1850–1890, which is the complete result set (totalResults: 2). The 4 FamilySearch collections shown are the complete collections_search results for Cook County (scope: Illinois, 4 collections). Holdings not indexed or digitized by FamilySearch are not represented in these counts.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library (Chicago) | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, newspaper microfilm | In-person; some digitized online |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance/title records, photographs, personal papers | In-person; contact museum for access |
| IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County records post-1871 (court, probate, land) | In-person; contact IRAD |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives for access |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person / mail request |
| NARA (Chicago regional / Washington, D.C.) | Federal records: military, passenger lists, naturalizations | In-person / online finding aids |

## Records NOT online

- Pre-fire (pre-October 1871) deeds, probate files, tax rolls, and court records: largely destroyed in the fire; limited reconstructed copies exist at IRAD and Chicago History Museum but are not fully digitized
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records at the Chicago History Museum: physical access required
- Catholic parish registers not yet in the FamilySearch Church Records collection: contact the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives
- City directories at the Newberry Library (1840s onward): in-person or microfilm access
- Sexton and burial registers for individual cemeteries: contact each cemetery directly

## Known record losses

The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse. According to Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), the fire destroyed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls held in the courthouse. The FamilySearch Wiki's Cook County, Illinois Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) confirms the courthouse loss also eliminated most probate files and many church registers. # Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (c. 1860–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837 (formal formation dates not returned by place-search tools — Wikipedia confirms the city's existence by the time of the 1871 fire)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois
- **Population during period:** The 1871 fire left more than 100,000 residents homeless, indicating a major urban center (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire). The place_population tool returned no data for this location.
- **Economy:** Major Midwestern commercial and transportation hub — rail terminus, meatpacking, lumber, grain trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Large immigrant population including Irish, German, Scandinavian, and other European groups — important for identifying records in multiple languages and across church denominations
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant among Irish and German immigrants), Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, and many others
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left 100,000+ homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with the bulk of the city's civil records (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were stable during the 1860–1880 period. No jurisdictional splits during this window affect record-holding.
- The defining event for record access is not a boundary change but a records-destruction event: the Great Chicago Fire of October 1871 eliminated most civil records generated before that date.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Illinois Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — no specific registration level or start year could be confirmed from tool results. Cook County collections on FamilySearch begin in 1871 for births, deaths, and marriages, almost certainly because pre-fire records were destroyed rather than because registration began that year.
- **What exists (post-fire):** FamilySearch holds Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records; collection ID 2024189); Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947 (980,000 records; collection ID 1913456); Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920 (620,000 records; collection ID 1756321). All three are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch (collections_search result, scope: Illinois).
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 vital records are almost entirely absent through civil sources — they were destroyed in the fire. No county-level civil vital records survive from before October 8, 1871.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the primary substitute for pre-fire vital events. The federal census (1850, 1860, 1870) names household members and can establish approximate birth years and places of origin.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, and many others serving the large immigrant population
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 (285,000 records; collection ID 1803978). Catholic parish registers are held at the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories). Some church registers survived the fire; others were destroyed with the rest of the courthouse district.
- **Language:** Many early records are in German, Norwegian, or other immigrant languages depending on the congregation.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, and 1870 are all available. The 1870 federal census for Chicago survived the Great Fire because originals were held in Washington, D.C. — it is the single most reliable pre-fire source for household composition (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The 1880 census covers the post-fire period. Both are indexed and searchable.
- **State census:** Illinois conducted state censuses — the 1865 and 1885 schedules fall within or near the target period and can fill intercensal gaps.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding each census and serve as a substitute for missing death records.
- **Access:** Federal census years (1870, 1880) are indexed and searchable via Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, court suits
- **Date range:** Pre-fire probate and court records were largely destroyed in 1871. Post-1871 records survive.
- **Where held:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University holds Cook County records post-1871 (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories). FamilySearch has digitized one volume of pre-fire reconstructed court records (DGS 009982110: 38 images, 1865–1871) — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image**.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Illinois is a public land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal land patents filed at the General Land Office — available via the BLM GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov/)
- **Types:** Pre-fire deeds were destroyed in the courthouse fire. The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds. FamilySearch holds a partially indexed volume of post-fire property re-recordings (DGS 009982111: 112 images, 1871–1880, 41% name-indexed — searchable by name for roughly half the volume; the remaining images must be browsed individually).
- **Pre-fire substitute:** Insurance company records, particularly the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection held at the Chicago History Museum, are the primary substitute for pre-fire property ownership (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (post-fire originals); IRAD at NEIU; Chicago History Museum (insurance/title records); BLM GLO for federal patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) is the primary conflict for this period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, Civil War draft registrations (1863). These federal records were held in Washington, D.C. and were NOT destroyed in the Chicago fire.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA: https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Several historic Chicago cemeteries date to this period. Specific cemetery names were not confirmed by a tool result in this survey — consult the Chicago History Museum or Newberry Library for cemetery directories.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has extensive Chicago-area coverage.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual cemeteries and potentially at the Chicago History Museum.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago had active newspapers before and after the fire. Some pre-fire papers survived because their offices were outside the burned district; post-fire coverage extensively documented the disaster and its aftermath, including lists of survivors and displaced families.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Chicago newspaper collections. The Newberry Library holds Chicago newspapers on microfilm (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, fire-era casualty and survivor lists (fall 1871), legal notices, property recovery filings under the Burnt Record Act.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is an inland city. Primary ports of entry for families arriving by 1870 were New York, Baltimore, New Orleans, and other coastal ports.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (held by NARA in Washington — unaffected by the fire); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (pre-1906 filed in any court of record; Cook County court naturalizations were largely destroyed in 1871 — also check state and federal courts and neighboring county courts). Alien registrations are a 20th-century record type.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for passenger lists and federal naturalization records. FamilySearch and Ancestry for digitized arrivals.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest page for all family members when researching a family's arrival.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and personal property tax rolls
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls were in the Cook County Courthouse and were destroyed in 1871. Post-fire tax records survive.
- **Where held:** Post-fire tax records at the Cook County Assessor and IRAD at NEIU.
- **Substitute value:** City directories (Newberry Library, 1840s onward) serve as a substitute for missing tax and census years, confirming residence and occupation between enumerations.

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Available from the 1840s onward, held at the Newberry Library (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). These are the primary substitute for any pre-fire civil record — they list heads of household with occupation and street address.
- **Insurance and title records:** The Chicago History Museum holds the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection, the leading source for pre-fire property ownership.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000); Birth Certs 1871–1940 (1,450,000); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000); 2 digitized volumes: browse-only pre-fire court records (DGS 009982110) and partially indexed post-fire property re-recordings (DGS 009982111) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (all years including 1870 and 1880) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Chicago newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records, Civil War pension files | Subscription |
| NARA | Passenger lists, federal court records, military records (unaffected by fire) | Free in-person; some online via Fold3/Ancestry |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 matching digitized volumes for Cook County 1850–1890, which is the complete result set (totalResults: 2). The 4 FamilySearch collections shown are the complete collections_search results for Cook County (scope: Illinois, 4 collections). Holdings not indexed or digitized by FamilySearch are not represented in these counts.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library (Chicago) | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, newspaper microfilm | In-person; some digitized online |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance/title records, photographs, personal papers | In-person; contact museum for access |
| IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County records post-1871 (court, probate, land) | In-person; contact IRAD |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives for access |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person / mail request |
| NARA (Chicago regional / Washington, D.C.) | Federal records: military, passenger lists, naturalizations | In-person / online finding aids |

## Records NOT online

- Pre-fire (pre-October 1871) deeds, probate files, tax rolls, and court records: largely destroyed in the fire; limited reconstructed copies exist at IRAD and Chicago History Museum but are not fully digitized
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records at the Chicago History Museum: physical access required

# Locality Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** French Louisiana (Territoire de la Louisiane) founded 1699; New Orleans established 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (from 1718)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (French Empire); transferred to Spanish Empire 1762 by the Treaty of Fontainebleau
- **Population during period:** Population data for the colonial period was not returned by tools; estimates suggest a few thousand European colonists and a larger enslaved African population by mid-century
- **Economy:** Fur trade, tobacco, indigo, rice, and later sugar; economy depended heavily on enslaved and indentured labor
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers, German and Swiss immigrants, Indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans, Acadians arriving in the 1760s–1770s, and Spanish colonial administrators from 1769
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — the only legally recognized church under both French and Spanish colonial rule; all official vital events recorded by Catholic parishes under the Code Noir
- **Key historical events:** Colony founded 1699; New Orleans founded 1718; Code Noir enacted (required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons); Treaty of Fontainebleau 1762 ceded western Louisiana to Spain; Spanish administration effectively began 1769; colony briefly retroceded to France 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes
- **1699–1762:** French Louisiana — administered by France under the Conseil Supérieur (Superior Council); records primarily in French
- **1762–1800:** Spanish Louisiana — Treaty of Fontainebleau ceded the colony to Spain; Spanish colonial administration (Cabildo) replaced French governance in 1769; records shift to Spanish from 1769
- **1800–1803:** Briefly retroceded to France under the Treaty of San Ildefonso
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase transferred the territory to the United States
- **Important:** The 1700s spans both French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769) colonial regimes. Records in the same repository may be in two different languages and administrative traditions. Researchers must search both the French-era Conseil Supérieur records and the Spanish-era Cabildo records for events across the century.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed during the French or Spanish colonial period. Catholic sacramental registers are the only vital record source for this entire era.
- **What exists:** Catholic parish baptismal, marriage, and burial registers from 1720 (St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans). The Code Noir legally required the baptism of all enslaved persons, so enslaved individuals appear in baptismal registers alongside free colonists.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925", ~987,654 records); FamilySearch volume DGS 004330991 (264 images, Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803) — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and Spanish.** Originals held at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.
- **Gaps:** Records prior to 1720 are extremely sparse or lost. No statewide U.S. civil registration applies to the colonial period at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Superior Council notarial acts for marriage contracts and estate proceedings; civil contracts filed before notaries in the New Orleans Notarial Archives.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic — the only legally recognized denomination in French Louisiana. Protestant worship was prohibited under the Code Noir.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"); FamilySearch volume DGS 004330991 (264 images, browse-only); Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (originals)
- **Language:** Records are in French during the French colonial period and transition to Spanish after 1769. Researchers must read colonial French and Spanish script or obtain specialist assistance.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds census rolls (recensements) for the French colonial period. These are administrative enumerations, not standardized family censuses. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census covering Louisiana was 1810; the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses do not cover Louisiana.
- **Access:** ANOM census rolls are physical records in France; some are accessible via Gallica (gallica.bnf.fr). No FamilySearch colonial census collection was returned for this period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** The Conseil Supérieur handled court proceedings, estate inventories, land grants, and contracts during the French colonial period. The Cabildo performed equivalent functions under Spanish rule.
- **Date range:** French colonial court records ca. 1699–1769; Spanish colonial records 1769–1803
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** DGS 004330992 (149 images, French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council records, Louisiana, 1699–1769) — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and Spanish.**
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (Collection 2078341, ~456,789 records)
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — holds Superior Council records, partially digitized. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot (arpent) system along waterways; Spanish grants followed different conventions from 1769 onward
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French Crown concessions and Spanish grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America.
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, mortgages, bills of sale
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (public access); Louisiana State Land Office; American State Papers: Public Lands (digitized and available online). (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (Seven Years' War, 1754–1763); colonial militia service throughout the period
- **Record types:** French colonial militia muster rolls, military correspondence, officer commissions
- **Where held:** ANOM in Aix-en-Provence holds French colonial military records. No Louisiana-specific colonial military collection was returned by FamilySearch tools for this period.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (New Orleans, established 1789, the oldest surviving cemetery); earlier burials typically in church grounds
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — coverage of French colonial-era burials is sparse given the age of the records
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are contained within Catholic sacramental books (see Church records)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Louisiana newspaper, the *Moniteur de la Louisiane*, began in 1794 — at the very end of the Spanish colonial period. No newspapers from the French colonial period are known to this survey.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Libraries and the Historic New Orleans Collection hold early Louisiana newspaper microfilm
- **Content value:** Formal obituaries and marriage notices did not exist for most of the 1700s; the notarial record serves this function instead

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the principal port of entry for the colony
- **Record types:** French colonial passenger and settler lists; Acadian deportation and resettlement records (1755–1770s); Superior Council contracts naming settlers
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) holds French colonial emigration/immigration records. No specific FamilySearch immigration collection for this colonial period was returned.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax and tribute rolls; property assessments under French and Spanish administrations
- **Date range:** French and Spanish administrative fiscal records span the 1700s
- **Where held:** ANOM (France) and Louisiana Historical Center; not identified in FamilySearch collections for this period
- **Substitute value:** Can partially substitute for missing census data to establish residence and property ownership

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds notarial acts from the 1730s — marriage contracts, wills, bills of sale, manumissions, and property transfers. These are a critical source unique to Louisiana's civil-law tradition and frequently name family members and places of origin.
- **Superior Council / Cabildo records:** Civil and criminal cases, estate inventories, and administrative decisions — held at the Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans.
- **Enslaved persons records:** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of enslaved persons; baptismal registers are the primary genealogical source for enslaved individuals in this period. Notarial bills of sale also name enslaved individuals and sometimes their origins.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (Collection 1612905, ~987,654 records); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (Collection 2078341, ~456,789 records); 2 browse-only digitized volumes (DGS 004330991: 264 images, sacramental registers 1720–1803; DGS 004330992: 149 images, Superior Council notarial acts 1699–1769) | Free |
| Gallica — Bibliothèque nationale de France (gallica.bnf.fr) | Some ANOM colonial records digitized; search for Louisiana colonial records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records post-1803; some territorial records | Free (online finding aids) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Louisiana 1700–1800; both were returned in the single response page (complete set). Both are browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records (French colonial), Cabildo records (Spanish colonial); partially digitized | In-person; contact for access |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, New Orleans | Notarial acts from 1730s: marriage contracts, wills, bills of sale, manumissions | In-person; public access |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls (recensements), military records, emigration records | In-person; some digitized via Gallica |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers from St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes | Contact archives for access |
| Louisiana State Land Office, Baton Rouge | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person / written inquiry |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Post-colonial state records; some territorial records | In-person / online catalog |

## Records NOT online
- French colonial census rolls / recensements (held at ANOM, France; partial digitization via Gallica)
- French and Spanish colonial military muster rolls and correspondence (held at ANOM)
- Full notarial archives from the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (partial digitization only)
- Most Superior Council and Cabildo administrative records beyond the two FamilySearch browse-only volumes
- Acadian resettlement records (held primarily at ANOM and Canadian archives)

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Louisiana colonial records were stated by the tools used in this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Louisiana record types returned only generic content during this survey and could not be consulted on this point — verify at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for any known losses before concluding a record set is intact.

## Research tips
- **Catholic registers are the essential starting point.** The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana; all baptisms, marriages, and burials were recorded by Catholic parishes. Begin with St. Louis Cathedral registers (from 1720) via FamilySearch Collection 1612905 before any other record class. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Records are in French and Spanish.** The colony shifted from French to Spanish administration in 1769. Documents from before 1769 are in French; post-1769 records are predominantly in Spanish. Researchers must be able to work in both languages or engage a translator fluent in colonial-era handwriting in each.
- **Search notarial acts for vital data.** Marriage contracts, wills, and estate inventories filed before notaries name family members, relationships, and places of origin not found elsewhere. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds records from the 1730s. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **For enslaved ancestors, start with baptismal registers and notarial acts.** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of enslaved persons; many appear in the same sacramental registers as free colonists. Bill of sale notarial acts may provide additional detail including origins. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **ANOM in France is indispensable for French colonial research.** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence) holds administrative records, census rolls, correspondence, and emigration records for French Louisiana. Some records are accessible via Gallica (gallica.bnf.fr). (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Browse-only volumes require image-by-image examination.** Both FamilySearch digitized volumes for the colonial period (DGS 004330991 and DGS 004330992) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — you must page through every image manually. They are in French and Spanish.

| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (Collection 1612905, ~987,654 records); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (Collection 2078341, ~456,789 records); 2 browse-only digitized volumes (DGS 004330991: 264 images, sacramental registers 1720–1803; DGS 004330992: 149 images, Superior Council notarial acts 1699–1769) | Free |
| Gallica — Bibliothèque nationale de France (gallica.bnf.fr) | Some ANOM colonial records digitized; search for Louisiana colonial records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records post-1803; some territorial records | Free (online finding aids) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Louisiana 1700–1800; both were returned in the single response page (complete set). Both are browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records (French colonial), Cabildo records (Spanish colonial); partially digitized | In-person; contact for access |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, New Orleans | Notarial acts from 1730s: marriage contracts, wills, bills of sale, manumissions | In-person; public access |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls (recensements), military records, emigration records | In-person; some digitized via Gallica |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers from St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes | Contact archives for access |
| Louisiana State Land Office, Baton Rouge | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person / written inquiry |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Post-colonial state records; some territorial records | In-person / online catalog |

## Records NOT online
- French colonial census rolls / recensements (held at ANOM, France; partial digitization via Gallica)
- French and Spanish colonial military muster rolls and correspondence (held at ANOM)
- Full notarial archives from the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (partial digitization only)
- Most Superior Council and Cabildo administrative records beyond the two FamilySearch browse-only volumes
- Acadian resettlement records (held primarily at ANOM and Canadian archives)

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Louisiana colonial records were stated by the tools used in this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Louisiana record types returned only generic content during this survey and could not be consulted on this point — verify at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for any known losses before concluding a record set is intact.

## Research tips
- **Catholic registers are the essential starting point.** The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana; all baptisms, marriages, and burials were recorded by Catholic parishes. Begin with St. Louis Cathedral registers (from 1720) via FamilySearch Collection 1612905 before any other record class. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Records are in French and Spanish.** The colony shifted from French to Spanish administration in 1769. Documents from before 1769 are in French; post-1769 records are predominantly in Spanish. Researchers must be able to work in both languages or engage a translator fluent in colonial-era handwriting in each.
- **Search notarial acts for vital data.** Marriage contracts, wills, and estate inventories filed before notaries name family members, relationships, and places of origin not found elsewhere. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds records from the 1730s. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **For enslaved ancestors, start with baptismal registers and notarial acts.** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of enslaved persons; many appear in the same sacramental registers as free colonists. Bill of sale notarial acts may provide additional detail including origins. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **ANOM in France is indispensable for French colonial research.** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence) holds administrative records, census rolls, correspondence, and emigration records for French Louisiana. Some records are accessible via Gallica (gallica.bnf.fr). (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Browse-only volumes require image-by-image examination.** Both FamilySearch digitized volumes for the colonial period (DGS 004330991 and DGS 004330992) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — you must page through every image manually. They are in French and Spanish.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Coal Mining Region (1860–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this query; see county histories and census schedules directly
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; Schuylkill County was the core of the Pennsylvania Coal Region alongside Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, Welsh, German immigrant populations from the 1820s–1870s; followed by Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian immigrants by the 1880s–1900s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish and later Slavic/Italian ethnic parishes), Welsh Congregational and Calvinist, Methodist, Lutheran, Reformed, Presbyterian, Greek Catholic
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (1875–1877); Great Railroad Strike (1877); founding of United Mine Workers of America (1890); repeated mine disasters throughout the period

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has been stable since its 1811 formation; no boundary changes affect the 1860–1910 research window
- Lackawanna County was created from Luzerne County in 1878 — for families in the Scranton/Carbondale coal area, pre-1878 records are under Luzerne County
- Adjoining counties for cross-border research: Luzerne (north), Carbon (east), Berks (south), Lebanon (southwest), Dauphin (west), Northumberland (northwest)

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania statewide death registration is evidenced by the FamilySearch Death Certificates collection beginning in 1906; the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records were not accessible during this survey and could not confirm the specific level and year of each registration requirement — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records directly
- **What exists:** Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (FamilySearch collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records with images); County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records); Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records); Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch.org (indexed + images for death certificates and marriages); Pennsylvania State Archives for originals
- **Gaps:** No indexed birth certificates or death certificates before 1906 on FamilySearch; births before statewide registration must be sought in church records
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers; newspaper birth and death notices; cemetery records; census mortality schedules (1860–1880)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian ethnic parishes), Welsh Congregational, Methodist, Lutheran, Reformed, Presbyterian, Greek Catholic
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; some parishes kept separate registers for each event
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has a collection for Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985, ~1,245,830 records, ~982,415 persons indexed with ~607,220 images); individual parish archives and diocesan archives (Diocese of Allentown for the Schuylkill area)
- **Language:** English for most Protestant registers; Latin for Roman Catholic sacramental records; Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, or Italian for ethnic Catholic parishes
- **Note:** Ethnic parishes are the critical source for immigrant mining families — identifying the specific parish (by nationality and township) is essential before searching

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 available (1890 destroyed); all list occupation, enabling identification of mining families
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860, 1870, 1880 schedules list individuals who died in the year preceding enumeration — especially valuable for mining accident victims
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct statewide intercensal enumerations during this period
- **Access:** Federal census 1860–1880 and 1900–1910 are indexed and online at FamilySearch and Ancestry (subscription); mortality schedules are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994) covers this period; 3,200,560 images but 0 indexed records — browse-only, must be examined image by image
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Register of Wills, Pottsville (originals); FamilySearch microfilm (browse-only)
- **Note:** Miners who died intestate (without a will) generate administration files; miners who owned property or tools may have inventories naming heirs

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is not a public land survey state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property was not accessible during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property directly
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records; mining company leases
- **Date range:** County deed books from formation (1811)
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville (originals); many deeds microfilmed by FamilySearch

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865), Spanish-American War (1898), World War I draft (1917–1918)
- **Record types:** Civil War service and pension records at NARA; Pennsylvania adjutant general records at Pennsylvania State Archives; WWI draft cards (Fold3); bounty land warrants (pre-period but may name relatives)
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC / St. Louis); Pennsylvania State Archives; Fold3.com (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; Military Records at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Catholic, Protestant, and municipal cemeteries throughout Schuylkill County mining communities
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Schuylkill County cemeteries; coverage is partial and volunteer-dependent
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual cemeteries or churches; contact the specific cemetery or historical society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville) published throughout this period and carried mining accident reports, obituaries, marriage notices, and naturalization announcements
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized historical newspapers; Pennsylvania State Library and Historical Society of Schuylkill County hold microfilm
- **Content value:** Mining accident reports name the victim and often nationality; obituaries frequently name birthplace in Ireland, Wales, or Eastern Europe

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden through 1890, Ellis Island from 1892)
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry); naturalization declarations and petitions at Schuylkill County courts; Pennsylvania State Archives holds Schuylkill County naturalization records 1840s–1906
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds original passenger lists; FamilySearch and Ancestry for digitized indexes
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members. Post-1895 manifests include last residence and contact name in the US.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property and personal property tax lists
- **Date range:** Available from county formation; annual lists
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County archives and Pennsylvania State Archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can identify a miner's presence in a township in years between federal censuses

### Coal mining-specific records
- **Mine Inspector reports:** Published annually from 1870; list fatal accidents with name, age, nationality, and cause of death; held at Pennsylvania State Archives and accessible as a print series
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill County, 1870–1900:** FamilySearch volume 002240015, 410 images, 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable — indexed + images
- **Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne County, 1870–1895:** FamilySearch volume 002240016, 287 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna County, 1878–1900:** FamilySearch volume 002240017, 199 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only
- **UMWA records:** United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) membership rolls and grievance files; held at the Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton, and at Penn State University's Special Collections
- **Company records:** Employment records and pay ledgers survive fragmentarily at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Schuylkill County Church Records; PA County Marriages; PA Probate Records (browse-only); PA Death Certificates (from 1906); Mine Worker Employment Cards (indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Miners' Journal | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives holdings | Free catalog; some fees for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 23 digitized volumes matching this place and period; the 3 detailed above are the first page only. The remaining 20 volumes were not examined — request further pages before concluding a record type is absent from FamilySearch's digitized holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, probate files, naturalization records, court minutes | In-person; some records on microfilm at FamilySearch |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Mine Inspector reports, Schuylkill Co. naturalization records, state-level records | In-person; online catalog at phmc.pa.gov |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville | Local histories, newspaper archives, family files, mining company records | In-person; contact for access |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton | Mining community records, UMWA collections, ethnic community materials | In-person |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County | Contact diocese for access |

## Records NOT online
- Birth records before 1906 (pre-statewide registration): must use church baptism registers, held at parishes, diocesan archives, or on FamilySearch microfilm
- Most colliery payroll ledgers and company employment records (where they survive): physical only at Pennsylvania State Archives or local historical societies
- Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne County) and Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna County) in FamilySearch: present as browse-only images with no name index — must be read image by image
- UMWA membership and grievance files: physical at Anthracite Heritage Museum and Penn State Special Collections
- Schuylkill County tax lists and court minute books: largely on microfilm at FamilySearch or physical at the courthouse

## Known record losses
No tool result returned during this survey stated that a specific Schuylkill County record set was destroyed. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmed loss. Confirm the survival of any specific record series with the Schuylkill County courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives before assuming destruction.

## Research tips
