# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Mississippi Territory created 1798; Alabama Territory split off 1817; Alabama statehood December 14, 1819
- **Administrative centers:** Washington / Natchez (Mississippi Territory); St. Stephens (Alabama Territory)
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), then Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
- **Population during period:** No population data returned for this period; settlement was sparse and growing rapidly after the Creek War of 1813–1814
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, trade with Creek and Cherokee nations
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations; Anglo-American settlers arriving from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia (accelerating after Creek War 1813–1814); French Creole and Spanish colonial population in the Mobile District
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist and Baptist circuit riders (Anglo-American settlements); Catholic parishes (French colonial foundation, Mobile District)
- **Key historical events:** Creek War (1813–1814) opened most of present-day Alabama to Anglo-American settlement; U.S. seizure of the Mobile District from Spain (1813)

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: most of present-day Alabama was Spanish-claimed West Florida (southern portion) or under Georgia/North Carolina claims (northern portion)
- 1798: Mississippi Territory established, covering present-day Mississippi and southern Alabama above 31° N
- 1804: Mississippi Territory expanded to include the full present-day Alabama extent north of 31° N
- 1813: United States seized the Mobile District from Spain; the coastal belt and Mobile Bay came under U.S. authority
- 1817: Alabama Territory separated from Mississippi Territory
- 1819: Alabama statehood

The Mobile District split is geographic, not temporal: events in the coastal/Mobile Bay area before 1813 are in Spanish records, while the interior was under Mississippi Territory from 1798. Do not assume a single filing jurisdiction for all pre-1819 Alabama events.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration during the territorial period. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Alabama Vital Records returned only generic content and provided no specific registration dates. County-level marriage records appear in the FamilySearch collection from 1809.
- **What exists:** County marriage bonds and licenses from 1809 (collection 1598408, Alabama, County Marriages 1809–1950, 612,345 records with images). No systematic birth or death registration before statehood.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration before statehood. Pre-1809 marriages may survive only in church registers.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial records; territorial census substitutes; estate files naming heirs

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, French colonial foundation 1702); Methodist from ca. 1790s; Baptist from early 1800s
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; confirmations. Catholic registers in the Mobile District are the earliest extant vital records for that area.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1986396, "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (156,789 records, 78,394 images — indexed with images). French and Spanish colonial church records for the Mobile District are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville; microfilm copies are at the Mobile Municipal Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Language:** Pre-1763 Catholic records in French; 1780–1813 in Spanish

### Census records
- **Territorial census:** Mississippi Territory censuses taken in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama; physical originals held at ADAH. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Federal census:** 1810 federal census covers Alabama Territory.
- **FamilySearch indexed collections:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (collection 2016756, 287,634 records — **index only, no images**); "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890" (collection 1927171, 198,340 records — **index only, no images**). Both are name-indexed but have no accompanying images on FamilySearch.
- **Access:** Name-indexed on FamilySearch; physical originals at ADAH for the territorial censuses

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration, territorial court proceedings
- **Date range:** Territorial court records begin 1798 with the creation of Mississippi Territory
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1537764, "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (438,210 records) starts 1809. "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920" (collection 1855293, 245,670 records, 122,835 images) covers territorial period records; search this for pre-1809 court activity in the territory. Physical territorial court records are at ADAH and the Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a federal land state; township-and-range)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government via the General Land Office; first federal land sales in Alabama Territory began after 1817. Spanish and British grants preceded American control in the Mobile District.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (BLM GLO); private land claims (Spanish/British grants confirmed by U.S.); territorial grants; county deed books
- **Date range:** Spanish and British land grants predate 1798; federal grants begin the territorial period
- **Where held:** BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents — **free, online, searchable**. FamilySearch collection 1919694, "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907" (312,450 records, 156,225 images) covers the Mississippi Territory period. Library of Congress holds copies of Spanish colonial records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812; territorial militia service
- **Record types:** Territorial militia rolls; pension files and bounty land warrants for War of 1812 veterans; service records. Territorial records include militia rolls. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C.) holds federal service and pension records. ADAH holds territorial militia rolls. Fold3 (fold3.com) has military records (subscription).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Early cemeteries were mostly family plots; formal church and public cemeteries grew with Anglo-American settlement after 1800
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has indexed many Alabama cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records from the territorial period are sparse; ADAH holds transcripts and surveys of early Alabama cemeteries

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Mobile Gazette (Mobile, early territorial period); Huntsville Republican (Huntsville, ca. 1816)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com has historical Alabama newspapers; physical collections at ADAH and University of Alabama Libraries
- **Content value:** Land sale notices, estate settlement announcements, early legal notices

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the primary port of entry for the Alabama region
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at Mobile; naturalization petitions in territorial courts (pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal passenger arrival records and naturalization files; Mobile Municipal Archives holds local port records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and early county tax lists; property assessments
- **Date range:** Tax lists from the territorial period are among the earliest name sources
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial-era tax records; some tax list data is incorporated in FamilySearch's census substitutes collection (2016756)
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax assessments name heads of household nearly every year and are the primary vital-record substitute for the pre-1819 period when no civil registration existed

### Colonial records (Mobile District)
- The Mobile District was under French (1702–1763), British (1763–1780), and Spanish (1780–1813) administration. Events in this area before 1813 are in colonial records, not U.S. territorial records:
  - Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France (French era)
  - Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain (Spanish era), with copies at the Library of Congress
  - Mobile Municipal Archives holds microfilm of both series
  (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Alabama, County Marriages 1809–1950; Alabama, Probate Records 1809–1985; Alabama, Compiled Census & Substitutes Index 1810–1890; Alabama, Church Records 1803–1950; Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records 1798–1907; Mississippi, County Court Records 1799–1920; Mississippi, Compiled Census & Substitutes 1792–1890 | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama Territory and state | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |

**Coverage of digitized volumes:** The volume_search tool returned 0 digitized image volumes for Alabama (or Mississippi Territory) in the 1780–1820 window across multiple searches, including searches filtered by land, census, vital, military, court, probate, and religious record types. There are no FamilySearch browse-only image volumes catalogued under "Alabama" or "Mississippi Territory" for this period. The FamilySearch collections listed above are name-indexed record sets; browse-only pre-statehood volumes, if they exist, are not separately catalogued under these pre-statehood place names in FamilySearch's Records Management Service.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Mississippi Territory censuses 1801/1805/1808/1810; territorial court records; county records; militia rolls; tax lists | In-person; catalog at archives.alabama.gov |
| Mississippi Dept. of Archives and History (MDAH), Jackson, MS | Mississippi Territory records 1798–1817 including present-day Alabama events | In-person; mdah.ms.gov |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington, D.C. | Federal land records, military service/pension files, naturalization records | In-person; online through Ancestry and Fold3 |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial church records; port records | In-person; contact for access |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Copies of Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District | In-person; some digitized |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District | In-person; some microfilm at Library of Congress |

## Records NOT online
- Mississippi Territory territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (originals at ADAH; 1810 is indexed in census substitutes collection)
- Territorial court minute books and case files
- Most early county deed books from before the FamilySearch indexed collections begin
- French and Spanish colonial church registers for the Mobile District (originals in France and Spain; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- Early county estate and guardianship files before 1809
- Militia rolls and muster lists (physical at ADAH)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Alabama territorial record set was destroyed or lost. The absence of FamilySearch digitized volumes for the pre-1820 period is a digitization and cataloguing gap, not necessarily a record loss. When a search returns nothing, contact ADAH directly before concluding that records do not survive.

## Research tips
- **Search both Alabama and Mississippi collections on FamilySearch.** Around 1800, the area was Mississippi Territory; territorial-era collections are filed under Mississippi on FamilySearch. The land records (1798–1907), court records (1799–1920), and census substitutes (1792–1890) filed under Mississippi overlap with the territorial period for present-day Alabama. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **The Mobile District requires completely separate research.** Events in the coastal/Mobile Bay area before 1813 are in Spanish colonial records held in European archives and at the Mobile Municipal Archives — a FamilySearch county-level search will miss them entirely. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Tax lists and militia rolls are vital-record substitutes.** No civil birth or death registration existed during the territorial period. Annual tax assessments name heads of household nearly every year and are the most reliably surviving record series.
- **The BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) is a key free online resource.** Federal land patents for Alabama are searchable and free online and are often the earliest federal document naming a specific settler with an exact township-and-range location.
- **FamilySearch has no browse-only image volumes for Alabama 1780–1820.** The volume_search confirmed zero digitized volumes under this place and period. Researchers wanting to browse original document images must use physical repositories or microfilm at ADAH or the FamilySearch Library in Salt Lake City.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama returned only generic content in this survey.** The specific pages for Alabama Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate, and Census were not retrievable. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy directly before relying on the gaps identified here.

  - Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France (French era)
  - Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain (Spanish era), with copies at the Library of Congress
  - Mobile Municipal Archives holds microfilm of both series
  (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Alabama, County Marriages 1809–1950; Alabama, Probate Records 1809–1985; Alabama, Compiled Census & Substitutes Index 1810–1890; Alabama, Church Records 1803–1950; Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records 1798–1907; Mississippi, County Court Records 1799–1920; Mississippi, Compiled Census & Substitutes 1792–1890 | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama Territory and state | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |

**Coverage of digitized volumes:** The volume_search tool returned 0 digitized image volumes for Alabama (or Mississippi Territory) in the 1780–1820 window across multiple searches, including searches filtered by land, census, vital, military, court, probate, and religious record types. There are no FamilySearch browse-only image volumes catalogued under "Alabama" or "Mississippi Territory" for this period. The FamilySearch collections listed above are name-indexed record sets; browse-only pre-statehood volumes, if they exist, are not separately catalogued under these pre-statehood place names in FamilySearch's Records Management Service.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Mississippi Territory censuses 1801/1805/1808/1810; territorial court records; county records; militia rolls; tax lists | In-person; catalog at archives.alabama.gov |
| Mississippi Dept. of Archives and History (MDAH), Jackson, MS | Mississippi Territory records 1798–1817 including present-day Alabama events | In-person; mdah.ms.gov |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington, D.C. | Federal land records, military service/pension files, naturalization records | In-person; online through Ancestry and Fold3 |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial church records; port records | In-person; contact for access |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Copies of Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District | In-person; some digitized |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District | In-person; some microfilm at Library of Congress |

## Records NOT online
- Mississippi Territory territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (originals at ADAH; 1810 is indexed in census substitutes collection)
- Territorial court minute books and case files
- Most early county deed books from before the FamilySearch indexed collections begin
- French and Spanish colonial church registers for the Mobile District (originals in France and Spain; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- Early county estate and guardianship files before 1809
- Militia rolls and muster lists (physical at ADAH)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Alabama territorial record set was destroyed or lost. The absence of FamilySearch digitized volumes for the pre-1820 period is a digitization and cataloguing gap, not necessarily a record loss. When a search returns nothing, contact ADAH directly before concluding that records do not survive.

## Research tips
- **Search both Alabama and Mississippi collections on FamilySearch.** Around 1800, the area was Mississippi Territory; territorial-era collections are filed under Mississippi on FamilySearch. The land records (1798–1907), court records (1799–1920), and census substitutes (1792–1890) filed under Mississippi overlap with the territorial period for present-day Alabama. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **The Mobile District requires completely separate research.** Events in the coastal/Mobile Bay area before 1813 are in Spanish colonial records held in European archives and at the Mobile Municipal Archives — a FamilySearch county-level search will miss them entirely. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Tax lists and militia rolls are vital-record substitutes.** No civil birth or death registration existed during the territorial period. Annual tax assessments name heads of household nearly every year and are the most reliably surviving record series.
- **The BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) is a key free online resource.** Federal land patents for Alabama are searchable and free online and are often the earliest federal document naming a specific settler with an exact township-and-range location.
- **FamilySearch has no browse-only image volumes for Alabama 1780–1820.** The volume_search confirmed zero digitized volumes under this place and period. Researchers wanting to browse original document images must use physical repositories or microfilm at ADAH or the FamilySearch Library in Salt Lake City.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama returned only generic content in this survey.** The specific pages for Alabama Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate, and Census were not retrievable. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy directly before relying on the gaps identified here.

Here is the locality research guide produced by the subagent:

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860–1900)

### Core County Covered
**Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania** (southern anthracite field, 1860–1900)

---

### Key Finding: Specialized Coal-Region Index

The FamilySearch Wiki page **"Pennsylvania Coal Region Records"** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) is the most important specialized resource and describes:

- A **payroll-derived colliery worker index** naming approximately **41,000 workers**, with occupations and sometimes parish of origin — far more useful for finding an Irish miner than census records alone.
- **Catholic diocesan boundary information** for all five anthracite counties.
- **Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments** (see below).

---

### Record Types & Repositories

| Record Type | Coverage / Notes |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch digitized images | Most records are image-only (no name index); deed records are ~20% searchable by name |
| **Naturalization records** | Schuylkill County courthouse; critical for Irish immigrants |
| **Catholic church registers** | Held at the **Philadelphia Archdiocesan Archives** — NOT Scranton — because Schuylkill County remained under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1961 |
| **PA State Tax Assessments** | Triennial assessments from 1853; record occupation and sometimes birthplace; held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**; fill gaps between censuses; not yet online |
| US Federal Census | 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (1890 largely destroyed) |
| Church records (Lackawanna/Luzerne) | Diocese of Scranton (est. 1868) covers the northern anthracite fields |

---

### The Five Anthracite Counties

1. **Schuylkill** (southern field) — surveyed above
2. **Luzerne** (northern field)
3. **Lackawanna** — split from Luzerne County in **1878**; important for post-1878 records
4. **Carbon**
5. **Northumberland**

> ⚠️ Separate locality surveys are needed for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties.

---

### Important Diocesan Boundary Note

Many researchers assume all northeastern Pennsylvania Catholic records are in Scranton — **this is wrong for Schuylkill County**. Use the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Archives for Schuylkill County records throughout this entire period. The Diocese of Scranton covers the northern counties (Luzerne, Lackawanna).

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. Search the **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** for your Irish ancestors.
2. Check **Schuylkill County naturalization records** for Irish miners.
3. Request church registers from the **Philadelphia Archdiocesan Archives**.
4. Search the **Pennsylvania State Archives** triennial tax assessments for occupation and birthplace data between census years.
5. Run separate locality surveys for Carbon, Luzerne, Lackawanna, and Northumberland counties.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks County (southern portion) and Northampton County (northern portion)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880) → 172,927 (1900) [U.S. Census]
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; Schuylkill was the core of the southern anthracite field; the Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company was the dominant operator
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic immigrant community from the 1840s onward; Welsh, English, German, and later Eastern European miners also present — ethnic composition directly shapes which church registers to prioritize
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (primary for Irish-born miners), Welsh Methodist, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Presbyterian, Lutheran, Episcopal
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (1876–1879) generated Schuylkill County Quarter Sessions court records; Civil War draft (1863) and service records cover the peak Irish-immigration decade; repeated colliery disasters created coroner and company records

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County boundaries have been stable since formation in 1811; no splits or additions occurred during 1860–1900
- Records predating 1811 are held in Berks County (southern territory) and Northampton County (northern territory) — search both parent counties for any event before 1811

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page Pennsylvania_Vital_Records returned only generic content during this survey; no specific year or level can be confirmed from a page fetched in this run. The generic Genealogy_Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) notes that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s but does not name Pennsylvania or a year — consult the Pennsylvania_Vital_Records wiki page directly for registration level and date
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume of Marriage Records, 1870–1910 (94 images, browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; imageGroup 007936753)
- **Gaps:** No indexed birth or death collection was returned for this county and period; pre-statewide-registration records may be sparse or held only in physical repositories
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish baptismal registers; coroner inquests (especially for mine fatalities); newspaper death and marriage notices in the Miners' Journal

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (multiple parishes established 1840–1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrants); Welsh Methodist; Lutheran; Presbyterian; Episcopal
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; confirmation records are a separate dated event, often years after baptism, and name both the confirmand and sponsors
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume of Church Records, 1842–1895 (187 images, browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; in English and German; imageGroup 007936751). **Diocesan key:** before 1868 all five anthracite counties fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia. After 1868, Schuylkill and Carbon remained with Philadelphia (Diocese of Allentown not erected until 1961); Luzerne and Lackawanna transferred to the Diocese of Scranton; Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg. Request Schuylkill County Catholic registers from the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- **Language:** English and German; researchers must read the original language for German entries

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Decennial censuses available for 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 — all covering Schuylkill County
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules name individuals who died in the year preceding enumeration — relevant for mine accident fatalities and Irish immigrants who died young
- **1890 census:** Largely destroyed nationally; 1890 Schuylkill records are not available

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced (saved as **loc_001** in the project):

---

## Vermont — Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide (Late 1700s)

### Jurisdictional Overview
Vermont in the late 1700s passed through **three distinct governing authorities**, and understanding which one was in force determines where to look for records:

1. **New Hampshire Grants (1749–1764)** — Governor Benning Wentworth issued 129 township grants beginning in 1749, creating the earliest documentary footprint for settlers in the territory.
2. **New York's competing claim (1764–1777)** — The Crown assigned the territory to New York, so New York also issued patents and administered courts. Land records may exist under *both* New Hampshire and New York systems for the same ground.
3. **The Vermont Republic (1777–1791)** — Vermont declared independence and governed itself until admission to the Union in March 1791.

### The Records Gap
Vermont had **no civil registration** before statehood, and statewide birth, marriage, and death recording did not begin until **1857**. This means the standard vital-records approach simply does not work for this period.

---

### Key Record Types for Pre-Statehood Vermont

| Record Type | Why It Matters | Where to Look |
|---|---|---|
| **Land Records** | The primary documentary trail; may exist under NH, NY, *and* VT Republic systems for the same parcel | Vermont State Archives; county land records |
| **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** | ~1,800 early grantees listed — the closest thing to a pre-statehood census | FamilySearch; Vermont State Archives |
| **Church Records** | Births, marriages, deaths recorded by congregations when no civil record existed | Individual church repositories; NEHGS |
| **Tax Lists** | Identify residents by name; often precede censuses | Town clerks; Vermont State Archives |
| **Town Meeting / Proprietors' Records** | Document land divisions, local governance, early settlers | Town clerks; Vermont State Papers series |
| **Probate Records** | Wills, inventories, administrations name family members | County probate courts; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Town Histories (1860s–1900s)** | Frequently reprint proprietors' records and early documents no longer available in original | Libraries; HathiTrust; Google Books |

---

### Most Important Finding Aid
The **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** is the single most useful entry point — it lists approximately 1,800 early grantees across the township grants and is the closest analog to a census for the territory before 1791. If your ancestor received a land grant or was associated with a grantee, this is where to start.

---

### Key Complication
Because land records may exist under **three different government systems** (New Hampshire, New York, and the Vermont Republic) for the same piece of ground, a search limited to one jurisdiction will miss the others. Always check all three.

---

### Next Steps
- Identify the specific **town** where your ancestors lived. Vermont town records were kept independently, and survival varies considerably by town.
- Check the **FamilySearch Wiki pages** for Vermont vital records, land, church, probate, census, and naming customs at familysearch.org/en/wiki/ for current collection details and microfilm holdings.
- Consult published **town and county histories** — they frequently preserve records (proprietors' votes, early deeds, settler lists) that no longer survive in original form.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1750–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont declared independence in 1777 and operated as the Vermont Republic. The territory was previously the New Hampshire Grants (NH governor Wentworth issued 129 township grants, 1749–1764), then claimed by New York Colony (1764–1777) after the Privy Council set the Connecticut River as the NY–NH boundary. Vermont was admitted to the Union as the 14th state on March 4, 1791.
- **County seat / administrative center:** The Vermont Republic organized counties beginning ca. 1778; administrative functions operated at both the town and county level. The town was the primary unit of local government.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New Hampshire (grants 1749–1764), then New York Colony (1764–1777), then Vermont Republic (1777–1791).
- **Population during period:** No population figure was returned by the tools for the pre-statehood period. Vermont is included in the published 1790 Federal Census (enumerated in 1791 after March 4 statehood).
- **Economy:** Agriculture (subsistence farming), timber, and early milling; the land dispute between NH grantees and NY patentees was the defining economic and legal struggle of the era.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English settlers from Connecticut and Massachusetts; some Scots-Irish settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (dominant, reflecting New England settlement patterns); Baptist; Presbyterian; Episcopal/Anglican; Methodist (arriving later in the period).
- **Key historical events:** NH Wentworth grants (1749–1764); NY claim and grant conflict (1764–1777); Green Mountain Boys' resistance; Vermont's declaration of independence (1777); Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Vermont Republic (1777–1791); U.S. statehood (March 4, 1791).

## Boundary changes
- **1749–1764:** Territory granted by New Hampshire governor Benning Wentworth as the New Hampshire Grants (129 townships).
- **1764:** Privy Council assigned the Connecticut River as the NY–NH boundary, placing Vermont under New York colonial authority; NY refused to recognize NH grants and issued competing patents.
- **1777:** Vermont declared independence and organized as the Vermont Republic with its own constitution and government; counties formed beginning ca. 1778.
- **1791 (March 4):** Vermont admitted to the United States as the 14th state. Records generated after this date are under the State of Vermont.
- **Critical implication:** Land records for the same parcel may exist under three competing jurisdictions — NH, NY, and Vermont Republic. Search all three before concluding that land documentation is absent.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Vermont Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) states that statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857 at the state level — far after the pre-statehood period. No civil vital registration existed during ca. 1750–1791.
- **What exists:** Some town clerk records go back to the 1770s but survive unevenly (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). These are not formal civil registration but town-level recording where a clerk noted events.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices; Vermont State Archives for state-level holdings. Records are not centralized.
- **Gaps:** Civil vital registration is entirely absent for the target period. Town-level recording is inconsistent and many towns have nothing before 1800.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); family bibles; cemetery inscriptions; probate files naming family members; town proprietors' records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (most common, reflecting CT and MA settlement); Baptist; Presbyterian; Episcopal/Anglican; Methodist.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives; denominational archives; Vermont Historical Society; FamilySearch microfilm (extent not confirmed by tool results for this survey).
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Church records are the primary substitute for absent civil vital registration in this period. The FamilySearch Wiki topic pages for Vermont Church Records returned only generic content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Church_Records directly for current coverage.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Vermont is included in the published 1790 Federal Census. Vermont was admitted March 4, 1791, and the census enumeration for Vermont was conducted in 1791 after statehood. This is the only federal enumeration for the period; it lists heads of household, with other household members counted by age and sex only.
- **State/provincial census:** The Vermont Republic conducted no known systematic census before 1791.
- **Other enumerations:** Vermont Republic tax lists (1778–1791) serve as the primary pre-census substitute; town proprietors' records enumerate original landowners.
- **Access:** The 1790 Federal Census is indexed and available on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, inventories, guardianships; county court minute books and civil suit records.
- **Date range:** Vermont Republic organized counties ca. 1778 and probate courts operated from that point. Pre-1777, probate would have been under NY or NH jurisdiction.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (many records have been transferred to the Vermont State Archives); NARA holds some federal-era materials.
- **Digitization:** The FamilySearch Wiki topic pages for Vermont Probate Records returned only generic content during this survey — confirm current digitization at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Probate_Records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Vermont uses the original-colony metes-and-bounds system, not the federal rectangular survey).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Three overlapping systems apply for the pre-statehood period:
  1. New Hampshire grants (1749–1764): NH governor Wentworth issued 129 township grants. The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees and is identified by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) as the earliest systematic resident list for the territory.
  2. New York colonial patents (1764–1777): NY issued competing grants over the same territory.
  3. Vermont Republic grants (1777–1791): Vermont's own government issued grants resolving the conflict.
- **Types:** Township grants, individual deeds, proprietors' records, tax records, bounty land grants for Revolutionary War service.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives (Secretary of State's land records); individual town clerks (deeds recorded at the town level); New Hampshire State Archives (NH grants); New York State Archives (NY colonial patents).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (preceding the period, relevant to early settlers); Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Vermont Republic militia service (1777–1791).
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; Green Mountain Boys and Vermont militia muster rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pension files — available on Fold3, https://www.fold3.com/; free access at https://www.archives.gov/); Vermont State Archives for Vermont Republic militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burial grounds and church cemeteries; many dating to the 1760s–1780s in established towns.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Vermont cemeteries; coverage for pre-1791 burials varies.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are held by town offices. The Vermont Old Cemetery Association has conducted surveys.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont's earliest newspapers date to the early 1780s (e.g., the Vermont Gazette, ca. 1781). Coverage for the pre-statehood period is sparse.
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society; state and university libraries; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized holdings.
- **Content value:** Pre-1791 newspapers occasionally carry land notices, legal notices, and death notices, but coverage is very limited.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Vermont was settled primarily by internal migration from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and other New England colonies — not direct overseas immigration. Port arrival manifests are generally not relevant for this population.
- **Relevant record types:** Track migration through land records, church records, and probate files connecting Vermont settlers to their New England origins. No formal federal naturalization process existed before the Naturalization Act of 1790; NARA holds post-1790 naturalization records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children; when researching a family that did emigrate from overseas (Scots-Irish, etc.), examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Vermont Republic property tax and poll tax lists; town-level assessment records.
- **Date range:** Vermont Republic tax records from ca. 1778; some town-level tax records from the early settlement period.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives; individual town offices.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for the absent federal census before 1791 and for tracking residents not appearing in land records.

### Other record types
- **Town proprietors' records:** A critical record class for this period. Proprietors were the original grantees of a town's grant; their records document the first land divisions and name the earliest settlers. Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Vermont in the late 1700s was not yet a state — it was first the New Hampshire Grants (where governor Wentworth issued 129 township grants beginning in 1749), then disputed territory under New York's competing claim (1764–1777), and finally the self-governing Vermont Republic (1777–1791) before admission to the Union in March 1791. The biggest practical complication is that land records may exist under three different government systems (New Hampshire, New York, and Vermont Republic) for the very same piece of ground, so a search limited to one jurisdiction will miss the others. # Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1750–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont declared independence in 1777 and operated as the Vermont Republic. The territory was previously the New Hampshire Grants (NH governor Wentworth issued 129 township grants, 1749–1764), then claimed by New York Colony (1764–1777) after the Privy Council set the Connecticut River as the NY–NH boundary. Vermont was admitted to the Union as the 14th state on March 4, 1791.
- **County seat / administrative center:** The Vermont Republic organized counties beginning ca. 1778; administrative functions operated at both the town and county level. The town was the primary unit of local government.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New Hampshire (grants 1749–1764), then New York Colony (1764–1777), then Vermont Republic (1777–1791).
- **Population during period:** No population figure was returned by the tools for the pre-statehood period. Vermont is included in the published 1790 Federal Census (enumerated in 1791 after March 4 statehood).
- **Economy:** Agriculture (subsistence farming), timber, and early milling; the land dispute between NH grantees and NY patentees was the defining economic and legal struggle of the era.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English settlers from Connecticut and Massachusetts; some Scots-Irish settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (dominant, reflecting New England settlement patterns); Baptist; Presbyterian; Episcopal/Anglican; Methodist (arriving later in the period).
- **Key historical events:** NH Wentworth grants (1749–1764); NY claim and grant conflict (1764–1777); Green Mountain Boys' resistance; Vermont's declaration of independence (1777); Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Vermont Republic (1777–1791); U.S. statehood (March 4, 1791).

## Boundary changes
- **1749–1764:** Territory granted by New Hampshire governor Benning Wentworth as the New Hampshire Grants (129 townships).
- **1764:** Privy Council assigned the Connecticut River as the NY–NH boundary, placing Vermont under New York colonial authority; NY refused to recognize NH grants and issued competing patents.
- **1777:** Vermont declared independence and organized as the Vermont Republic with its own constitution and government; counties formed beginning ca. 1778.
- **1791 (March 4):** Vermont admitted to the United States as the 14th state. Records generated after this date are under the State of Vermont.
- **Critical implication:** Land records for the same parcel may exist under three competing jurisdictions — NH, NY, and Vermont Republic. Search all three before concluding that land documentation is absent.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Vermont Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) states that statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857 at the state level — far after the pre-statehood period. No civil vital registration existed during ca. 1750–1791.
- **What exists:** Some town clerk records go back to the 1770s but survive unevenly (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). These are not formal civil registration but town-level recording where a clerk noted events.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices; Vermont State Archives for state-level holdings. Records are not centralized.
- **Gaps:** Civil vital registration is entirely absent for the target period. Town-level recording is inconsistent and many towns have nothing before 1800.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); family bibles; cemetery inscriptions; probate files naming family members; town proprietors' records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (most common, reflecting CT and MA settlement); Baptist; Presbyterian; Episcopal/Anglican; Methodist.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives; denominational archives; Vermont Historical Society; FamilySearch microfilm (extent not confirmed by tool results for this survey).
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Church records are the primary substitute for absent civil vital registration in this period. The FamilySearch Wiki topic pages for Vermont Church Records returned only generic content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Church_Records directly for current coverage.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Vermont is included in the published 1790 Federal Census. Vermont was admitted March 4, 1791, and the census enumeration for Vermont was conducted in 1791 after statehood. This is the only federal enumeration for the period; it lists heads of household, with other household members counted by age and sex only.
- **State/provincial census:** The Vermont Republic conducted no known systematic census before 1791.
- **Other enumerations:** Vermont Republic tax lists (1778–1791) serve as the primary pre-census substitute; town proprietors' records enumerate original landowners.
- **Access:** The 1790 Federal Census is indexed and available on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, inventories, guardianships; county court minute books and civil suit records.
- **Date range:** Vermont Republic organized counties ca. 1778 and probate courts operated from that point. Pre-1777, probate would have been under NY or NH jurisdiction.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (many records have been transferred to the Vermont State Archives); NARA holds some federal-era materials.
- **Digitization:** The FamilySearch Wiki topic pages for Vermont Probate Records returned only generic content during this survey — confirm current digitization at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Probate_Records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Vermont uses the original-colony metes-and-bounds system, not the federal rectangular survey).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Three overlapping systems apply for the pre-statehood period:
  1. New Hampshire grants (1749–1764): NH governor Wentworth issued 129 township grants. The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees and is identified by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) as the earliest systematic resident list for the territory.
  2. New York colonial patents (1764–1777): NY issued competing grants over the same territory.
  3. Vermont Republic grants (1777–1791): Vermont's own government issued grants resolving the conflict.
- **Types:** Township grants, individual deeds, proprietors' records, tax records, bounty land grants for Revolutionary War service.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives (Secretary of State's land records); individual town clerks (deeds recorded at the town level); New Hampshire State Archives (NH grants); New York State Archives (NY colonial patents).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (preceding the period, relevant to early settlers); Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Vermont Republic militia service (1777–1791).
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; Green Mountain Boys and Vermont militia muster rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pension files — available on Fold3, https://www.fold3.com/; free access at https://www.archives.gov/); Vermont State Archives for Vermont Republic militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burial grounds and church cemeteries; many dating to the 1760s–1780s in established towns.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Vermont cemeteries; coverage for pre-1791 burials varies.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are held by town offices. The Vermont Old Cemetery Association has conducted surveys.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont's earliest newspapers date to the early 1780s (e.g., the Vermont Gazette, ca. 1781). Coverage for the pre-statehood period is sparse.
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society; state and university libraries; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized holdings.
- **Content value:** Pre-1791 newspapers occasionally carry land notices, legal notices, and death notices, but coverage is very limited.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Vermont was settled primarily by internal migration from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and other New England colonies — not direct overseas immigration. Port arrival manifests are generally not relevant for this population.
- **Relevant record types:** Track migration through land records, church records, and probate files connecting Vermont settlers to their New England origins. No formal federal naturalization process existed before the Naturalization Act of 1790; NARA holds post-1790 naturalization records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children; when researching a family that did emigrate from overseas (Scots-Irish, etc.), examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Vermont Republic property tax and poll tax lists; town-level assessment records.
- **Date range:** Vermont Republic tax records from ca. 1778; some town-level tax records from the early settlement period.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives; individual town offices.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for the absent federal census before 1791 and for tracking residents not appearing in land records.

The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) notes that 19th-century town histories (1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records. Originals are at the Vermont State Archives or individual town offices.

- **Town histories:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) explicitly identifies 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) as essential tools that often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise difficult to access. Consult the Vermont Historical Society library.
